f.main_result: At 3 months the occlusive cap generated more tissue than the perforated cap (89.9% vs 55.9%, P<0.05) and more mineralized bone (34.0% vs 24.3%).

f.population: 94 patients with a non-carious cervical lesion associated with a single gingival recession (Miller I-IV)
f.intervention: Five approaches chosen by the position of the predetermined maximum root coverage relative to the lesion: CAF; bilaminar; odontoplasty + restoration + CAF; restoration + CAF; restoration alone
outcomes: periodontist VAS evaluation of root coverage, color match and emergence profile
IM-GM distance, probing depth, keratinized tissue height
f.main_result: Patient and periodontist esthetic satisfaction was very high across all lesion types and Miller classes at 1 year, and correlated with color match rather than amount of root coverage.
f.funding_coi: Self-supported by the authors; no conflicts of interest

f.intervention: Proposed classification of facial peri-implant soft tissue dehiscence/deficiency at single implants in the esthetic zone, with a recommended treatment per class
f.main_result: Four classes by crown-margin position relative to the homologous tooth and implant-head bucco-lingual position, each with papilla-height subclasses a/b/c, each linked to a suggested surgical approach.
f.funding_coi: Partly supported by the University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Further studies are needed to explore the classification's validity.

f.population: Bone dehiscence defects on teeth of Beagle dogs
f.intervention: Repositioned flaps with an interpositioned connective tissue graft or a collagen matrix
f.comparison: Repositioned flaps sutured onto instrumented dentin without graft (control)
outcomes: Force needed to detach the flap from the wound bed at 1, 3, 7 and 14 days
f.main_result: Flap resistance to tearing was highest with the connective tissue graft, 6.03 N median at day 7 versus 2.31 N in controls and 3.26 N with collagen matrix.
f.funding_coi: Clinical Research Foundation (CRF) for the Promotion of Oral Health, Brienz; no conflict of interest declared

f.population: Patients with severe chronic periodontitis and an isolated interproximal vertical bony defect in the anterior segments
f.intervention: Simplified papilla preservation at the defect combined with a coronally advanced buccal flap at adjacent teeth and enamel matrix protein
f.main_result: At 1 year, clinical attachment gain was 5.9 mm, probing depth reduction 6.0 mm and radiographic bone gain 5.0 mm, with no significant increase in gingival recession (0.1 mm).
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: Two patients with deep infrabony defects at maxillary central incisors with interdental and buccal gingival recession
f.intervention: Connective tissue graft wall technique with enamel matrix derivative through a palatal incision
f.main_result: At 1 year, interdental clinical attachment gain was 9 and 6 mm in the two cases, with improved papilla position, complete root coverage and radiographic bone fill.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: Implants placed with static computer-assisted guides in clinical studies
f.intervention: Static computer-aided implant surgery with surgical guides
f.main_result: Total mean error was 1.2 mm at the entry point, 1.4 mm at the apical point and 3.5 degrees angular deviation.
f.limitations: Data heterogeneity and non-standardised measuring methods.

f.population: 3D printed surgical guides from five resin/printer combinations
f.intervention: Steam autoclaving with cycle 1 (121 C, 20.5 min) or cycle 2 (134 C, 5.5 min)
f.comparison: Original STL file and pre-autoclaving scans
outcomes: Linear dimensional change along x, y and z axes
f.main_result: Most guides showed minor but significant shrinkage from 3D printing itself and from both autoclaving cycles, varying by resin.
f.funding_coi: Guides supplied free or at reduced cost by Dentalstudio Sankt Augustin GmbH and 3D Agency oHG; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: A single-model approach and no sleeves placed in the resin guide.

f.population: Fifteen participants with single tooth loss, multiple missing teeth or radiographic artifacts
f.intervention: Reducing CBCT field of view from full arch to quadrant or adjacent teeth before superimposition with intraoral scans
f.comparison: Full-arch field of view aligned by an expert
outcomes: Trueness and precision of CBCT-to-intraoral scan alignment at implant apex and shoulder
f.main_result: Largest mean discrepancy 0.10 mm and maximum 1.44 mm occurred with artifacts; precision depended on field-of-view volume but not on operator expertise.
materials_brands: Straumann Bone Level implant 4.1 x 10 mm (virtual)
f.funding_coi: Open Access funding by Projekt DEAL; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Pilot design with a limited number of clinical scenarios and software operators.

f.population: Consecutive partially edentulous patients
f.intervention: Implant placement with the Navident dynamic computer-assisted navigation system
f.comparison: Standard freehand placement
outcomes: Angular and linear deviation of implants
Patient satisfaction, pain and quality of life
f.main_result: Mean angular deviation was 4.02 degrees with dynamic navigation versus 7.97 degrees freehand (p < .001), at the cost of 14 min longer surgery.
f.sample_size: 30 patients with 22 implants in each group
f.funding_coi: Not funded by any grant-giving organization; one author reports grants and fees from Avinent, Inibsa, Dentaid and Nobel Biocare

f.population: Four systematic reviews on all-ceramic implant-supported crowns, computer-assisted manufacturing, computer-assisted implant planning and surgery, and patient-reported outcomes
f.main_result: Limited evidence (49 non-randomized trials) shows excellent 3-year outcomes of all-ceramic implant crowns, and optical impressions improve patient comfort over conventional ones.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared

f.population: 48 cast models mounted in mannequin heads with a tooth gap on each side
f.intervention: Implant placement with a CAD-CAM guide based on virtual planning
f.comparison: Free-hand implant placement
outcomes: Lateral, vertical and angular deviation from planned implant position
f.main_result: Lateral deviation at the implant base was 0.18 and 0.24 mm with guides versus 0.7 and 0.49 mm free-hand; angular deviation did not differ between groups.
f.funding_coi: Swissmeda and Dentsply Sirona supplied funding, software and study material; investigators declare no conflict of interest

f.population: In vitro: ten sterile two-piece implants inoculated with subgingival plaque from periodontitis patients; in vivo: twenty partially edentulous patients, one implant each
f.intervention: Irrigation-brush-irrigation of the internal implant chamber with 10% H2O2, 0.2% chlorhexidine, 70% alcohol or 0.9% NaCl
f.comparison: Repeated irrigation alone (irrigation-irrigation) and NaCl as irrigant
outcomes: relative reduction of total bacterial counts (real-time PCR)
f.main_result: 10% H2O2 gave the highest relative reduction of total bacterial counts (in vitro 87.1% vs CHX 56.9%, alcohol 43.7%, NaCl 42.7%; in vivo 51.4% vs alcohol 30.4%, NaCl 26.3%, CHX 7.1%); adding a brush gave no benefit (p = 0.088)
f.sample_size: In vitro 40 implants (80 samples); in vivo 20 implants in 20 patients (40 samples)
f.funding_coi: Authors' own institutions; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: In vivo difference between irrigants not significant, probably because of the small sample size

f.main_result: No decisive evidence that computer-assisted implant surgery is superior to conventional procedures in safety, outcomes, morbidity or efficiency; accuracy is cumulative-error dependent and lowest with bone-supported guides.
The accuracy, efficacy and complication rate of computer-guided implant treatment remain within acceptable clinical limits, provided each step of the 6-step digital workflow is verified.

Identifying the etiology (lip, crown, altered passive eruption, vertical maxillary excess) is the key step because it dictates the treatment: crown lengthening, lip repositioning, Botox or orthognathic surgery.
f.funding_coi: No disclosures

f.main_result: Periodontists can treat gummy smile and short tooth syndrome with a biological approach (re-exposing the CEJ) or a restorative approach; misdiagnosing altered eruption risks esthetic and periodontal failure.
f.funding_coi: No disclosures

f.main_result: The authors propose an adult classification of gummy smile and short tooth syndrome causes, used with an outside-in diagnostic process, to predict outcomes and determine treatment.
f.funding_coi: No disclosures

f.population: Patients with gummy smile (authors' clinical experience)
f.intervention: Hyaluronic acid filler injections (RD Dynamic Restructuring) guided by the Mercado-Rosso classification
f.main_result: Treatment maintains 70-80% of its effectiveness after 10 months, with retreatment suggested at 10 and 18 months.
f.funding_coi: Medical writing and publication fees funded by Teoxane SL; Dr Mercado received a Teoxane grant
f.limitations: A first step: the classification should be validated and treatment approaches evaluated in a cohort of patients.

f.main_result: Gummy smile has soft-tissue to hard-tissue origins, so the clinician must distinguish them to choose the strategy that meets patient expectations.
f.funding_coi: Editorial-board relationships of some authors with the journal

f.population: Partially edentulous patients receiving at least one posterior implant
f.intervention: Permanent abutment placed at implant placement (no disconnection)
f.comparison: Healing abutment with two disconnection/reconnection cycles before definitive prosthesis
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss at 6 months was 0.13 mm (test) vs 0.28 mm (control), not significantly different; mucosal dimensions did not differ.
f.funding_coi: Sponsored by Straumann USA; no conflicts of interest reported

f.population: 20 patients with a single missing tooth in the anterior maxilla (FDI 13-23)
f.intervention: Fixed implant-supported provisional crown with soft tissue conditioning (dynamic compression technique) for 6 months before the final crown
f.comparison: Final crown inserted directly without a provisional phase
f.main_result: Combined modPES+WES was 15.6 (group 1, with provisional) vs 12.2 (group 2); modPES differed significantly (P=.018), WES did not; bone loss was similar.
materials_brands: Straumann Bone Level Implant RC SLActive
f.funding_coi: Financial support from Straumann Group; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Small sample size

f.population: 22 periodontally healthy patients with a single failing tooth in the aesthetic zone (15-25), thick gingival biotype, intact buccal bone wall
f.intervention: Flapless single immediate implant (NobelActive) with bovine bone particles in the buccal gap and immediate non-functional screw-retained provisional crown; CTG when early complications appeared
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss was 0.12 mm at 1 year and 0.19 mm at 5 years, but mid-facial recession rose from 0.28 to 0.53 mm and 8 of 17 implants showed aesthetic complications.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; Nobel Biocare provided free materials; authors declare collaboration agreements with implant companies

f.population: Partially edentulous patients treated with one to three dental implants (at least 8.5 mm long, 4.0 mm wide, torque of at least 35 Ncm)
f.intervention: Definitive screw-retained metal-ceramic partial fixed prosthesis in occlusion within 1 week of implant placement
f.comparison: Immediate non-occluding provisional acrylic prosthesis within 24 h, replaced by definitive prosthesis after 4 months
outcomes: chair time and number of visits
f.main_result: No significant difference in 3-year marginal bone loss (1.13 mm occlusal vs 1.03 mm non-occluding; P = 0.779); the immediate definitive prosthesis needed significantly less chair time and fewer visits
materials_brands: Zimmer-Biomet implants (with bone substitutes and resorbable membranes)
f.funding_coi: Zimmer-Biomet, the implant manufacturer, supported the trial; data belonged to the authors
f.limitations: Small sample size (25 patients per group originally included); one centre did not deliver 1- and 3-year data

f.population: 35 consecutive patients (mean age 36.8 years) with a failing maxillary anterior tooth, 35 single implants
f.intervention: Immediate placement and provisionalization of single implants in the esthetic zone
f.comparison: Thick (14 sites) vs thin (21 sites) gingival biotype
f.main_result: All 35 implants remained in function (100% success); mean facial gingival level change was -1.13 mm at latest follow-up vs -0.55 mm at 1 year, and thin biotype lost more (-1.50 vs -0.56 mm)
materials_brands: Replace threaded hydroxyapatite-coated tapered implant (Nobel Biocare)
f.funding_coi: Nobel Biocare partially funded the research

f.population: Two patients; case 1 was a 53-year-old woman with a root rest of the maxillary right premolar
f.intervention: Chairside gingival recontouring with a provisional implant restoration whose base was built up with light-curing composite
outcomes: gingival contour and emergence profile after provisional restoration
f.main_result: Four to six weeks after the provisional restoration the gingiva reformed in harmony with the adjacent dentition
f.follow_up: 4 to 6 weeks with the provisional restoration before the final impression
f.funding_coi: Research funds from Chosun University Dental Hospital; no conflict of interest reported

f.population: 41 patients receiving 127 immediately loaded implants (76 maxillary, 51 mandibular)
f.intervention: Immediate occlusal loading of Brånemark implants, restored the same day (71%) or within 11 days, in full contact in centric occlusion
outcomes: implant loss by region, parafunction and GBR
f.main_result: Cumulative implant success rate 82.7% at 1 year (22 of 127 implants lost); 66% success in the posterior maxilla vs 91% elsewhere; bruxers lost 41% vs 12%
f.limitations: Larger controlled studies with bigger samples are needed

f.population: Completely edentulous patients treated with full-arch immediate prostheses on Morse taper hydrophilic implants
f.intervention: Full-arch immediate prosthesis on 4 hydrophilic implants with bicortical anchorage
f.comparison: Full-arch immediate prosthesis on 5 or 6 implants without bicortical anchorage
f.main_result: Overall implant survival 99.7% (391 of 392) and prosthesis survival 100%, no group differences; bicortical implants had significantly higher primary stability (P<0.001)
f.funding_coi: All authors report personal fees from Neodent; one author holds a Neodent patent

f.population: Edentulous patients with complete dentures receiving two interforaminal implants for a mandibular bar-retained overdenture
f.intervention: Immediate loading of two primarily splinted implants (one platform-switched, one platform-matching abutment)
f.comparison: Delayed loading 3 months after placement
f.main_result: Peri-implant bone loss was significantly smaller with immediate loading when baseline was implant placement (p = .017) but not when baseline was loading (p = .084); overall mean bone change -0.96 mm; platform switching equivalent
f.funding_coi: Materials provided by Schilli Implantology Circle and C+M; authors declare no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Small sample size and short follow-up of 3 years

f.main_result: Immediate loading is generally sound but should not be applied indiscriminately, because of unfavorable stress distribution, for maxillary anterior single implants, single molar implants, unsplinted overdenture implants and maxillary anterior partial fixed prostheses

f.population: Patients needing a single-tooth implant restoration, mostly posterior sites
f.intervention: One-piece zirconia implant with immediate temporization for single-tooth replacement
outcomes: probing depth, attachment level, bleeding and plaque indices
f.main_result: Six posterior implants were lost (3-year cumulative survival 90.8%); mean marginal bone loss 1.45 mm, with 35% of implants losing at least 2 mm
materials_brands: One-piece y-TZP zirconia implant with ZiUnite surface (Nobel Biocare)
f.funding_coi: Grant and implants from Nobel Biocare; two authors were Nobel Biocare lecturers

f.intervention: Immediate loading of dental implants and the role of primary stability
f.main_result: Good primary stability is the core issue for immediate loading; it depends on bone density and quality, implant shape, design, surface and surgical technique.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest and no external funding
f.limitations: Further research needed in poor bone, multiple implants and augmentation situations.

f.population: 9 patients with sites rendered edentulous by an impacted maxillary canine, plus 1 patient with a failing mandibular bridge
f.intervention: Implants placed through impacted canines, encroaching on the root or crown, without extracting the impacted tooth
f.main_result: All implants were restored and none failed during 1 to 8 years of follow-up; one soft tissue infection after 2 weeks was treated successfully
f.funding_coi: Two authors received an open-sponsoring grant from Nobel Biocare France
f.limitations: More implants and longer follow-up are needed before advocating the protocol

f.population: 30 patients with original single-implant crowns in the anterior maxilla in function for 14 to 20 years
f.intervention: 3-D measurement of movement of teeth adjacent to anterior maxillary single-implant crowns on scanned study casts
f.main_result: Adjacent teeth moved 0 to 2.5 mm; incisal movement >1 mm in 30% of patients, significantly associated with LAFH of 70 mm or more; CDA rating satisfactory in 87% of patients
f.funding_coi: Funded by Folktandvarden Stockholms lan AB and foundations; Nobel Biocare Services AG grants to one author
f.limitations: Small number of patients, facial-type classification, head posture uncertainty, model matching and ongoing attrition of the adjacent tooth

f.population: Partially edentulous patients with implant restorations followed more than 20 years
f.intervention: Observation of changes in position of teeth relative to static implant restorations as adult craniofacial growth continues
f.main_result: Continued adult craniofacial growth can change occlusion, open interproximal contacts and alter anterior esthetics (incisal edge, gingival margin, facial contour) around implant restorations
f.limitations: Continued adult growth causing problems is not common but is not predictable

f.population: 120 teeth in 58 patients aged 18 to 50 with subgingival crown preparations
f.intervention: Retraction cords (racemic epinephrine, aluminum sulfate) placed dry, water-saturated or Hemodent-saturated for 10 minutes
f.comparison: Nonmedicated cord; dry and water-saturated placement
f.main_result: Hemodent-saturated cords controlled bleeding in 44 of 60 tests versus 2 of 60 for dry or water-saturated cords; epinephrine and aluminum sulfate cords did not differ and both beat nonmedicated cord

f.intervention: Systematic approach to gingival deflection and hemorrhage control with contemporary materials, chosen by clinical situation
f.main_result: Consistent and successful gingival deflection is achieved by controlling hemorrhage first, then choosing technique by clinical situation

f.population: Alginate impression material cubes (n = 6 per group) infected by sucking by three volunteers
f.intervention: Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.2% or sodium peroxysulphate 1% used as mixing liquid and post-setting soak solution for alginate
f.comparison: Tap water as mixing liquid
f.main_result: Chlorhexidine gluconate and sodium peroxysulphate mixed into alginate and used as a 45-min soak gave no bacterial growth, whereas water-mixed or non-soaked groups did

f.intervention: Roll of composite resin, VPS tray adhesive and occlusal registration material applied around an open-tray impression coping

f.population: 59 studies (3 clinical, the rest in vitro) on multi-unit implant impression accuracy
f.intervention: Multi-unit implant impression materials, splinting, pickup vs transfer technique and implant angulation
f.main_result: PVS and PE are the preferred materials; pickup is marginally better than transfer especially with more implants; splinting evidence inconclusive; 20 to 25 degree angulation reduces accuracy
f.limitations: Nearly 95% of included studies were in vitro

f.main_result: Accurate impression is the main requisite of an implant-supported prosthesis; impression technique is key to success

f.intervention: Open- or closed-tray impression with Straumann SP and BLT impression components, plus bite registration and color assessment
materials_brands: Straumann Impression Post and Impression Cap (SP and BLT)

f.population: Partially and completely edentulous patients (4 clinical and 72 in vitro studies)
f.intervention: Splinted vs nonsplinted, open-tray vs closed-tray and digital vs conventional implant impression techniques
outcomes: effect of splinting, tray type, impression material, angulation and connection type
f.main_result: The splinted technique was more accurate for partially and completely edentulous patients; open-tray was more accurate than closed-tray for completely edentulous patients only; material had no effect.
f.funding_coi: Authors report no financial interest in the companies whose materials are included
f.limitations: Insufficient data on digital impressions and on the effect of connection type

f.population: 6 internal-connection implants at 0, 15 and 25 degrees angulation mounted in an experimental device
f.intervention: Direct acrylic-resin splinted impression technique with polyether
f.comparison: Direct nonsplinted and indirect snap-fit techniques
outcomes: 3D positional deviation of impression copings measured with a coordinate measuring machine
f.main_result: At 25 degrees the splinted technique was most accurate (0.39 mm) and snap-fit least accurate (0.85 mm); no difference between splinted and nonsplinted at 0 or 15 degrees.
f.limitations: in vitro nature of the experiment

f.population: 41 in vitro studies on implant impression accuracy
f.intervention: Implant impression techniques (splint, pick-up, transfer) and clinical factors
f.main_result: More studies favoured the splint technique (7 splint, 3 nonsplint, 7 no difference); polyether and VPS did not differ in 10 of 11 studies.

f.population: Maxillary metal reference model with two implants
f.intervention: One-step and two-step putty/wash PVS with closed custom and stock trays
f.comparison: Regular viscosity PVS with closed custom trays
outcomes: implant replica linear and angular displacement
f.main_result: Putty/wash PVS was more accurate than regular viscosity PVS (more linear displacement with regular body, P<.001); viscosity did not affect surface detail reproduction.
f.sample_size: 50 impressions (40 putty/wash PVS, 10 regular viscosity PVS) on one reference model
f.funding_coi: Funded by a grant from Tehran University of Medical Sciences

f.population: Reference master model with 4 implants at 0, 5 and 10 degrees simulating an all-on-4 prosthesis
f.intervention: Recently introduced PVS impression materials (Hydrorise, Honigum), with and without splinting
f.comparison: Well-established polyether materials
outcomes: accuracy and precision as linear 3D error
f.main_result: Hydrorise PVS (about 29-31 µm) was significantly more accurate than polyether (about 44 µm; P<.001); viscosity did not affect accuracy; splinting improved accuracy only in HIH+L.

f.population: Partially or completely edentulous patients in clinical studies with at least 10 patients
f.intervention: Digital implant impressions with intraoral scanners and scanbodies
f.comparison: Conventional implant impressions / reference dataset
f.main_result: Eight clinical studies reported linear deviations from 40 ± 20 µm to 360 ± 46 µm, with the oldest (2014) study at 1000 ± 650 µm; recent scanners judged clinically acceptable.
f.funding_coi: No funding; no conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: The number of clinical studies is low and study designs differ considerably

f.main_result: Astringent metal-salt agents are preferred over epinephrine-based agents given similar therapeutic effect and fewer systemic adverse effects.

f.population: 7 definitive casts, each with 3 implants at various angulations
f.intervention: Closed tray and open tray impression techniques
outcomes: implant angulation error of definitive casts
f.main_result: Impression technique had no significant main effect (P=.22); accurate casts can be made with open or closed tray for 3 implants angled up to 15 degrees.
materials_brands: GC Fujirock EP type IV dental stone

f.main_result: Gingival retraction methods are classified as mechanical, chemo-mechanical, cordless and surgical, and a combination may be needed.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no financial interests

f.intervention: Use of alginate impression material and methods of disinfecting alginate impressions
f.main_result: Impression disinfection is needed to prevent cross-contamination, but prolonged immersion in disinfectant causes liquid absorption, swelling and dimensional change of alginate impressions

f.population: 79 included studies, 77 experimental, one RCT and one retrospective; 75 in vitro and four in vivo
f.intervention: Conventional and digital implant impressions
f.comparison: Conventional versus digital implant impressions
outcomes: three-dimensional deviations between impression posts and scan bodies
f.main_result: Accuracy data for digital and conventional implant impressions are of low evidence level with high heterogeneity and insufficient in vivo data for clinical recommendations
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: Low evidence level and insufficient in vivo data

f.population: Acrylic resin cast with five internal connection implants
f.intervention: Repeated cleaning, steam sterilization and reuse of impression copings (10 cycles) with direct and indirect techniques
f.comparison: Resin cast measurements (control)
outcomes: positional accuracy of implant replica heads in x, y and z
f.main_result: No significant differences in x, z, angular or radial displacement over 10 reuses; only the y-axis in the open tray technique changed (P = .02)
f.sample_size: 40 polyether impressions with four sets of five impression copings
f.funding_coi: Funded by Dental Research Center of Tehran University of Medical Sciences; no conflicts of interest

f.population: Partially dentate mandibular acrylic resin master model with two internal connection implants
f.intervention: Reuse of impression copings for 10 polyether impressions and of scanbodies for 10 digital scans
f.comparison: Master model measurements
outcomes: discrepancy in x, y, z axes
f.main_result: Reuse up to 10 times did not consistently affect accuracy; no significant differences for most cycles, with isolated differences in casts 2, 4, 6, 8 and scan 2
f.sample_size: 10 casts and 10 digital scans, one implant pair
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: Two reference acrylic resin models with five internal connection implants each
f.intervention: Square and conical impression copings of two implant systems with open-tray and close-tray techniques
f.comparison: Reference resin models (control)
outcomes: positional accuracy of implant replica heads
f.main_result: Less inaccuracy with the less retentive Replace Select copings than Implantium (p < .001); no significant difference between direct and indirect techniques
f.funding_coi: Funded by a grant from Tehran University of Medical Sciences; no financial interest declared

f.population: 24 replicas of a metal matrix with two implants at 90 and 65 degrees
f.intervention: Four pick-up impression techniques with square copings, unsplinted or splinted with acrylic resin or a prefabricated bar
f.comparison: Metal matrix image (control)
outcomes: difference in implant angulation from control
f.main_result: All groups differed from control; angular difference was highest with unsplinted T1 (1.019 degrees) and lowest with the prefabricated bar T4 (0.325 degrees)

f.intervention: One-step/double-mix impression with polyvinyl siloxane and double cord gingival displacement
f.main_result: The quality of final impressions plays a major role in the success of the prosthetic rehabilitation

f.population: Cultured V-79 fibroblasts
f.intervention: Four chemical retraction agents (25% and 10% aluminium chloride, 25% aluminium sulphate, tetrahydrozoline) at several concentrations and exposure times
f.comparison: Untreated control cultures
f.main_result: 25% aluminium chloride was the most cytotoxic (damaged all cells within 1 min, t50 0.5 min) and tetrahydrozoline the least (t50 7 min).
f.sample_size: 192 samples in the dye exclusion test

f.intervention: Segmental impression technique using sectional trays to capture multiple preparations in stages
f.limitations: Fitting stock sectional trays is difficult in patients with limited mouth opening.

f.population: Metal master cast with three internal-connection implant analogs, parallel and with 10 degrees mesial angulation
f.intervention: Four impression coping types: pick-up or transfer, long or short
f.comparison: Pick-up versus transfer coping, long versus short, parallel versus angulated
outcomes: difference in analog distance between master cast and experimental cast (error rate)
f.main_result: Pick-up type copings gave a significantly lower error rate than transfer type; coping length and 10 degree angulation made no significant difference.

f.population: Three definitive casts each with 3 linearly positioned implant analogs at 0, 30 and 40 degrees angulation
f.intervention: Abutment-framework open tray impression technique
f.comparison: Closed tray and resin-splinted open tray techniques
outcomes: vertical gap between reference frameworks and analogs
f.main_result: Open tray techniques gave significantly smaller vertical gaps than closed tray, and the A-F technique was superior and unaffected by implant angulation.
f.sample_size: 10 impressions per technique on each of 3 definitive casts

f.population: Published studies on the accuracy of implant impressions
f.intervention: Different implant impression materials and techniques
f.main_result: More studies found splinted impressions more accurate than non-splinted; with 3 or fewer implants pick-up and transfer mostly did not differ, with 4 or more pick-up was more accurate; polyether and VPS were recommended.

f.population: Probands with induced mild gingivitis, palatal half of upper premolars
f.intervention: 3M Astringent Retraction Paste
f.comparison: Double-cord technique with aluminum chloride
outcomes: marginal gingiva height change over 12 months
f.main_result: Displacement was comparable in the horizontal direction and only somewhat better for the cord technique vertically.
f.funding_coi: Supported in part by 3M Oral Care; authors declare no conflict of interest

f.population: 20 patients receiving implant-supported single crowns
f.intervention: Intraoral scanning (iTero) implant impression
f.comparison: Conventional polyether impression
f.main_result: Patients rated convenience higher with intraoral scanning (78.6) than conventional impressions (53.6), and scanning was faster (14.8 vs 17.9 min).

f.population: Three master models simulating partially edentulous mandible with 2 implants, parallel or angulated
f.intervention: Splinted direct and indirect impression techniques with polyether, VPS and vinyl polyether silicone
f.comparison: Technique, material and implant angulation compared against each other
f.main_result: For 10 and 20 degree angulated implants, VPS with the splinted direct technique was most accurate and vinyl polyether silicone with the indirect technique least accurate.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; no conflicts of interest declared

f.population: Stone master model with 5 parallel implant analogs at different subgingival depths (0, 2, 4 mm)
f.intervention: Open-tray impressions with medium-body polyether or putty plus light-body VPS; implant D at 4 mm with an extended impression coping
f.comparison: Implants at 0, 2 and 4 mm depth, polyether versus VPS, standard versus extended coping at 4 mm
f.main_result: Depth did not affect VPS accuracy, but 4-mm-deep implants impressed with polyether showed greater horizontal distortion than 0-mm implants (P=.02); a 4-mm coping extension eliminated the difference.
f.limitations: The measured vertical and horizontal distortions did not completely describe the 3-D distortion, and axial rotation could not be detected.

f.population: Master casts with two implant replicas angulated 10° from each other for each of two connection systems (external butt joint; internal tapered conical)
f.intervention: Assembly of four impression coping types, resin splinted abutments and final prosthesis with 30 Ncm tightening, then 250 N cyclic loading for 1,000,000 cycles
f.comparison: External butt joint versus internal tapered conical connection
f.main_result: The internal tapered conical connection showed more axial displacement than the external connection in impression copings, resin splinted abutments and final prosthesis (P = 0.0001), and more after 250 N cyclic loading.
f.funding_coi: Shinhung MST Co. provided the implant components
f.limitations: Conclusions apply only within the limitation of the implant types tested (Sola/Luna, Shinhung).

f.population: Thirty gypsum and 30 digitally milled models made from a single-implant maxillary reference model
f.intervention: Digital impression (iTero with scannable abutment) leading to milled models
f.comparison: Gypsum models from closed-tray conventional VPS impression
f.main_result: Milled models from digital impressions had comparable accuracy to gypsum models; fossae (P<0.001) and vertical implant displacement (P=0.020) differed significantly.
materials_brands: Straumann Bone Level implant and Scanbody
f.funding_coi: Funded by the ITI Foundation research grant; no conflict of interest declared

f.population: 32 in vitro studies on implant impression accuracy published 2009 to 2013
f.intervention: Open versus closed, splinted versus non-splinted impression techniques, materials, coping designs and optical devices
f.main_result: The most accurate results came from an optical intraoral system with powder, or the open technique with splinted squared transfer copings and polyether.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Only 2009 to 2013 publications, and all included studies were in vitro.

f.population: 102 impressions of stainless steel dies similar to ADA specification 19
f.intervention: Impressions with two hydrophilic VPS materials (Reprosil, Aquasil Monophase) under dry, moist and wet conditions
f.comparison: Dry versus moist versus wet conditions; Aquasil versus Reprosil
f.main_result: Moisture did not significantly change dimensional accuracy (change 0.005% or less) but only dry conditions gave clinically acceptable surface detail; only 47% Aquasil and 11% Reprosil impressions were satisfactory when wet.
f.funding_coi: Funded in part by the Rinehart Foundation
The authors have nothing to disclose

f.population: Stainless-steel master model of a mandible with 5 implant analogs; 16 stone casts
f.intervention: 4 implant impression techniques (tapered unsplinted, squared unsplinted, squared splinted with acrylic, squared with lateral extension)
f.comparison: the 4 techniques compared against each other and the master model
outcomes: dimensional accuracy of implant positions on casts (Deviation Index)
f.main_result: Maximum distortion difference between techniques was only 0.31% (P=.022), clinically negligible.
f.sample_size: 4 casts per technique, 5 implants per cast

f.population: Six PVS impression materials in two consistencies, 12 groups
f.intervention: Mixing with the MIXPAC T-Mixer tip
f.comparison: Conventional helical mixing tip
f.main_result: The T-Mixer tip reduced material waste (P<.001) by about 24 to 29% and in general gave similar dimensional stability and detail reproduction.
materials_brands: Virtual Monophase and Light Body (Ivoclar Vivadent)
f.funding_coi: No specific grant funding

f.population: Eight Beagle dogs with clinically healthy gingiva
f.intervention: 10 minutes of exposure to cords impregnated with four chemical retraction agents (Racestyptine, Gingiva Liquid, Rastringent, Visine)
f.comparison: Untreated control gingiva
outcomes: area of inflammatory connective tissue infiltration under sulcular and junctional epithelium
f.main_result: Racestyptine (25% aluminum chloride) caused the largest and most persistent inflammation, while Visine (tetrahydrozoline) caused the least and could be recommended.

f.population: Two master models with four implants each, parallel or with 5° convergence/divergence, 80 impressions
f.intervention: Open-tray pick-up impressions with polyether or addition silicon and standard or shortened coping connection
f.comparison: Parallel versus nonparallel implants, polyether versus addition silicon, standard versus shortened coping
outcomes: four reference distances between impression copings on casts
f.main_result: Impressions of angulated implants were significantly less accurate than parallel ones (p < 0.0001); addition silicon was better for nonparallel implants and polyether with standard copings for parallel implants.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Further clinical investigations are needed to confirm these in vitro results.

f.population: Master models with implant analogs, 10 specimens per group in six groups
f.intervention: Open-tray impressions with custom, plastic-metal combination or polycarbonate stock trays, with splinted or non-splinted pick-up copings
f.comparison: Splinted versus non-splinted copings; three tray types
f.main_result: Tray type made no significant difference, but splinted copings gave smaller vertical discrepancy than non-splinted in all three trays (p<0.05); e.g. custom tray 24.68 vs 50.09 um.

f.population: Polymeric resin model of a maxillary arch with one standard implant (3.75 x 10 mm) at the right second premolar site
f.intervention: Gold machined UCLA abutments used as impression copings
f.comparison: Square impression copings roughened by sandblasting and coated with polyether adhesive
outcomes: Rotational position change of the implant hexagon in the master casts (angles MIA and PIA)
f.main_result: Rotational variation was much smaller with UCLA abutment copings (SD 4.36 and 5.56 min) than with roughened square copings (SD 36.34 and 34.39 min for MIA and PIA).

f.population: Ten edentulous jaws (seven maxillae, three mandibles), four implants each
f.intervention: Splinted pick-up impression technique
f.comparison: Transfer impression technique
outcomes: 3D discrepancy of scan body positions on digitized casts
Clinical fit of bar suprastructures (Sheffield test)
f.main_result: Mean discrepancy of scan bodies 2, 3 and 4 was 192, 282 and 366 µm, rising with span length; fit on the splinted pick-up cast was good in 10 of 10 cases versus acceptable or poor on the transfer cast.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared; funding not stated

f.population: Thirty consecutive patients with Straumann tissue level implants in the non-aesthetic zone
f.intervention: Intraoral scan (iTero) of the implants
f.comparison: Analogue impression with polyether material
f.main_result: Patients significantly preferred the intraoral scan, mainly for taste and preparatory activities, but perceived its duration more negatively; the analogue impression took less time overall.
f.funding_coi: Part of a larger project subsidized by ITI, Basel; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Small cohort of patients

f.population: Three adult patients aged 38 to 60 years at implant placement
f.intervention: Implant placement with long-term follow-up of implant position
f.main_result: Continued craniofacial growth can lead to infraocclusion of the implant-supported crown and to diastema, negatively affecting esthetics and chewing.
f.limitations: Lack of standardization of the evidence and a limited number of cases

f.main_result: Planning parameters: at least 8 mm crown height space for cement-retained restorations, 15 mm as the critical distance for full-arch (PFM below, hybrid above), 1.5 mm from adjacent teeth and 3 mm between implants.
f.funding_coi: CE lesson underwritten by an unnamed sponsor

f.population: 42-year-old man with skeletal class III malocclusion, worn maxillary teeth and missing mandibular molars
f.intervention: Orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, immediate implants, and full mouth rehabilitation
f.main_result: After orthodontics, two-jaw surgery, 8 immediate implants and full mouth restorations, no tooth movement was seen over the 2-year follow-up.

f.intervention: Increasing occlusal vertical dimension
f.main_result: Increase in OVD should follow restorative and esthetic needs, be minimal, and above 5 mm is rarely indicated; it is a safe procedure with self-limiting symptoms.

f.intervention: Increase of the vertical dimension of occlusion
f.main_result: Permanent VDO increase of up to 5 mm is safe and predictable, symptoms are self-limiting within about 2 weeks, and fixed restorations are preferable to removable splints.
f.follow_up: From 5 days to more than 2 years across included studies
f.limitations: Significant heterogeneity in study design and few available studies

f.main_result: The vertical dimension can often be increased if reconstruction starts with condyles in centric relation and stays within the patient's neuromuscular adaptation, tested first with reversible modalities.

f.population: endodontically treated posterior teeth
f.intervention: direct composite resin restorations
f.comparison: indirect restorations (mostly complete crowns)
f.main_result: For the short term (2.5 to 3 years), low-quality evidence suggests no difference in tooth survival or restoration quality between direct composite resin and indirect restorations.
f.funding_coi: Dutch society for dental science research grant
f.limitations: Overall risk of bias was serious to critical for observational studies because of confounding by restorative indication.

f.population: plastic dentoform teeth (mandibular left first molar) with onlay preparations
f.intervention: CAD-CAM nanoceramic resin onlays on a conventional (1.2-mm modified shoulder) or modified (flat cuspal reduction) preparation, from direct or indirect digital impressions
f.comparison: direct vs indirect digital impression; conventional vs modified preparation
f.main_result: Conventional preparation had smaller mean marginal discrepancy (59 um) than modified preparation (69 um, P<.001); direct 66 um vs indirect 62 um (P=.027).

f.population: 32-year-old man with severe dental erosion
f.intervention: ultrathin CAD-CAM composite resin occlusal veneers on posterior teeth and bilaminar anterior veneers (palatal composite, labial ceramic)
f.main_result: Restorative treatment was completed within 1 month with a noticeable improvement in oral health and appearance.
f.funding_coi: FAPERJ grant; support from Sirona Brazil, Kappler, Ivoclar Vivadent, 3M ESPE, AdDent, Bisco, Dental Design
f.limitations: Clinical performance of ultrathin occlusal veneers still needs research.

f.population: 7 in vitro studies of implant-level impressions; clinical studies of single metal- or zirconia-based abutments/reconstructions
f.intervention: internal connection abutments/reconstructions
f.comparison: external connection abutments/reconstructions
f.main_result: No study directly compared internal and external connections for impression accuracy; screw loosening was the most frequent mechanical complication of metal abutments/reconstructions in both designs.
f.sample_size: 7 in vitro studies; 14 clinical studies on metal and 5 on zirconia abutments/reconstructions
f.follow_up: inclusion required mean follow-up of at least 3 years (metal) or 1 year (zirconia)
f.funding_coi: IS advisor for VITA; department collaborations with 3M ESPE, Straumann, Astra, Ivoclar, DeguDent, Sirona
f.limitations: In vitro studies used different protocols so data could not be compared.

f.population: implant sites in healed ridges (buccal bone wall thickness) and single implant sites with soft tissue augmentation
f.intervention: simultaneous bone augmentation and soft tissue augmentation (connective tissue grafts)
f.main_result: Healed sites with buccal bone wall under 1.5 mm had more vertical bone loss and less favorable outcomes; soft tissue augmentation gave stable outcomes from 1 to 5 years.
f.sample_size: two systematic reviews; first included 16 studies (12 clinical, 4 preclinical)

f.population: partially edentulous patients with missing single or multiple teeth undergoing dental implant therapy
f.intervention: additive manufacturing of implant restorations
f.comparison: subtractive manufacturing of implant restorations
f.main_result: Titanium base abutments showed no significant 1-year survival difference vs customized abutments; monolithic zirconia posterior multi-unit prostheses are recommended.
f.sample_size: 67 publications critically reviewed in three systematic reviews
f.funding_coi: International Team for Implantology (ITI)
f.limitations: Clinical performance of additive restorations and long-term RCT data remain lacking.

f.population: Patients with a single implant as the distal element in the posterior mandible, placed either in keratinized mucosa (n=63) or alveolar mucosa (n=35)
f.intervention: SLA implants placed within keratinized mucosa versus alveolar mucosa, with free gingival graft added in 11 alveolar-mucosa cases
f.comparison: Implants placed in alveolar mucosa without keratinized mucosa
outcomes: need for antibiotic or surgical therapy
f.main_result: Over 10 years antibiotic/surgical therapy was needed in 12.7% of KT versus 51.4% of AM patients (P<0.001), and 42.9% of AM patients reported discomfort during oral hygiene versus none of KT patients.
f.sample_size: 128 patients enrolled (one implant each), 98 analysed at 10 years

f.population: Eleven human cross-sectional or longitudinal studies of dental implants with differing widths of keratinized mucosa
f.intervention: Width of keratinized mucosa around dental implants
f.comparison: Implants lacking adequate keratinized mucosa
f.main_result: Wide KM was associated with lower plaque index, gingival index, mucosal recession (WMD -0.60 mm) and attachment loss (WMD -0.35 mm); bleeding, probing depth and bone loss did not differ significantly.
f.funding_coi: Authors report no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Limited number of studies (n=11), heterogeneity, publication bias, and English-only articles

f.population: 15 edentulous patients with four implant-retained mandibular overdenture implants each (36 implants evaluated)
f.intervention: Implants with at least 2 mm of keratinized mucosa on the buccal surface
f.comparison: Implants with no keratinized mucosa on the buccal surface
outcomes: peri-implant crevicular fluid IL-1 beta and TNF-alpha
f.main_result: After 12 months implants with KM had lower TNF-a levels and lower plaque and gingival index values than implants without KM (P<0.05).
f.sample_size: 36 implants (19 with KM, 17 without) in 15 patients
f.funding_coi: Supported by Gazi University Scientific Project and Research Support Foundation

f.population: 19 publications (17 human and 2 animal studies) on implants with varying keratinized mucosa
f.intervention: Presence or width of keratinized mucosa around implants
f.main_result: Evidence that keratinized mucosa is needed around implants to maintain health and tissue stability is limited; an inadequate width (<2 mm) was linked to higher plaque scores in 5 of 12 studies.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no personal conflict of interest
f.limitations: Marked heterogeneity in study design and data precluded statistical analysis

f.intervention: Soft tissue grafting to increase attached mucosa at dental implants
f.main_result: Soft tissue grafting may be important to prevent peri-implant tissue breakdown and should be considered when implants are placed; a decision tree guides technique selection.

f.intervention: Direct-indirect composite veneer technique with extra-oral heat tempering

f.population: Disks of light-cured resin cement and flowable composite, bare or luted to 1 mm feldspathic porcelain discs
f.intervention: Accelerated artificial aging (ASTM G154-06, 300 h) of the luting agents with and without porcelain cover
f.comparison: Light-cured resin cement vs flowable composite, each bare or covered by 1 mm porcelain
f.main_result: Flowable composite changed most (delta E 18.16) vs resin cement (5.41); porcelain-covered groups changed little (1.65 and 1.21)
f.follow_up: 300 hours of accelerated aging (about 1 year of clinical function)

f.population: Porcelain veneers laid on a fireproof abutment modelled on a maxillary central incisor
f.intervention: Three preparation designs (feather, bevel, incisal overlap with palatal chamfer) loaded at 45 degrees until first fracture
f.comparison: The three preparation designs compared with each other
f.main_result: Fracture localisation depended significantly on preparation design (chi-square 11.22, p=0.024); incisal fractures dominated feather (66.7%) and palatal chamfer (72.4%), combined fractures dominated bevel (53.6%)
f.sample_size: 90 veneers, 30 per design (the results table lists 63)
f.funding_coi: No financial support; no competing interests

f.population: 80 healthy human molars with flattened occlusal surfaces
f.intervention: Ceramic laminate veneers (0.5 and 1.0 mm) bonded with light-cured, conventional dual or self-adhesive dual cement, then 580 h accelerated artificial aging
f.comparison: Unrestored teeth and cement-only samples as controls
f.main_result: Greatest color change with 0.5 mm veneers and light-cured cement, lowest with 1.0 mm veneers and conventional dual cement; self-adhesive cement was independent of thickness
f.sample_size: 80 molars (60 veneered, n=10 per thickness-cement group) plus control teeth and 30 cement samples
f.funding_coi: FAPESP grant
f.limitations: Single ceramic shade, single cement color and a single aging method

f.population: 40 included studies on incisal preparation designs for ceramic veneers (anecdotal reports, surveys, in vivo and in vitro studies)
f.intervention: Incisal preparation designs: window, feathered edge, palatal chamfer, butt joint
f.comparison: Comparison among incisal preparation designs
f.main_result: In vitro studies showed palatal chamfer raises ceramic fracture risk while butt joint least affects tooth strength; incisal ceramic is the commonest fracture site
f.sample_size: 40 studies (13 anecdotal, 3 surveys, 8 in vivo, 16 in vitro)
f.limitations: Lack of standardization of modeling structures and finite element analysis type

f.population: Published studies on bonded porcelain laminate veneers meeting Cochrane trial criteria
f.intervention: Veneer preparation extending past the dentin–enamel junction
f.comparison: Veneers bonded to dentin vs etched enamel
f.main_result: Strong evidence that veneers bonded to dentin carry greater failure risk than those bonded to etched enamel

f.population: 40 porcelain laminate veneers on 3D-printed dies of a scanned typodont maxillary central incisor preparation
f.intervention: Veneers made by pressing (VITA PM9) or CAD-CAM milling (VITA Blocs Mark II) and cemented with RelyX Veneer or Variolink-N
f.comparison: Press vs CAD-CAM milling, and RelyX Veneer vs Variolink-N
f.main_result: Press veneers cemented with RelyX Veneer had the smallest cervical marginal and internal gaps; gaps were larger incisally than cervically and all within clinically acceptable values
f.sample_size: 40 veneers (20 pressed, 20 milled; 10 per cement within each)
f.funding_coi: Grant from Jordan University of Science and Technology

f.population: In vitro studies testing fracture strength of teeth restored with porcelain laminate veneers
f.intervention: Feathered incisal edge, butt joint and palatal chamfer preparations
f.comparison: Non-prepared teeth and the designs against each other
outcomes: frequency of root, coronal and ceramic fracture
f.main_result: Feathered edge and palatal chamfer reduced fracture strength by 76.53 N and 102.82 N versus unprepared teeth, while butt joint did not differ (p=0.37)
f.sample_size: 8 studies (7 on fracture strength, 6 on failure frequency)

f.population: Dental literature on porcelain, all-ceramic and composite veneers (PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus)
f.intervention: Different veneer preparation designs and material types
f.comparison: Porcelain vs composite veneers and different preparation designs
f.main_result: Clinician preference decides the design, but incisal overlap seems most predictable; porcelain veneers last well, composite veneers fail faster
f.funding_coi: No financial support; no competing interests
f.limitations: Evidence is controversial and further clinical trials with longer observation are needed

f.population: 47 patients with 223 restorations (154 metal-ceramic crowns, 25 posterior gold crowns, 22 anterior ceramic veneers, 22 anterior ceramic crowns) in one London practice
f.intervention: Crowns and veneers placed by one operator under a strict preventive policy with annual follow-up
f.main_result: Mean survival of metal-ceramic crowns was 47.53 years (6 failures in 154); all other restorations survived 50 years

f.population: Feldspathic ceramic blocks bonded with two luting agents (microsticks) and film-thickness specimens
f.intervention: Thermocycling (6,000 cycles, 5-55 C) of ceramic-luting agent bonds; film thickness per ISO 4049
f.comparison: Dual-cured resin cement (Variolink II) versus flowable resin (Filtek Z350 Flow); dry versus thermocycled
f.main_result: Luting agent did not affect uTBS (p=0.4467); thermocycling gave higher uTBS (20.5 vs 13.9 MPa); film thickness was similar between agents.
f.sample_size: 16 ceramic blocks, n=8 per luting agent; n=8 per agent for film thickness

f.population: Porcelain disks (enamel and dentin porcelain, 0.5-1 mm) over simulated A2 and C4 substrates
f.intervention: Mono- and bilayer enamel/dentin porcelain combinations of different thicknesses
f.comparison: Monolayer versus bilayer; higher-value (A2) versus lower-value (C4) background
f.main_result: Increased porcelain thickness, particularly dentin layer, and increased opacity gave better masking; delta E was higher over the C4 background.

f.intervention: Indirect resin composite versus porcelain veneers for anterior teeth
f.comparison: Direct versus indirect techniques; porcelain versus resin composite
f.limitations: No clinical follow-up similar to that of ceramic materials is available for resin composite veneers.

f.main_result: Bonding protocol must match ceramic type: HF etching plus silane for silica-based ceramics, air-particle abrasion plus phosphate-monomer primer for zirconia.

f.population: Typodont maxillary central incisor replicas with three veneer preparations, zirconia CAD/CAM veneers
f.intervention: Shoulder with wings veneer preparation design
f.comparison: Feather edge and shoulder preparations
f.main_result: The shoulder with wings preparation gave the smallest cervical absolute margin discrepancy and overhang, comparable to shoulder in proximal areas.
f.funding_coi: Supported by 3M New Zealand; authors declare no competing interests.

f.population: Flowable resin composite films (Tetric N-Flow A1) light-activated through ceramic discs
f.intervention: Light-activation through ceramic discs of shades A1 and A3, 0.5, 0.7 and 1.0 mm
f.comparison: Control without ceramic interposition
f.main_result: Control showed highest DC (71.9%); all groups with interposed ceramic had lower DC (about 62-65%), lowest with 0.7 and 1 mm A3.
f.funding_coi: Supported by PIBIC/CNPq

f.population: 70 patients, 30 with bruxism activity, with 323 IPS Empress porcelain laminate veneers
f.intervention: Porcelain laminate veneers in bruxers, with or without occlusal splint
f.comparison: Patients without bruxism
f.main_result: Of 13 fractures and 29 debondings, 8 fractures and 22 debondings occurred in bruxers; debonding was about 3 times more likely and fracture risk was higher without splint.

f.population: 40 extracted sound human maxillary central incisors with lithium disilicate laminate veneers
f.intervention: Luting with pre-heated restorative resin composite
f.comparison: Photo-polymerizing resin cement (Variolink Esthetic LC)
f.main_result: Composite-luted veneers had higher fatigue survival (mean load 1165 N vs 762.5 N) and load to failure (927.59 vs 629.4 N) than cement-luted.

f.population: 28 patients treated with 125 porcelain laminate veneers
f.intervention: PLVs with incisal overlap or incisal bevel, bonded to enamel, minimal or severe dentin exposure
f.comparison: Incisal bevel versus incisal overlap; enamel versus minimal versus severe dentin exposure
f.main_result: Overall 2-year survival was 91.2%; PLVs bonded to severe dentin exposure failed more often than those bonded to enamel or minimal dentin exposure.
f.funding_coi: Supported in part by Hacettepe University Scientific Research Projects Coordination Unit

f.population: 10 participants, 0.3-mm lithium disilicate laminate veneers on maxillary second premolars, no tooth preparation
f.intervention: Light-polymerizing cement on one side
f.comparison: Dual-polymerizing cement on the contralateral side
f.main_result: Color change did not differ between light- and dual-polymerizing cement; at 24 months 40% and 20% of veneers exceeded acceptable color thresholds, with marginal discoloration from 1 year.

f.intervention: Microscopic minimally invasive tooth preparation guided by a target restorative space (TRS) guide plate
f.main_result: Specialist consensus strongly recommends microscope use for 0.1 mm accuracy, diagnostic wax models with preparation guides, enamel-confined preparation, and 0.3-0.5 mm mini-chamfer supragingival or equigingival margins.
f.funding_coi: Chengdu Science and Technology Benefiting Project grant; no competing interests declared

f.main_result: Reported clinical success of ceramic veneers ranged from 75% to 100% (18 months to 20 years); veneer preparation into dentin adversely affects survival.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared

f.population: 32 extracted human maxillary central incisors
f.intervention: Veneer preparation with incisal shoulder finish line, with or without palatal chamfer, restored with pressable IPS Empress veneers luted with Rely-X Veneer
f.comparison: Shoulder finish line alone versus shoulder with palatal chamfer; non-worn versus worn tooth
f.main_result: A palatal chamfer margin gave higher load to failure than a shoulder finish line alone (166.67 N vs 131.84 N on non-worn teeth; 119.56 N vs 90.56 N on worn teeth), and worn teeth with a shoulder line failed at lower load than non-worn teeth.
f.sample_size: 32 extracted maxillary central incisors in 4 groups of 8

f.population: 21 studies (2 clinical, 19 in vitro) on porcelain laminate veneers
f.intervention: Pressed and milled porcelain laminate veneers and preparation designs, assessed for marginal and internal fit
f.comparison: Pressed versus milled fabrication; butt joint versus palatal chamfer preparation
f.main_result: Marginal gap did not differ between pressed and milled veneers (P=.600); pressed had a smaller internal gap (P=.030); butt joint preparation gave a smaller marginal gap than palatal chamfer (mean difference -14.02 um, P=.002).

f.population: Disc-shaped specimens (5 mm x 2 mm) of two light-cured composites, five per group
f.intervention: Curing with three LED units and one halogen unit for 20, 40 or 60 s
f.comparison: Quartz-tungsten halogen unit (Optilux 501)
f.main_result: LED units cured both composites as effectively as the halogen unit when exposure was 40 s or longer; bottom hardness rose significantly from 20 to 40 s with no further gain at 60 s.
f.sample_size: Five specimens per experimental group, two composites

f.population: Resin composite samples in steel moulds (5 mm diameter, three 2 mm increments) simulating a Class II cavity
f.intervention: Incremental exposure of five composites to seven blue LED curing devices at 7 mm distance
f.main_result: All five composites were sufficiently polymerized with at most 20 s exposure per increment, but Bluephase 16i and L.E.Demetron II failed the manufacturer-recommended times for four of five composites.
f.funding_coi: Supported by Ivoclar Vivadent, DENTSPLY and sds Kerr

f.population: 21 included studies of high-power (>=2000 mW/cm2) LED light-curing units; 32 marketed units identified
f.intervention: High-power LED light-curing units (>=2000 mW/cm2) for resin-based materials
f.comparison: Low-power LED light-curing units
outcomes: adverse events on patients oral condition
f.main_result: Thirty-two marketed units delivered 2000-6000 mW/cm2 (highest FlashMax P3); evidence that high-power units are the best clinical option is still very scarce.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest

f.main_result: Clinical long-term success of CAD/CAM glass-ceramic restorations is well proven and monolithic lithium disilicate shows high long-term survival for crowns and FDPs; long-term data on monolithic zirconia and polymer-infiltrated ceramic are still lacking.
f.funding_coi: No financial support; no conflicts of interest declared

f.population: Three randomized or quasirandomized trials of glass-ceramic posterior restorations on adult vital teeth
f.intervention: Self-adhesive resin cement for cementing glass-ceramic posterior restorations
f.comparison: Conventional resin cements
f.main_result: No clinical difference between self-adhesive and conventional resin cements in tooth and restoration integrity at 1 year.
f.funding_coi: CNPq Scientific Initiation Program (ProIC/DPP/UnB)

f.population: Specimens of four pressable glass-ceramics, 85 per material
f.intervention: Novel lithium disilicate glass-ceramic HS10PC (estetic ceram)
f.comparison: IPS e.max Press LT and HT; IPS Empress Esthetic as control
f.main_result: HS10PC showed similar flexural strength, hardness, indentation modulus, fracture load and wear to IPS e.max Press; lithium disilicate ceramics outperformed leucite-reinforced IPS Empress Esthetic.
f.funding_coi: Supported by estetic ceram (manufacturer of HS10PC)
f.limitations: No a priori power analysis was performed to determine sample size.

f.population: Enamel specimens from 24 extracted human permanent molars and 6 antagonist rods per material
f.intervention: Pin-on-disk wear testing of enamel against monolithic zirconia, lithium disilicate glass ceramic and composite resin
f.comparison: Enamel against enamel
f.main_result: Monolithic zirconia and composite resin caused significantly less enamel wear depth than glass ceramic and enamel (P<.001).
f.sample_size: 24 antagonist specimens (6 per material) against enamel from 24 molars
f.funding_coi: Chulalongkorn University graduate school thesis grant
f.limitations: Authors note conclusions hold only within the limitations of this in vitro study.

f.population: Sixty ceramic discs (full contour zirconia or lithium disilicate pressed on zirconia) and 60 antagonists (extracted teeth, PFM crowns, full contour zirconia crowns)
f.intervention: Three-body chewing simulation of ceramic discs against different antagonists
f.comparison: Zirconia versus lithium disilicate discs, each against teeth, PFM crowns and zirconia crowns

f.main_result: No clinical consensus exists on the best surface conditioning for high-strength ceramics, and dual-cure cements can be incompatible with simplified adhesives.
f.limitations: Clinical trials are required to understand real performance of new ceramics, luting agents and surface treatments.

f.population: Sixty-three lithium disilicate (IPS e.max Press) blocks luted to dentin of extracted human third molars
f.intervention: Etching with 1%, 5% or 10% hydrofluoric acid and luting with Bis-GMA/TEGDMA or Bis-GMA/TEGDMA/UDMA light-cured resin cement
f.comparison: HF concentrations and the two resin cement matrices against each other
outcomes: microtensile bond strength at 24 h and 6 months
f.main_result: 10% HF gave higher and more stable microtensile bond strength than 1% with the BisGMA/TEGDMA cement; with the UDMA cement HF concentration made no difference, and water aging lowered bond strength except 10% HF with BisGMA/TEGDMA.
f.follow_up: 24 hours and 6 months of water storage
f.funding_coi: Funded by Fapesp and NIH/NIDCR; authors declare no conflict of interest

f.population: 104 lithium disilicate (IPS e.max Press) blocks
f.intervention: Etching with 5% or 10% hydrofluoric acid with previous heating of the acid (70 °C), the ceramic (85 °C) or both
f.comparison: Unheated control etching at each HF concentration
f.main_result: Heating raised the bond strength of 5% HF to that of unheated 10% HF, while 5% HF without heating gave significantly lower values than 10% HF.

f.population: Lithium disilicate-based ceramic plates (100 plates, 10 groups)
f.intervention: Five ceramic primers (silane agents) applied with or without post-silanization heating at 100 °C for 1 min, then RelyX CRA dual-cure resin cement
f.comparison: Unheated primed plates and the different primers against each other
f.main_result: Heating the primer did not improve bond strength; Clearfil Ceramic Primer gave the lowest values (37.4 and 31.8 MPa) versus about 43-49 MPa for the other silanes.
f.funding_coi: Supported by FAPEAM and CNPq
f.limitations: Long-term effects of post-silanization heating were not evaluated and need further study.

f.intervention: Review of hydrofluoric acid etching, silane, abrasion and silica coating protocols for preparing porcelain and high-strength ceramic surfaces for bonding
f.main_result: No single HF concentration and etching time is optimal for all porcelains, and both under- and over-etching are possible; alumina and zirconia cores cannot be etched with HF.

f.population: 45 ceramic specimens: feldspathic, alumina and zirconia (15 each)
f.intervention: Etching with 40% hydrofluoric acid gel for 2 minutes followed by SEM
f.comparison: Unetched control specimens of each ceramic
f.limitations: Conclusions drawn within the limitations of the SEM-only investigation.

f.population: Ten samples and ten cusp-shaped abraders per restorative material (gold alloy, two lithium disilicates, feldspathic porcelain, zirconia, three heat-cured composites)
f.intervention: Two-body wear in a dual-axis chewing simulator for 120,000 cycles with each material opposing itself
f.comparison: Type 3 gold alloy as the traditional reference
f.main_result: Monolithic zirconia (Katana ML) wore least, total volumetric loss 0.052 mm3, while IPS e.max Press wore most, 0.796 mm3; gold alloy 0.220 mm3.
f.funding_coi: Authors certify no proprietary, financial or personal interest
f.limitations: Conclusions apply only to an in vitro model of a material opposing itself.

f.population: 90 CAD-CAM bar specimens (12×4×3 mm) of lithium disilicate, lithium disilicate-strengthened aluminosilicate glass ceramic and zirconia
f.intervention: Mastication simulation (1,200,000 cycles, 5-55 °C) before 3-point flexural strength testing
f.comparison: Nonaged specimens and the three materials against each other
f.main_result: Zirconia (1136 MPa) was far stronger than lithium disilicate (304 MPa) and lithium aluminosilicate glass ceramic (202 MPa); aging reduced both glass ceramics by about 14.5% but zirconia only 4.3% (not significant).
f.funding_coi: Materials supplied by Ivoclar Vivadent AG and Institut Straumann AG

f.population: Sixty subjects needing a single implant crown in the maxillary or mandibular anterior or premolar region
f.intervention: Immediate or early placed bone-level tapered implants restored with buccally micro-veneered lithium-disilicate or zirconia crowns bonded to titanium-base abutments
f.comparison: Lithium-disilicate (n = 30) versus zirconia-ceramic (n = 30) crowns
f.main_result: At about 13 months implant survival was 98.3% and restoration survival 100%, with a 3.7% technical complication rate and no difference between the two ceramics (p = .558).
f.funding_coi: Funded with financial and material support from Institut Straumann AG; authors report grants and non-financial support from the company.

f.population: CAD/CAM glass-ceramic specimens cut from blocks (30 per material per test)
f.intervention: Zirconia reinforced lithium silicate glass-ceramic (Vita Suprinity)
f.comparison: Lithium disilicate glass-ceramic (IPS e.max CAD)
f.main_result: Vita Suprinity had higher fracture toughness (2.31 MPa m0.5), flexural strength (443.63 MPa), elastic modulus (70.44 GPa) and hardness (6.53 GPa) than IPS e.max CAD (P < 0.001) but a higher brittleness index (2.84).
f.sample_size: 30 specimens per material for fracture toughness, flexural strength and hardness

f.population: Cylindrical specimens of 5 dental ceramics, a Type III gold alloy and human enamel (n=10 each)
f.intervention: 2-body wear test in a dual-axis mastication simulator for 120 000 cycles against zirconia cusps
f.comparison: Human enamel and Type III gold alloy as controls
f.main_result: Gold alloy wear depth (0.223 mm) was closest to enamel (0.217 mm); only milled, unglazed Celtra Duo wore more (0.320 mm, P<.05), and glaze firing removed the difference.
f.sample_size: 10 specimens per material (7 groups plus enamel control)
materials_brands: IPS e.max Press and IPS e.max CAD (Ivoclar Vivadent)

f.population: Standardized human enamel specimens (n¼72) opposing ceramic specimens
f.intervention: Monolithic Y-TZP zirconia, lithium disilicate and feldspathic porcelain with rough, smooth (polished) or glazed surfaces in a 3-body wear simulator, 50 000 cycles
f.comparison: Three ceramics (zirconia, lithium disilicate, feldspathic porcelain) and three surface finishes against each other
f.main_result: Smooth zirconia caused the least enamel wear (1.26 mm2) and glazed groups the most (ZG 5.58, PG 4.2, EG 3.29 mm2); zirconia wear was similar to feldspathic porcelain and polished surfaces wore enamel less than glazed ones.
f.sample_size: 72 ceramic specimens in 9 groups of 8, with 72 enamel specimens
f.limitations: Findings are limited to this in vitro setting.

f.population: Zirconia, lithium disilicate, veneering porcelain and enamel specimens (n = 8) with extracted molar cusps as antagonists
f.intervention: Adjusted (A), adjusted and polished (AP) or adjusted and glazed (AG) zirconia and lithium disilicate, 400,000 chewing-simulator cycles
f.comparison: Veneering porcelain and enamel as controls
f.main_result: Veneering porcelain caused the most enamel wear (2.15 mm3); polished lithium disilicate (0.36 mm3) and zirconia (0.33 mm3) caused the least, comparable to enamel-enamel wear.
f.limitations: Results apply only to the materials used and the test conditions.

f.population: Ceramic specimens (n=10 per test; n=8 for wear) with isolated human molar cusps for wear
f.intervention: 5Y-ZP (Katana UTML) tested for flexural strength, translucency, bond strength and wear
f.comparison: 3Y-TZP (Katana HT) and lithium disilicate (e.max CAD)
f.main_result: Flexural strength was 1194 MPa (Katana HT), 688 MPa (Katana UTML) and 450 MPa (e.max LT); bond strength and opposing enamel wear did not differ and 5Y-ZP showed no measurable wear.
f.funding_coi: Supported partially by a grant from Kuraray.

f.population: CAD/CAM block specimens (bars n = 10; hardness n = 2) and human incisor and premolar enamel
f.intervention: Flexural, hardness and 400,000-cycle wear testing of lithium disilicate, lithium silicate/zirconia, three resin composites and a polymer infiltrated ceramic
f.comparison: Human enamel and the other CAD/CAM materials
f.main_result: E.max CAD and Celtra Duo were stronger, stiffer and harder than the resin composites and Enamic; resin composites and the infiltrated ceramic wore less than enamel and caused less opposing enamel wear than the glass ceramics.
f.sample_size: 10 bars per material for flexural testing
f.funding_coi: All materials were provided by their manufacturer.

f.population: Human enamel specimens (n¼5) opposing lithium disilicate glass ceramic (n¼5) and Type III gold (n¼5)
f.intervention: Ball-on-flat reciprocating friction-wear test with 9.8 N load for up to 1100 cycles in distilled water
f.comparison: Type III gold versus lithium disilicate glass ceramic against enamel
f.main_result: Type III gold had a lower steady-state friction coefficient (0.25 vs 0.64, P=.009) and caused less enamel wear damage than lithium disilicate; lithium disilicate showed abrasive wear, gold adhesive wear.
f.funding_coi: Kirkpatrick Bequest Fund Scholarship (Grant PL108227), Sir John Walsh Research Institute.

f.population: Hemispherical styli of four ceramics and enamel against flattened enamel antagonists (8 specimens per group)
f.intervention: 100,000-cycle two-body wear test of lithium disilicate, leucite-reinforced glass, yttria-stabilized zirconia and feldspathic porcelain styli
f.comparison: Human enamel styli and the four ceramics against each other
outcomes: enamel antagonist height and volume loss
f.main_result: Zirconia (Aadva Zr) showed the smallest stylus wear and caused the least enamel wear, while leucite-reinforced glass, lithium disilicate and feldspathic porcelain were closer to enamel.

f.population: Pressible lithium disilicate glass-ceramic disks with different surface finishes
f.intervention: Pin-on-disk abrasive wear against alumina pins at 5 N and 25 N contact loads
f.comparison: Different initial surface finishes (28 to 1846 nm roughness) and loads
f.main_result: Initial surface finish and contact load significantly affected friction coefficients, wear volumes and surface roughness changes; wear and friction increased with load, with three-body wear dominant on rough and two-body wear on fine surfaces.
f.funding_coi: Supported by James Cook University Collaboration Grants Scheme and NIDCR grant 2R01 DE017925; authors declare no conflict of interest.

f.population: 335 patients with 627 posterior teeth (premolars, molars) restored with single crowns
f.intervention: Pressed monolithic lithium disilicate single crowns with feather-edge margins, cemented with resin-based self-etching cement
f.main_result: Nine crowns fractured and four teeth were extracted; overall survival was 97.93%, lower for second molars

f.population: One patient with moderate dental biocorrosion
f.intervention: Full-mouth rehabilitation with ultrathin CAD-CAM ceramic occlusal veneers (posterior) and bilaminar veneers (maxillary anterior: lingual direct composite plus labial ceramic veneers)
outcomes: clinical integrity of restorations at 1.5 years
f.main_result: At 1.5-year reevaluation the restorations were well integrated with no cracks or chipping in the posterior restorations
f.funding_coi: FAPERJ research grant; manufacturers supplied discounts/materials

f.intervention: Narrative review of lithium disilicate and zirconia dental ceramics: properties and indications
f.main_result: Lithium disilicate and zirconia are materials of choice for modern prosthetic dentistry owing to their properties and versatility
f.funding_coi: No competing interests declared

f.population: 20 glazed IPS e.max CAD lithium disilicate discs (10 adjusted and polished) tested against zirconia spheres
f.intervention: Ball-on-disc reciprocating tribometer wear test in artificial saliva (100,800 cycles, 8.5 N)
f.comparison: Glazed versus glazed-then-polished surfaces of lithium disilicate and zirconia
f.main_result: Mixed surface-treatment pairs lost more volume than matched pairs, but friction and volume loss did not differ significantly among the four groups; roughness did
f.limitations: The zirconia counter bodies could not be analyzed

f.population: Lithium disilicate glass-ceramic bar (N = 40) and plate (N = 32) specimens made from remelted IPS e.max Press glass
f.intervention: Two-step heat treatment at 765, 810, 855 or 915 °C to produce different crystal sizes (G1-G4)
f.comparison: Heat-pressed (GC-P) and original ingot (GC-O) lithium disilicate controls
f.main_result: Medium-sized crystals (G3) gave the highest flexural strength, hardness, elastic modulus and fracture toughness and the lowest wear loss
f.funding_coi: National Natural Science Foundation of China and Shaanxi Natural Science Foundation grants

f.intervention: Review of lithium disilicate ceramics: properties, manufacturing, in vitro and in vivo survival and clinical indications
f.main_result: Lithium disilicate is considered one of the most promising dental materials in digital dentistry
f.funding_coi: No competing interests declared

f.intervention: Celtra Duo zirconia-reinforced lithium silicate CAD blocks for crowns, partial crowns, inlays, onlays and veneers

f.population: Eight commercial chairside CAD/CAM materials
f.intervention: Elastic constants by resonant ultrasound spectroscopy, resonant beam technique and pulse-echo; microstructure by SEM, EDX, Raman and XRD
f.main_result: Young's modulus ranged from 10.9 (Lava Ultimate) to 201.4 (e.max ZirCAD) and Poisson's ratio from 0.173 (Empress CAD) to 0.47 (Lava Ultimate)
f.funding_coi: Materials donated by the manufacturers
f.limitations: For materials with a considerable polymeric fraction, all tested methods show important limitations

f.population: 48 glass-ceramic samples (1.5 mm) of six A2 MT ceramics (96 surfaces)
f.intervention: Thermocycling (10,000 cycles) with glazed or polished surfaces
f.comparison: Heat-pressed versus milled feldspathic, lithium disilicate and ZLS ceramics; glazed versus polished
f.main_result: Thermocycling reduced translucency and opalescence in all samples and roughened glazed surfaces; ZLS ceramics changed most and heat-pressed lithium disilicate least
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest

f.population: 140 ZLS ceramic discs (12 mm diameter, 1.2 mm thick) of Vita Suprinity and Celtra Duo
f.intervention: Crystallization firing of two ZLS glass-ceramics
f.comparison: Fired versus unfired discs of each material
f.main_result: Fired Celtra Duo had the highest characteristic strength (251.25 MPa) and unfired Vita Suprinity the lowest (106.95 MPa)

f.population: Blocks of pre-crystallized ZLS and lithium metasilicate (becoming lithium disilicate) glass ceramic, sliced to 5 x 10 x 10 mm
f.intervention: Diamond grinding with a computer-assisted high-speed handpiece and coarse diamond burs, simulating dental adjustment of ZLS
f.comparison: Lithium disilicate glass ceramic (IPS e.max CAD) ground under the same conditions
f.main_result: ZLS needed higher forces (tangential 0.56-2.03 N vs 0.43-1.59 N) and energy (1228-312 vs 912-253 J/mm3) than LDGC, while edge chipping depth did not differ (101 vs 110 um at the highest removal rate).
f.funding_coi: National Natural Science Foundation of China, Natural Science Foundation of Tianjin and an Australia-China science fund

f.population: Monolithic CAD/CAM posterior crowns (mandibular first molar form) on composite dies and milled bars of four materials
f.intervention: Fracture-strength testing of adhesively cemented monolithic crowns and three-point flexural testing of bars of lithium disilicate, ZLS, a high-performance polymer composite and a PICN
