f.main_result: Combined PES and WES ranged from 16 to 20 at 24 months versus 14 to 18 at restoration delivery, with mean PES 9.33 and WES 8.33.
f.limitations: The technique may initially be technique-sensitive.

f.population: One 23-year-old woman missing maxillary right central and lateral incisors, restored with two adjacent implants
f.intervention: Interimplant papilla reconstruction at second-stage surgery by joining two elevated connective tissue pedicle flaps
f.main_result: The reconstructed papilla was still shorter than on the contralateral side, but the area refilled with papilla at 1 year after proximal modification of the crowns.
materials_brands: NobelProcera angulated screw channel zirconia crowns
f.funding_coi: Supported by the Science and Technology Department of Sichuan Province
f.limitations: The technique does not address vertical bone resorption and needs adequate keratinized tissue.

f.population: Maxillary anterior interproximal sites bordered by teeth, implants and pontics (clinical data over five years plus the 1998 data)
f.intervention: Re-analysis of the height of bone to papilla tip at interproximal sites for each tooth/implant/pontic combination
f.comparison: Six restorative classes (tooth-tooth, tooth-pontic, pontic-pontic, tooth-implant, implant-pontic, implant-implant)
outcomes: predictably achievable papilla height from the most coronal interproximal bone
f.main_result: Achievable soft tissue height above the interproximal bone differs by class, from 3.5 mm between two implants to 6.5 mm between tooth and pontic.
f.follow_up: five years of added clinical data

f.population: Literature on interdental and interimplant papillae from the last 30 years
f.intervention: Review of techniques to create or maintain interdental/interimplant papillae, plus the authors' esthetic triangle approach
f.main_result: Bone support is the foundation for papilla; bone augmentation, soft tissue grafts and esthetic restorations are used, and an esthetic triangle of bone volume, soft tissue thickness and restorations is proposed.
f.funding_coi: Partially supported by the University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund; no financial interests declared

f.population: Literature on peri-implant and interdental papilla (review, articles and case reports)
f.intervention: Narrative review of limitations of papilla preservation, affecting factors and methods to maintain or augment inter-implant papilla
f.main_result: Among contributing factors, crestal bone levels play a major role in the presence of peri-implant papilla; surgical techniques and implant design changes such as platform switching are used to preserve it.

f.population: 9 partially edentulous patients (mean age 65) with 23 immediately restored implants
f.intervention: Computer-assisted flapless guided implant surgery with premade immediate screw-retained provisional restorations
outcomes: distance from contact point to bone
f.main_result: Papilla fill was 91% between implants and 71% between implant and tooth, with bone mostly above the platform at about 545 days.

f.population: Anterior implant sites needing peri-implant soft tissue augmentation (literature review)
f.intervention: Soft tissue grafting (free gingival graft, subepithelial connective tissue graft, roll flap, envelope flap) around anterior implants
outcomes: peri-implant soft tissue thickness and contour
f.main_result: Soft tissue augmentation techniques can optimize anterior implant esthetics, but the need for them remains controversial and lacks literature support; envelope technique gave a mean 0.8 mm mucosal thickness gain.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no conflict of interests
f.limitations: Need for soft tissue augmentation lacks literature support; long-term clinical trials needed

f.population: 30 patients, 288 interproximal sites (anterior, premolar and molar)
f.intervention: Probing the distance from the base of the contact point to the crest of bone and recording papilla presence or absence
outcomes: presence or absence of the interproximal papilla
f.main_result: Papilla was present almost 100% of the time at 5 mm or less from contact point to bone crest, 56% at 6 mm and 27% at 7 mm or more.

f.population: 17 nonsmoking periodontitis patients with one deep intrabony defect and a narrow interproximal space
f.intervention: Papilla amplification flap combined with titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membranes for guided tissue regeneration
f.main_result: Clinical attachment gain was 4.7 mm and probing depth reduction 6.3 mm at 1 year; primary closure was obtained in 100% of cases and maintained in 65% at 6 weeks.

f.population: Illustrative clinical cases needing implant placement or augmentation in the esthetic zone
f.intervention: Papillae-sparing incisions with a pedicle flap for implant placement and soft- or hard-tissue augmentation
f.main_result: Papillae-sparing incisions give access to bone for implants and grafting without inducing recession of adjacent papillae.

f.population: Adjacent implants in 33 patients from five private offices
f.intervention: Probing of papilla height from crest of bone between two adjacent implants
f.main_result: Mean papilla height between two adjacent implants was 3.4 mm (range 1-7 mm).

f.population: Published in vitro and in vivo studies on PEEK CAD-CAM dental prostheses
f.intervention: Literature review of PEEK for CAD-CAM fabricated dental prostheses
f.main_result: PEEK is a viable alternative for CAD-CAM fixed and removable prostheses, but clinical data are scarce.
f.funding_coi: Not funded; no competing interests
f.limitations: Only a few clinical studies were identified, so long-term performance is unknown.

f.population: Patients with peri-implantitis-affected implants
f.intervention: Flap reflection, surface decontamination, EMD or PDGF, and GBR with bone graft and absorbable membrane and/or connective tissue graft
f.main_result: 98.8% survival; BoP eliminated in 91%; probing depth reduced 5.10 mm and bone gain 1.77 mm on average.
f.limitations: Randomized controlled trials and histological studies are still needed.

f.intervention: Antibiotics and surgical debridement with autogenous bone and a collagen membrane
f.comparison: Bovine-derived xenograft with collagen membrane
f.main_result: Bovine xenograft gave more radiographic bone fill than autogenous bone at 12 months, though success of both was limited.
f.funding_coi: Funded by BIOMET 3i; authors declare no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Success of both regenerative procedures was limited.

f.population: 24 partially dentate patients with moderate to advanced peri-implantitis
f.intervention: Anti-infective surgical protocol: open flap debridement, implant surface decontamination, systemic amoxicillin and metronidazole
f.main_result: 100% implant survival at 12 months; all implants had mean PD below 5 mm, 47% were BoP negative, 92% had stable or gained bone.

f.population: 29 patients with one implant with peri-implant mucositis
f.intervention: Non-surgical debridement plus 0.5% chlorhexidine gel for 4 weeks
f.comparison: Non-surgical debridement plus placebo gel
f.main_result: Adjunctive chlorhexidine gel gave no added benefit over mechanical cleansing; 38% of implants had complete BOP resolution at 3 months.
f.funding_coi: ITI research grant and Clinical Research Foundation; no conflict of interest

f.population: Titanium and zirconium disks contaminated with a six-species high-adherence biofilm; human gingival fibroblasts
f.intervention: Decontamination with titanium curette, ultrasonic scaler, glycine and erythritol air-polishing, Er:YAG laser, CHX, PVI, doxycycline, NaOCl
f.comparison: Untreated control disks
f.main_result: Air-polishing, ultrasonic scaler and Er:YAG laser reduced biofilm activity with favorable cytocompatibility, while chemical agents were cytotoxic.
f.funding_coi: Oral Reconstruction Foundation grant; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: In vitro design only

f.population: 117 patients with implant-supported restorations (450 implants) treated 2001-2013 at a university clinic
f.intervention: Association of smoking history and patient/implant variables with peri-implant status
f.comparison: Never-smokers versus former and current smokers
f.main_result: Smoke intensity (>23 pack-years) was associated with higher peri-implantitis risk; quitting more than 21 years earlier gave lower risk.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; no conflict of interest

f.population: 192 implants explanted due to peri-implantitis from 161 patients in 12 dental offices
f.intervention: Measurement of bone loss at explantation using explants and radiographs
f.main_result: Mean relative bone loss at explantation was 66.2%, higher in the mandible and for shorter implants.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared; Nobel offices received replacement implants
f.limitations: Highly selective sample.

f.population: 18 healthy volunteers wearing intraoral maxillary splints with material discs; human gingival fibroblasts in vitro
f.intervention: 24 h intraoral wear of splints carrying discs of eight implant materials (zirconia, noble alloy coatings, Pagalinor, hydroxyapatite, TiZr, TAN, TiGr4)
f.comparison: Titanium zirconium as the reference material against the other seven materials
f.main_result: Noble metal alloys (AgPt, AgAuPd, Pagalinor) had less biofilm mass and CFU than titanium or zirconia, with zirconia highest (9.1-fold biofilm mass and 18.5-fold CFU versus AgPt).
f.sample_size: 18 volunteers, two runs, two discs of each of 8 materials per run
f.funding_coi: Discs provided by Straumann AG; authors declare no competing interests

f.population: Patients with at least one dental implant with peri-implantitis (26 articles reporting 20 investigations)
f.intervention: Surgical treatment of peri-implantitis: access flap, resective, reconstructive and combined approaches
f.comparison: Reconstructive versus access flap versus resective surgery; with versus without barrier membrane
f.main_result: Reconstructive surgery gave significantly less mucosal recession than access flaps (WMD -1.35 mm), while resective surgery led to about 1.2 mm of recession and combined approaches the most (1.97 mm).
f.funding_coi: Self-funded for the EAO consensus conference; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: None of the included studies had low risk of bias, few comparisons were available for WMD, and heterogeneity was significant.

f.population: Patients with implant-supported reconstructions placed in 2003 in Sweden, examined 9 years later
f.intervention: Clinical examination (probing pocket depth, bleeding on probing) at 9 years tested as a screening test for history of bone loss
f.main_result: Each additional mm of PPD corresponded to 0.30 mm more bone loss; BoP sensitivity for bone loss >2 mm was 80.9% with 42.2% specificity, whereas PPD sensitivity was low.
f.sample_size: 1,578 implants in 427 patients with baseline radiographs
f.funding_coi: Grants from the Swedish Social Insurance Agency, Swedish Research Council, TUA and the Swedish Dental Society; some authors report personal fees or grants from implant companies outside the submitted work

f.population: Patients with peri-implantitis (7 human clinical trials) and 2 animal studies in beagle dogs
f.intervention: Lasers (CO2 or Er:YAG) for peri-implantitis implant surface detoxification, surgical or non-surgical
f.main_result: Lasers gave the same probing depth reduction as conventional decontamination for non-surgical therapy (WMD 0.00 mm, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.19).
f.sample_size: 9 studies (7 human clinical trials, 2 animal studies)
f.funding_coi: Partially supported by the University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Research on lasers for peri-implantitis is inadequate and the evidence is short-term.

f.population: Thirty subjects with peri-implantitis treated by access flap surgery
f.intervention: Supportive peri-implant care with ultrasonic PEEK tip plus glycine powder air polishing every 3 months
f.comparison: Same ultrasonic instrumentation with rubber cup and polishing paste
f.main_result: After 12 months PD changed -0.84 mm in the air-polishing test group versus +0.18 mm in controls (p<.001); healthy tissues were present at 83% of implants overall (87% vs 80%, p=.255).
materials_brands: EMS Instrument PI PEEK tip; Perio AIR-flow and Airflow Master Piezon (EMS)
f.funding_coi: Self-funded by the ETEP Research Group; no conflict of interest

f.population: Patients with advanced peri-implantitis combined supra- and intrabony defects (24 patients, 26 defects at 24 months)
f.intervention: Access flap, granulation tissue removal and implantoplasty, then surface decontamination with Er:YAG laser, plus natural bone mineral and collagen membrane
f.comparison: Plastic curets + cotton pellets + sterile saline for surface debridement/decontamination
f.main_result: At 24 months Er:YAG laser did not give significantly higher BOP reduction (75.0% vs 54.9%) or CAL gain (1.0 vs 1.2 mm) than plastic curets, and CAL was not significantly different from baseline in either group.
f.funding_coi: In part funded by Geistlich Biomaterials; materials provided by Elexxion AG and Geistlich; first author received lecture fees from Geistlich

f.population: Published systematic reviews on dental implant failure and survival (748 found, 149 analyzed)
f.intervention: Narrative synthesis of reviews on implant design, surface, augmentation, abutment connection and material
f.main_result: True dental implant failure rates are likely higher than published, and roughened collars, microthreads and platform switching maintain bone while augmentation does not raise success rates.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest

f.population: Nine cynomolgus monkeys with ligature-induced peri-implant mucositis around ITI titanium implants
f.intervention: Mechanical cleansing alone, or mechanical cleansing with 0.12% chlorhexidine irrigation and 0.2% CHX gel, for two months
f.comparison: Untreated control group
f.main_result: Mechanical therapy alone or with chlorhexidine resolved mucositis clinically and histologically, with no difference in PD reduction between them (group A had more recession and less CAL gain than B).

f.population: Dogs with implants having exchangeable intraosseous cylinders in the mandible and ligature-induced peri-implantitis
f.intervention: Three decontamination modalities (cylinder exchanged, sprayed in situ with saline, removed, cleansed and steam-sterilized) on machined, SLA or TPS surfaces
f.comparison: Pristine exchanged cylinder (T1) and surface types compared with each other
f.main_result: In situ saline cleansing (T2) gave the highest BIC and SLA surfaces the highest BIC (better than machined); bone crest height did not differ by implant type.

f.population: Titanium dental implants inoculated with a six-species subgingival biofilm
f.intervention: Direct current of 0.75, 1.5 and 3 V (anodic) and -0.75, -1.5 and -3 V (cathodic) for 5 min in a three-electrode system
f.comparison: Untreated biofilm and the different voltages and polarities against each other
f.main_result: 3 V and -3 V significantly reduced total live bacteria from 3.15x10^6 to 1.85x10^5 and 2.92x10^4 per mL; F. nucleatum was most affected; 0.75 V and -0.75 V had no effect.
f.funding_coi: Funded by an ITI grant; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Effects inside the abutment chamber were not examined, qPCR gives only an estimate of live bacteria, and only direct current was tested.

f.population: 79 treated-periodontitis patients (moderate or high IDRA risk) with implant-supported single crowns or FDPs, at least 5 years in function
f.intervention: Retrospective calculation of Implant Disease Risk Assessment (IDRA) risk at restoration delivery, related to peri-implantitis at most recent follow-up
f.comparison: moderate versus high IDRA-risk patients
outcomes: odds ratio high vs moderate risk
f.main_result: AUC of IDRA risk category for peri-implantitis was 0.613; peri-implantitis occurred in 12% at moderate and 27% at high risk (OR 2.727, not significant).
f.funding_coi: Funded by the authors' own institution; no conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Retrospective design, low patient number and no low-risk IDRA group (selection bias).

f.main_result: Peri-implantitis is best diagnosed with 2017 World Workshop case definitions; smoking, diabetes, periodontitis history and poor maintenance are key risk factors; mucositis responds to non-surgical therapy while peri-implantitis generally needs surgery (OFD, APF, GBR).
f.funding_coi: No external funding; authors declare no conflict of interest

f.population: 21 patients with 21 implants with advanced peri-implantitis (combined supra- and intrabony defects) at 4 years
f.comparison: Plastic curets + cotton pellets + sterile saline decontamination
f.main_result: At 48 months CPS sites tended to show larger BOP (85.2% vs 71.6%) and CAL (1.5 vs 1.2 mm) reductions than ERL, but outcomes were not influenced by decontamination method.
f.sample_size: 21 patients (21 implants) at 4 years; 32 patients at baseline
f.funding_coi: Long-term follow-up funded by authors' own department; materials supplied by Elexxion and Geistlich; F. Schwarz received lecture fees from Geistlich
f.limitations: Small number of patients, only descriptive statistics.

outcomes: diagnostic value of BOP for peri-implantitis
long-term biologic complications at augmented sites
implant survival in geriatric/systemically compromised patients

f.population: 32 partially edentulous patients with advanced peri-implantitis (38 combined supra- and intra-bony defects)
f.intervention: Flap surgery, granulation tissue removal and implantoplasty, then Er:YAG laser surface decontamination, with natural bone mineral and collagen membrane
f.comparison: Plastic curets + cotton pellets + sterile saline decontamination
f.funding_coi: Partly funded by Geistlich Biomaterials; materials provided by Elexxion and Geistlich; no conflict of interest declared

f.intervention: Introduction of the Implant Disease Risk Assessment (IDRA), an eight-vector functional diagram estimating a patient's risk of peri-implantitis
f.main_result: The IDRA combines eight evidence-based parameters and may be useful for identifying individuals at risk of developing peri-implantitis; it requires validation.
f.limitations: The tool requires validation through retrospective or prospective studies in multiple settings.

f.population: Partially dentate patients with a history of treated periodontitis receiving dental implants
f.intervention: Dental implants placed in patients treated for periodontitis
f.comparison: Periodontally healthy patients
f.main_result: Implants in treated periodontitis patients had more biological complications and lower success and survival (79.22-100% vs 91.67-100%) than in periodontally healthy patients.
f.limitations: High heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; conclusions limited by strength of evidence.

f.population: 18 cpTi cylindrical screw implants (4 x 13 mm, external hex, Zimmer Biomet)
f.intervention: Implantoplasty of the coronal 6 mm with tungsten carbide burs or diamond sonic tips, each followed by Arkansas finishing
f.comparison: Untreated control implants; burs versus sonic tips
f.main_result: Sonic diamond tips caused less material loss than burs but took longer (860 vs 453 s with finishing); fracture resistance did not differ from burs or controls (1.65 vs 1.51 vs 1.66 kN).
materials_brands: Komet tungsten carbide burs H379.310.023 and diamond sonic tips SF878K
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared

f.population: 180 stained implants (Replace Select Straight 4.3 x 13 mm) in resin peri-implant defect models of 30, 60 and 90 degrees
f.intervention: Surface decontamination for 2 min with air powder abrasion (glycine powder), sonic scaler with steel tip, or curette
f.comparison: Curette versus sonic scaler versus air powder abrasion across three defect angulations
outcomes: percent residual stain on implant surface
f.main_result: Air powder abrasion cleaned best (residual color 0.13-8.03%) versus sonic scaler (11.4-19.69%) and curette (48.1-57.13%) in all defect angles, with no SEM surface damage.
materials_brands: Nobel Biocare Replace Select Straight implants
Perio-Mate air powder unit with glycine powder (NSK)

f.population: 28 patients with 32 implants with peri-implantitis infrabony defects suitable for regenerative surgery
f.intervention: Regenerative surgery with Bio-Oss xenograft, resorbable collagen membrane and hydrogen peroxide surface detoxification, prosthesis removed or maintained
f.comparison: Prosthesis maintained versus removed after regenerative surgery
f.main_result: Regenerative treatment gave similar bone gain in both groups; success did not depend on removing the prosthesis.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest

f.population: Partially edentulous subjects previously treated with implant-supported fixed dental prostheses
f.intervention: Recall examination of existing implant-supported fixed prostheses (clinical, radiographic, questionnaires)
f.comparison: Cement-retained vs screw-retained and short-span vs long-span prostheses
f.main_result: Cumulative implant survival was 99.1%, peri-implantitis affected 5% and mucositis 84.1% of implants; mucositis was more likely with cement-retained (OR 6.8) and short-span prostheses (OR 2.3).
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no financial interest in companies whose materials are included

f.population: Patients with implants placed in a university setting, 83 patients with 168 implants analysed
f.intervention: Radiographic measurement of restoration emergence angle and profile in bone-level and tissue-level implants
f.comparison: Emergence angle >30 vs <=30 degrees; convex vs concave profile
f.main_result: In bone-level implants peri-implantitis prevalence was 31.3% with emergence angle >30 degrees versus 15.1% with <=30 degrees (p = .04); no such correlation in tissue-level implants.
f.sample_size: 96 patients with 225 implants (83 patients, 168 implants analysed)
f.funding_coi: University of Washington School of Dentistry research fund; no conflicts of interest

f.population: Patients with peri-implantitis treated surgically, from 17 long-term studies
f.intervention: Surgical therapy of peri-implantitis with at least 5 years follow-up
f.main_result: Mean long-term disease resolution after surgical peri-implantitis therapy was 58.6%, bone loss arrest 69.6%, retreatment need 27.2% and implant survival 88.6%.
f.funding_coi: Conflict of interest statement: none

f.population: 85 patients with peri-implantitis (cases) and 69 patients with healthy implants (controls)
f.intervention: Submucosal peri-implant microbial sampling analysed by culturing techniques
f.comparison: Patients with only healthy peri-implant conditions
f.main_result: Peri-implantitis was associated with P. gingivalis, P. intermedia, T. forsythia and F. nucleatum, most strongly P. intermedia (OR 15.1) and T. forsythia (OR 13.3).
f.funding_coi: Two authors declare stock ownership of LabOral International B.V. and LabOral Diagnostics; others none

f.population: Observational studies on peri-implantitis, healthy implants and periodontitis (26 included)
f.intervention: Systematic review of microbial biofilm profiles and microbiomes
f.comparison: Healthy implants or periodontitis
f.main_result: Peri-implantitis is a heterogeneous mixed infection with periodontopathic microorganisms and uncultivable anaerobic rods; sequencing of the entire microbiome improves identification.
f.funding_coi: Supported by the authors' institution (El Bosque University); no conflicts of interest

f.population: Ten systemically healthy non-smokers with a history of periodontitis
f.intervention: 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing of plaque samples from a peri-implantitis implant and periodontally healthy dental sites
f.comparison: Healthy dental sites in the same individuals
f.main_result: Diseased peri-implant sites were less diverse than healthy sites; Prevotella and Porphyromonas discriminated disease, Actinobacillus and Streptococcus health.

f.population: Systemically healthy human subjects with at least one osseointegrated dental implant
f.intervention: Peri-implantitis (exposure), bacterial presence/count in submarginal biofilm
f.comparison: Peri-implant health or mucositis
f.main_result: Peri-implantitis was associated with S. epidermidis (OR 10.28), F. nucleatum (OR 7.83), T. denticola (OR 6.11), T. forsythia (OR 4.25), P. intermedia (OR 3.79) and P. gingivalis (OR 2.46).
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest and no specific funding
f.limitations: Only 12 studies, all at moderate/high risk of bias, limiting external validity

f.population: Clinical studies of reconstructive therapy of peri-implantitis defects
f.intervention: Factors and techniques contributing to minimal invasiveness in reconstructive peri-implantitis treatment
f.main_result: Most minimally invasive flap techniques were case reports, with no controlled or randomized trials showing superiority over conventional access.
f.funding_coi: Open access funding by Universitat Bern; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Controlled or randomized trials are difficult to conduct because defects are not comparable

f.population: 47 peri-implantitis patients, 158 eligible peri-implantitis implants
f.intervention: CBCT classification of peri-implantitis defect morphology and severity
outcomes: associated patient, implant and site variables
f.main_result: Class Ib was the most prevalent defect (55%) and moderate the most frequent severity (50.6%); smoking, prosthesis type and distance to adjacent implant related to severity.
f.funding_coi: FEDICOM Foundation

f.population: Expert consensus meeting of 96 clinicians and researchers, based on two systematic reviews
f.intervention: Implant neck (collar design/surface) and abutment material characteristics
f.comparison: Rough vs machined collar; titanium vs zirconia abutments
f.main_result: Marginal bone levels were mainly influenced by the rough microstructure of the implant neck, not by abutment material; titanium abutments had higher bleeding on probing than zirconia.
f.sample_size: 96 experts; two systematic reviews (13 publications, 608 implants for abutment material)
f.funding_coi: Organized and supported by the Oral Reconstruction Foundation, Basel

f.population: 37 systemically healthy adults with peri-implantitis (one target implant/site per patient)
f.intervention: Non-surgical treatment plus systemic amoxicillin and metronidazole
f.comparison: Non-surgical treatment alone
f.main_result: Antibiotics group had a higher mean PIPD reduction at 12 weeks (2.28 vs 1.47 mm), not statistically significant; only 2 implants had a successful outcome.
materials_brands: EMS ultrasonic devices with PEEK fiber tip (PI instrument)
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest; funded by the authors' university departments (ACTA)
f.limitations: Local etiological factors such as implant positioning, excess cement and keratinized gingiva were not evaluated.

f.population: 39 patients with one implant with mild to moderate peri-implantitis in five specialist clinics
f.intervention: Debridement with an oscillating chitosan brush
f.comparison: Debridement with titanium curettes
f.main_result: No significant difference in PPD and BI changes between brush and curette at 6 months; disease eradication in 9.5% (brush) vs 5.9% (curette).
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Research Council of Norway and university grants; brush inventor holds the patent and two authors are shareholders in Labrida AS

f.population: 60 dyed implants (30 apically tapered, 30 fully tapered) in plastic models with porcine soft tissue
f.intervention: Cleaning for 150 s with curette, ultrasonic scaler or air powder waterjet with erythritol powder
f.comparison: Curette as control therapy; two implant designs compared
f.main_result: Cleaned surface ranged from 17.1% (FTAP, curette) to 45.5% (ATAP, air powder waterjet); titanium residues were highest with curette and near zero with waterjet.
materials_brands: Airflow One with Airflow Powder Plus (erythritol), EMS
f.funding_coi: Funded by the researchers' institution; implants provided by Straumann; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: No treatment modality removed more than 50% of the surface in either design; model lacks naturally matured deposits and vital soft tissue.

f.population: 43 patients diagnosed with peri-implantitis who underwent peri-implant surgery
f.intervention: Surgical treatment of peri-implantitis, with OHIP-14 recorded before and after
f.main_result: OHIP-14 scores were low and unchanged from baseline (7.2) to 36 months (7.0), with no significant changes.
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Faculty of Dentistry, University of Oslo; no conflicts of interest

f.intervention: Proposed three-type treatment-driven classification of facial peri-implant marginal mucosa defects with prosthetic and surgical management recommendations
f.main_result: Facial PMMDs are classified into three types by interproximal bone and papillary height loss; a bilaminar coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft is advised as primary surgical modality, with prosthetic correction when needed.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Literature on surgical management of single-tooth PMMDs is scant and dominated by case reports and case series.

f.population: Published literature on peri-implantitis prevention, histopathology and therapeutics (214 studies retrieved)
f.main_result: Peri-implantitis incidence is sustained and concerning, with no predictable treatment protocol; risk assessment, surgical/restorative expertise and strict maintenance are key.
f.sample_size: 214 studies retrieved from PubMed, Web of Science and Science Direct
f.funding_coi: No specific grant funding

f.population: Published literature on regenerative surgical treatment of peri-implantitis bone defects (857 PubMed records screened)
f.main_result: Regenerative techniques improve clinical and radiographic parameters, but no grafting material, membrane or decontamination method is shown superior; defect morphology is a key outcome factor.
f.funding_coi: No funding; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Not a systematic review; PubMed only and English only.

f.population: 99 patients with 458 dental implants, randomly selected from a university clinic database
outcomes: prevalence of peri-implant health and diseases
risk and protective indicators of peri-implantitis
f.main_result: Prevalence of peri-implantitis was 56.6% at patient level and 27.9% at implant level; smoking (OR 3.59) and moderate/severe periodontitis (OR 2.77) were among the risk indicators.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts; partly funded by an Osteology Foundation Young Research Grant
f.limitations: Cross-sectional design; baseline data on bone loss from 0-1 years after loading were unavailable, so case definitions relied on single-time bone levels.

f.population: 134 patients with 478 implants supporting fixed prostheses, without a regular maintenance program
f.comparison: Tissue-level versus bone-level implants
f.main_result: Peri-implantitis affected 20% of patients and 8.8% of implants; smoking and lack of keratinized mucosa were associated with it (OR 2.57 and 3.89).
materials_brands: Nobel Biocare Replace Select and Branemark MKIII

f.population: 159 longitudinal clinical studies on prevention or management of peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis
f.main_result: PPD and BOP were reported in 89% and 87% of 159 studies; patient-reported outcomes (6%) and adverse events (8%) were rarely reported and a primary outcome was defined in only 36%.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; no conflicts of interest

f.population: 30 edentulous patients with two mandibular implants each, 2 years in function
f.intervention: Internal implant decontamination (10% H2O2 + brush) plus sealant, CHX varnish or CHX gel
f.comparison: Decontamination alone (control)
outcomes: total bacterial counts (real-time PCR) in internal implant cavity
f.main_result: Internal bacterial counts fell about 4-fold after 12 months overall, with no difference between decontamination alone and added sealant or chlorhexidine (p = .348)
f.funding_coi: Own institutions; materials supplied by Ivoclar Vivadent, Hager und Werken and GSK; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Possibly underpowered to detect minor differences; homogeneous implant sample; PCR cannot distinguish live from dead bacteria

f.population: Patients with dental implants and peri-implant mucositis/peri-implantitis
f.intervention: Consensus evaluation of measures for managing peri-implant mucositis (patient and professional plaque control, adjuncts)
outcomes: clinical signs of inflammation after management
f.main_result: Meta-analysis estimated weighted mean prevalence of peri-implant mucositis 43% and peri-implantitis 22%; mechanical plaque control is effective, adjuncts add no benefit
f.sample_size: Prevalence meta-analysis of 1196 patients and 4209 implants (mucositis)
f.funding_coi: European Federation of Periodontology workshop, partly unrestricted grants from Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble
f.limitations: Included prevalence studies used convenience samples of limited size with varying follow-up

f.population: 63 patients with one circumferential peri-implant intraosseous defect each
f.intervention: Open flap debridement plus porous titanium granules
f.comparison: Open flap debridement alone
f.main_result: At 12 months radiographic defect fill was 3.6/3.6 mm with PTG versus 1.1/1.0 mm with OFD alone (P < 0.0001), with similar clinical improvements
f.funding_coi: Research grant from Tigran Technologies AB; several authors report industry grants and Tigran advisory roles
f.limitations: Biomaterial could not be distinguished from osseous tissue on radiographs, so new bone formation could not be verified

f.population: Implants treated for peri-implantitis in 12 included studies (390 implants)
f.intervention: Reconstructive surgical procedures for peri-implantitis
f.comparison: Open flap debridement (only one RCT available)
f.main_result: Weighted mean radiographic defect fill 2.17 mm (95% CI 1.46-2.87), PD reduction 2.97 mm, CAL gain 1.65 mm, BOP reduction 45.8%; no evidence versus nonreconstructive procedures
f.funding_coi: Partly supported by University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund; no conflicts declared
f.limitations: Mostly small case series with short follow-up and inconsistent methodologies

f.population: 138 patients (147 implants) with peri-implantitis
f.intervention: Reconstructive surgery using bone substitute material
f.comparison: Access flap surgery (control)
outcomes: composite outcome (implant not lost, no BOP/SOP, PPD <=5 mm, <=1 mm recession)
PPD, BOP, buccal keratinized mucosa, buccal recession
f.main_result: Composite success was 16.4% (test) vs 13.5% (control), not significant; buccal recession was lower in the test group (0.7 vs 1.1 mm).
f.funding_coi: Osteology Foundation Large Clinical Grant; several authors report honoraria/grants from Dentsply Sirona, Straumann, Geistlich etc.
f.limitations: No blinding to group allocation was performed.

f.population: 45 patients with peri-implantitis intraosseous defects
f.intervention: Bovine-derived xenograft (BDX) with collagen membrane
f.comparison: Autogenous bone graft with collagen membrane
f.main_result: Successful treatment at year five in 36% of implants with autogenous bone versus 78.3% with BDX; bone level change -0.7 mm versus +1.6 mm
f.sample_size: 45 patients enrolled; at year 5, 16 patients/25 implants (AB) and 23 patients/38 implants (BDX)
f.funding_coi: Biomet 3i funded the initial 12-month study; long-term follow-up self-funded; Renvert reports grants from Biomet 3i and Geistlich

f.population: 75 patients with one crater-like peri-implantitis defect around SLA tissue-level implants
f.intervention: Reconstructive surgery with deproteinized bovine bone mineral with 10% collagen (DBBMC)
outcomes: treatment success (PD, BOP, pus, bone loss)
f.main_result: At 5 years 51 of 75 patients remained, implant survival 80%, success in 29 patients (45.3%); outcome not related to defect configuration but to adherence to supportive therapy
f.funding_coi: Self-funded, no external funding

f.population: Six female Labrador dogs with experimental peri-implantitis
f.intervention: Reconstructive surgical therapy with bone substitute materials (DBBM, biphasic graft, DBBM with collagen membrane)
f.comparison: No augmentation (Group C)
f.main_result: Healing was superior around smooth-surface implants than moderately rough ones; benefit of bone substitutes was overall small
f.funding_coi: Swedish Research Council and TUA research funding; materials provided by Geistlich and Dentsply

f.population: Consecutive partially edentulous patients with at least one peri-implantitis implant
f.intervention: Local factors (surgical, implant, prosthesis-related) assessed as exposures
f.comparison: Peri-implantitis versus non-peri-implantitis implants
f.main_result: Implant malpositioning (tilt 10-30 degrees OR 5.84, 30 degrees or more OR 7.43) and medial position (OR 3.9) raised peri-implantitis odds; inside bony housing OR 0.13; Morse taper OR 0.43
f.funding_coi: Statistics covered by the university department; otherwise self-funded; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Cross-sectional design cannot establish a direct link between local factors and peri-implantitis

f.population: Granulation tissue biopsies from 39 peri-implantitis cases and 35 periodontitis controls
f.intervention: Identification of titanium particles in peri-implantitis granulation tissue (SEM/EDS) and immunohistochemistry
f.comparison: Periodontitis granulation tissue
outcomes: CD68, IL-6, Nf-kB and VEGF expression
f.main_result: Titanium particles were found in all peri-implantitis specimens without foreign body reaction; peri-implantitis showed higher CD68 and VEGF expression than periodontitis
f.funding_coi: Serbian Ministry of Education and Science, Medical Military Academy and Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts
f.limitations: No SEM/EDS analysis of periodontitis specimens, which were assumed particle-free

f.population: 51 peri-implantitis implants in 38 patients (BOP, PD ≥ 6 mm, bone loss ≥ 4 mm)
f.intervention: Regenerative approach: surface decontamination, enamel matrix derivative, PDGF with bovine or freeze-dried bone, collagen membrane or connective tissue graft
f.main_result: Probing depth fell 5.4 and 5.1 mm and bone level gain was 3.75 mm (group 1) and 3.0 mm (group 2); no implant lost bone
f.limitations: Lack of histology to determine nature of newly formed tissue

f.population: Patients in good general health requiring surgical treatment of peri-implantitis (16 RCTs)
f.intervention: Implant surface decontamination protocols (mechanical, chemical, physical, systemic antimicrobials) during surgical treatment
f.comparison: Other decontamination protocols, including placebo
f.main_result: No single decontamination method showed clear superiority; systemic antibiotics improved treatment success (RR 1.84) but Er:Yag laser added no PPD benefit.
f.funding_coi: Funded solely by the authors' institutions; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Most evidence rests on single RCTs and half of the trials were not at low risk of bias.

f.population: Human clinical trials of surgically treated peri-implantitis (21 articles, 12 case series)
f.intervention: Surgical treatment of peri-implantitis: access flap and debridement, resection, bone grafting, guided bone regeneration
f.main_result: Surgical procedures gave weighted mean PD reduction of 2.04 to 3.16 mm, and grafting with membranes gave greater PD reduction and 2.1 mm bone fill.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Lack of high-quality comparative studies to support the findings.

f.population: 40 participants with peri-implantitis and a contained intraosseous defect (one implant each)
f.intervention: Access flap with xenograft (DBBM) and collagen membrane (GBR), plus systemic antimicrobials
f.comparison: Access flap surgery alone (control), also with systemic antimicrobials
f.main_result: No significant clinical or radiographic differences between access flap and GBR at 12 months; PD reduction 4.2 vs 3.7 mm, MBL gain 1.7 vs 2.4 mm.
materials_brands: Amoxicillin 500 mg + metronidazole 400 mg for 7 days
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Osteology Foundation; first author reports speaking honoraria from Geistlich and Straumann among others
f.limitations: Sample of 40 participants is relatively small for a single-centre trial.

f.population: 75 patients with one peri-implantitis crater-like lesion, PD >= 6 mm
f.intervention: Implant decontamination then filling of the defect with deproteinized bovine bone mineral with 10% collagen
f.main_result: Treatment success was obtained in 37 (52.1%) of 71 implants examined at 1 year; PD fell by 2.92 mm and BOP from 71.5% to 18.3%.
f.sample_size: 75 patients, one implant each; 71 examined at 1 year
materials_brands: Bio-Oss Collagen (deproteinized bovine bone mineral with 10% collagen), Geistlich
f.funding_coi: Self-funded, no external funding; first author received grants from Straumann, Dentsply, Geistlich and Sunstar outside the work

f.population: 376 patients with 1095 dental implants treated 1999-2005 at a specialist clinic in Stockholm
f.intervention: Dental implant therapy (Astra Tech 65%, Nobel Biocare 35%)
f.main_result: Cumulative implant survival to 15 years was 82.6%; 65% of patients had at least one complication; implant loss was more frequent after treated severe periodontitis.
f.funding_coi: Grants from Stockholm County Council and Folktandvården Stockholms Läns Landsting AB; no conflict of interest

f.population: 27 patients with one peri-implantitis intrabony defect each (Class Ib, Ic or Ie)
f.intervention: Access flap surgery with natural bone mineral plus collagen membrane
f.comparison: Class Ib vs Class Ic vs Class Ie defect configurations (9 each)
f.main_result: Class Ie defects tended to show higher PD and CAL changes than Class Ib and Ic, with significant differences only at 6 months.
materials_brands: Natural bone mineral with collagen membrane (Geistlich Biomaterials)
f.funding_coi: Study materials provided by Geistlich Biomaterials; no conflict of interest declared

f.population: 72 titanium SLA implants placed 5 mm supracrestally in porcine ribs
f.intervention: Instrumentation with five decontamination protocols: metal scaler, PEEK scaler, round titanium brush, tufted titanium brush, glycine air-powder
f.comparison: Untreated control implants
f.main_result: Metal scaler damaged the surface, PEEK left plastic remnants, titanium brushes flattened threads and glycine air-powder caused minimal change.
f.funding_coi: Korean government research grants (KHIDI); no conflict of interest

f.population: 96 implants coated with ink in 3D-printed resin blocks simulating Ib, Ic and Ie peri-implant defects
f.intervention: Mechanical decontamination with air-polishing (glycine), rotating titanium brush, PEEK ultrasonic tip, stainless steel ultrasonic tip
f.comparison: Devices compared with each other (no untreated control)
outcomes: area of remnant ink on implant surface
f.main_result: Air-polishing with glycine and titanium brushes cleaned better than ultrasonic devices in all three defect configurations, though none removed all ink.
materials_brands: Air-Flow system with Perio Prophylaxis Powder (EMS)
f.funding_coi: Self-funded by the ETEP Research Group; no conflict of interest

f.population: Animals (ligature-induced peri-implantitis) and patients with dental implants; 7605 patients with 26,188 implants in clinical studies
f.intervention: Implants with different surface characteristics and/or materials
f.comparison: Modified versus non-modified implant surfaces
f.main_result: Modified surfaces showed greater bone loss in preclinical dog models, but clinical studies showed no difference in peri-implantitis incidence among implant surfaces.
f.sample_size: 18 preclinical experiments (25 publications) and 31 clinical publications with 7605 patients
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no relevant conflict of interest
f.limitations: Little information available on the impact of implant material.

f.population: Ten long-term clinical studies of three modern implant brands with moderately rough surfaces
f.intervention: Modern moderately rough oral implants
f.comparison: Older machined implants
f.main_result: Implants with peri-implant infection and bone loss leading to removal or surgery averaged 2.7% over 7 to 16 years; peri-implantitis plus failure is commonly below 5% over 10 years.
f.funding_coi: Consensus meeting sponsored by five major implant suppliers

f.main_result: CP titanium acts as a foreign body in live tissue, marginal bone loss may have immunological causes, and titanium allergy may exist only in rare cases.
f.limitations: Lack of universally accepted, tested patch tests makes titanium allergy diagnosis difficult; no universal definition of marginal bone loss prevented a systematic review.

f.main_result: Peri-implantitis-type marginal bone loss occurs in 1-2% of implants at 10+ years with trained clinicians and controlled systems; later bone loss mostly reflects treatment complications and foreign-body/immunological reactions, not infection.
Marginal bone loss around oral implants is attributed to a dis-balanced foreign body response, not a periodontitis-like infectious disease.
f.funding_coi: Supported economically by the Sylván Foundation

f.main_result: Osseointegration is redefined as a foreign body reaction in which interfacial bone forms as a defense reaction to shield the implant from the tissues.

A step-by-step decision process chooses among coronally advanced flap, CAF plus connective tissue graft and modified coronally advanced tunnel, based on non-carious cervical lesions, interdental attachment loss, buccal root displacement, then keratinized tissue and gingival thickness.
f.limitations: Few studies assess esthetic outcome beyond complete root coverage or compare techniques on esthetic outcome.

f.main_result: Saliva has roles in lubrication, buffering, mineralization, wound healing, taste and immune responses, and is a developing diagnostic fluid including for SARS-CoV-2.
f.funding_coi: NIDCR/NIH training program and grants

f.main_result: Intracrevicular margins do not cause periodontal disease; inflammation and bone loss occur only with large overhangs, and finish line design does not change periodontal response.

f.population: 7 adult monkeys with retained mandibular root tips
f.intervention: Self-tapping screw-type titanium implants placed in contact with retained root tips
f.comparison: Control implants placed in bone free of retained roots
f.main_result: Where implants contacted retained root tips, newly formed cementum covered the implant surface and a ligament-like space formed (8 of 14 test implants had root contact); controls were osseointegrated.
f.funding_coi: Astra Meditec and a Danish research foundation grant

f.population: 3 mongrel dogs, edentulous mandibular premolar regions
f.intervention: Titanium implants coated with cultured autologous periodontal ligament cells, placed with a void and covered by a membrane
f.main_result: Cementum-like tissue with a periodontal ligament-like layer and inserting collagen fibers formed on 37% of evaluated implant surfaces; no direct bone-to-implant contact.
materials_brands: Straumann commercially pure titanium screw implant, 8 mm x 4.1 mm
f.funding_coi: Korea Science and Engineering Foundation grant

f.population: Monkey mandibles with retained apical root portions
f.intervention: Plasma-sprayed titanium hollow-cylinder implants placed in close contact with retained roots
f.comparison: Implants without contact to retained roots
outcomes: cementum formation with inserting collagen fibers
f.main_result: Implants placed against retained roots showed cementum with inserting collagen fibers (a true periodontal ligament); implants without root contact osseointegrated.
f.funding_coi: ITI Foundation

f.population: 5 adult monkeys (Macaca cynomolgus) without periodontal destruction
f.intervention: Bodily labial movement of the central incisors and distal movement of first premolars with fixed orthodontic appliances for 3-4 months, into areas of varying keratinized gingiva width
f.comparison: Non-moved lateral incisors and first molars as controls; premolars moved into keratinized gingiva vs alveolar mucosa
f.main_result: About half of labially moved incisors showed small apical gingival margin displacement unrelated to initial keratinized gingiva width; attachment loss at premolars did not differ significantly between keratinized gingiva and alveolar mucosa sites.
f.follow_up: 3-4 months of orthodontic force plus 1 month retention

f.population: Low-income individuals with periodontitis (review)
f.intervention: Proposed low-cost therapy: mechanical pocket debridement, pocket irrigation with antiseptics (povidone-iodine, dilute sodium hypochlorite), systemic antibiotics for advanced disease, and self-care
f.main_result: The author proposes that povidone-iodine and dilute sodium hypochlorite could be first-choice antiseptics in an inexpensive multifaceted periodontal therapy, while noting that studies on cost-effectiveness and long-term outcome are still needed.
f.limitations: Most models for prevention and treatment have not been tested or compared in controlled studies; studies are needed to identify the most cost-effective method and long-term outcome.

f.population: Literature on patients with periodontitis and Alzheimer's disease / dementia (review)
outcomes: association between periodontal disease and Alzheimer's disease
f.main_result: Current clinical evidence shows an association, probably bidirectional, between periodontitis and Alzheimer's disease; causality is not established.
f.funding_coi: Research grants from the Osteology Foundation and the Alzheimer Society of Canada; no conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: A causal relationship between periodontal disease and Alzheimer's disease has yet to be established.

f.population: Patients undergoing implant treatment planning and follow-up (review)
f.intervention: Cone beam computed tomography imaging in implant dentistry
f.comparison: Conventional two-dimensional radiography and medical CT
f.main_result: CBCT is an adjunctive diagnostic modality, recommended mainly when clinical examination and conventional 2D radiography cannot supply satisfactory information, and it may be primary in selected implant cases; radiation dose optimisation (ALADA) is central.

f.population: Dental implants and implant patients in the long-term literature (review)
f.intervention: Implant surface topography (machined vs moderately rough) and patient factors in relation to peri-implant bone loss
f.main_result: Moderately rough implant surfaces give better survival than first-generation implants, but a systematic evaluation of the effect of topography on peri-implant bone loss is lacking.

f.population: Fully and partially edentulous patients treated with osseointegrated implants (historical review)
f.intervention: Osseointegrated dental implants over 50 years of development
f.main_result: Modern implant therapy gives excellent long-term results with success and survival rates above 95% in numerous 10-year studies.

f.population: Zirconia dental implants in the literature (review)
f.intervention: Zirconia (3Y-TZP) dental implants as an alternative to titanium
f.comparison: Titanium implants
f.main_result: Zirconia is a valuable alternative to titanium biologically, but early failure rates of tested zirconia systems were generally higher than titanium and long-term data are scarce.
f.funding_coi: Authors' clinical studies on titanium (Straumann) and zirconia (Dentalpoint) implants were supported by the respective manufacturers
f.limitations: Solid data on long-term outcomes of zirconia implants are scarce.

f.population: Dental implants and peri-implant tissues in the literature (review)
f.intervention: Periodontal diagnostic tools (probing pocket depth, bleeding on probing, radiography) applied to implants
f.main_result: Probing pocket depth and bleeding on probing are not reliable for monitoring peri-implant health and disease and lead to over-diagnosis; radiographic evaluation of crestal bone level over time is the most reliable tool.

f.population: Fixed implant prosthodontics workflows (review)
f.intervention: Digital technologies (scanning, CAD/CAM, milling, additive manufacturing, digital design of supra-implant mucosa architecture) in fixed implant prosthodontics
f.comparison: Conventional impression and gypsum cast workflow
f.main_result: Fully digital protocols for single-unit monolithic implant crowns on prefabricated titanium abutments should be considered in place of conventional manufacturing, but a complete digital approach for implant-supported fixed prostheses is not yet scientifically investigated and cannot be recommended for routine use.
f.limitations: Most digital systems were developed as closed processes, so results from one workflow may not transfer to others; further validation is needed.

f.population: Patients with inadequate bone height in the posterior maxilla (review)
f.intervention: Lateral and transcrestal sinus floor elevation, with or without grafting materials, with simultaneous or staged implant placement
f.main_result: Technique selection is based on residual bone height: transcrestal for single gaps with at least 5 mm, lateral with simultaneous implants for 3 mm or more, and lateral with staged grafting when under 3 mm.
Implant survival is not affected by placement or loading protocols given careful assessment and planning; evidence is of varying quality.
f.limitations: The literature is of varying quality, making strong evidence-based recommendations difficult.

f.main_result: Implant therapy in elderly patients is routine; morbidity is best minimized by avoiding augmentation through short and narrow-diameter implants and flapless surgery.
Data on covering peri-implant mucosal recessions are very limited; only shallow recessions (up to 2 mm) can be treated successfully with CAF plus subepithelial connective tissue graft or GBR.
f.limitations: Literature is scarce, limited to animal studies and case series of shallow recessions.

f.main_result: Pooled 5-year survival was 96.03% for cemented and 95.55% for screw-retained reconstructions (P = 0.686), but complications were significantly higher with cemented prostheses.

f.population: 52 implant sites in 38 patients with severe horizontal bone atrophy
f.intervention: Staged lateral ridge augmentation with autogenous block grafts protected by DBBM particles and collagen membranes, followed by implant placement
f.main_result: Ten-year implant success was 98.1% with minimal block graft resorption of 7.7%; chin grafts kept better than retromolar grafts.
f.sample_size: 38 patients with 52 implants examined at 10 years
f.funding_coi: Grant from the FDR Foundation, Basel; no conflicts of interest declared

f.population: 42 patients with severe horizontal bone atrophy
f.intervention: Staged horizontal ridge augmentation with autogenous block grafts covered with ABBM and a bioabsorbable collagen membrane
f.main_result: Mean crest width rose from 3.06 mm to 7.66 mm at re-entry (gain 4.6 mm) with only 0.36 mm surface resorption.

f.population: 28 subjects with maxillary incisors, canines and premolars scheduled for extraction
f.intervention: Bio-Oss Collagen placed in the fresh extraction socket, covered with a palatal soft tissue graft
f.comparison: Control sockets with no grafting
f.main_result: Cross-sectional ridge area was reduced about 25% in controls and 3% in grafted sites after 4 months, though buccal and palatal wall height loss was not prevented.

Esthetic outcomes can be achieved at postextraction sites irrespective of implant timing, but immediate placement needs strict case selection and early placement (type 2) with GBR is the option of choice in most instances.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest identified among group members
f.limitations: Esthetic data came predominantly from case series, with few RCTs and cohort studies and a minority at low risk of bias.

f.population: 37 human studies of postextraction ridge preservation
f.intervention: Postextraction ridge preservation (grafts and/or membranes in the socket)
f.comparison: Ungrafted sockets healing by clot alone, where compared
f.main_result: Ridge preservation is effective in limiting horizontal and vertical ridge alterations, with no evidence that one technique is superior and none that it improves ability to place implants.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest reported; ITI consensus conference proceedings
f.limitations: Techniques, methodologies, durations and materials varied so much that direct comparison was difficult.

f.population: 22 ridges with horizontal alveolar deficiency (crest width <4 mm) and at least two adjacent missing teeth
f.intervention: Mandibular ramus bone block grafts plus DBBM granules at the periphery and over the graft, covered by two layers of collagen membrane
f.comparison: Mandibular bone block grafts alone
f.main_result: Mean graft resorption was significantly lower with DBBM and collagen membrane (0.25 mm) than with block grafts alone (0.89 mm), but complications were more frequent in the test group.

f.population: Humans older than 18 years in good general health with at least one tooth to be extracted
f.intervention: Socket/ridge preservation after extraction (grafts, membranes, growth factors, flapless or flapped surgery)
f.comparison: Spontaneous healing of the socket without filling
f.main_result: Socket preservation gave significantly less ridge loss than spontaneous healing: bone height WMD 1.47 mm and width WMD 1.83 mm in favour of test groups, with a flapped approach favoured for width.
f.follow_up: At least 3 months after extraction (inclusion criterion)
f.limitations: The evidence gives no clear guidance on biomaterial or surgical procedure and no long-term implant outcome data

f.population: Zirconia-framework all-ceramic single crowns cemented on metal dies (in vitro)
f.intervention: Modified coping with 1 mm lingual margin, proximal strut and facial collar
f.comparison: Standard coping with 0.5 mm uniform thickness
f.main_result: Final fracture resistance was 3519 N (standard) vs 3570 N (modified), not significantly different (P=0.9).

f.intervention: Framework design rules for metal-ceramic crowns and bridges (connectors, CTE matching, heat resistance, preparation)
BEGO workflow for casting and ceramic veneering of non-precious alloy crowns and bridges

f.population: Literature on complete coverage tooth preparations
f.intervention: Complete coverage tooth preparation guidelines
f.main_result: Preparations should have 10-20 degrees total occlusal convergence, at least 4 mm occlusocervical height for molars and 3 mm for other teeth, and a ratio of 0.4 or greater.
f.sample_size: Literature of the last 50 years via MEDLINE and manual search

f.population: Hard and soft tissues surrounding osseointegrated dental implants
f.main_result: Keratinized mucosa width, mucosal thickness, supracrestal tissue height and buccal bone are linked to implant esthetics and health; respecting them can prevent esthetic complications.

f.population: Adults with tooth- or implant-supported fixed prostheses
f.intervention: Surgical soft tissue phenotype modification therapy (PhMT-s)
f.comparison: No surgical augmentation
f.main_result: Peri-implant soft tissue thickening reduced mucosal recession (WMD 0.36 mm, P=0.003); no controlled studies on tooth sites were found.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no conflicts of interest

f.main_result: Dental photography is a simple, available tool that can transform a practice and is needed for predictable esthetic dentistry.
f.funding_coi: No disclosures

f.intervention: Standardised 24-view photographic documentation for AACD accreditation

f.population: Beagle dogs, implants in fresh distal premolar sockets
f.intervention: Immediate placement of four different implant systems
f.main_result: No significant differences among the four implant systems; BIC 58.5-72.1% and buccal plate resorption about 2.5 mm.
f.funding_coi: Partly sponsored by Thommen Medical; no conflicts declared

f.population: Six male Doberman dogs, implants placed in the proximal tibia
f.intervention: Short-pitch, large-pitch (Intra-Lock MILO) and plateau (Bicon Integra-Ti) implant root shapes placed in tibia for 2 and 4 weeks
f.comparison: Comparison among the three implant designs and between 2 and 4 weeks
f.main_result: No significant difference in BIC among implant designs at 2 or 4 weeks (p > .75), although healing patterns differed with healing chambers
f.sample_size: 36 implants (12 per design; 6 per design per time point) in 6 dogs

f.population: Ten crossbred sheep, implants placed in the iliac crest (low-density bone)
f.intervention: Narrow-pitch (0.5 mm) implants tested for osseointegration after 0 days, 4 and 8 weeks
f.comparison: Wide-pitch implants (1.7 mm pitch)
f.main_result: Narrow-pitch implants gave higher BIC and primary stability from placement and better early bone formation than wide-pitch implants in low-density bone
f.sample_size: Ten sheep, three implants of each design per iliac crest (n = 5 per group)
materials_brands: Or-Vit narrow- and wide-pitch titanium implants
f.funding_coi: Grant from the Italian Ministry of Education (PRIN 2007); implants provided by Or-Vit

f.population: 12 female white New Zealand rabbits, implants placed in the tibiae
f.intervention: Square thread design implants (3.25 x 7 mm, custom-made titanium)
f.comparison: V-shaped and reverse buttress thread designs
f.main_result: Square-thread implants had significantly higher BIC (74.37%) than V-thread (65.46%) and reverse buttress (63.05%) and greater reverse torque, with no radiographic density differences
f.sample_size: 72 implants in 12 rabbits (24 per thread design)
materials_brands: BioHorizons custom-made titanium implants with RBM surface
f.funding_coi: University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund, BioHorizons research grant, and ICOI award
f.limitations: Further longitudinal investigation of bone changes after loading is required

f.population: Patients (1098) receiving 2310 implants in 25 included studies (17 RCTs, 8 prospective)
f.intervention: Platform-switching (PSW) implants
f.comparison: Regular platform (RP) implants
f.main_result: PSW implants had 0.41 mm less crestal bone loss than regular platform implants, with no significant difference in implant failure (RR 1.10)
f.funding_coi: Research Foundation of the State of São Paulo (FAPESP); no competing interests
f.limitations: RCTs should be done to explain the possible biases

f.population: 31 patients receiving implants in the posterior maxilla
f.intervention: Platform-switched implants with 4.3, 4.8 and 5.5 mm platforms restored with a 3.8 mm abutment
f.comparison: 3.8 mm platform control implants with no mismatching
f.main_result: Mean bone loss was 0.99, 0.82 and 0.56 mm in the test groups vs 1.49 mm in controls (P<0.005), with an inverse correlation between mismatching and bone loss
f.sample_size: 80 implants in 31 patients (69 implants analysed at 21 months)

f.population: 68 patients missing at least two teeth in the posterior mandible (single-crown implants)
f.intervention: Platform switched abutments on implants supporting single crowns
f.comparison: Platform matched abutments
outcomes: plaque index, sulcus bleeding and probing depth
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone level change from surgery to 12 months favoured platform switching (-0.40 vs -0.69 mm, p=0.004); success 97.3% vs 100%
f.sample_size: 68 patients, 146 implants (74 platform switch, 72 platform match)
f.funding_coi: Unrestricted grant of the Camlog Foundation; two authors are Camlog Foundation Board members

f.population: 23 individuals with bilaterally missing mandibular first or second molars
f.intervention: Platform-switched implants placed 2 mm below the alveolar crest (subcrestal)
f.comparison: Platform-switched implants placed at bone level (crestal)
f.main_result: At 36 months crestal bone loss was 0.45 mm (crestal) vs 0.3 mm (subcrestal) with no significant intra- or intergroup differences in BOP, PD or CBL
materials_brands: Straumann regular crossfit connection implants (4.1 mm diameter)
f.funding_coi: Funded by Deanship of Scientific Research, King Saud University (PRG-1437-38); no conflict of interest

f.population: 100 partially edentulous subjects (posterior region), 54 men and 46 women
f.intervention: Bone-level implants restored with platform switching (test)
f.comparison: Tissue-level implants restored with platform matching (control)
outcomes: marginal bone level change on periapical radiographs
f.main_result: Platform-switched bone-level implants lost less marginal bone: MBL change 0.61 mm (tissue-level, matching) vs -0.20 mm (bone-level, switching) baseline to 5 years, P < .001
f.funding_coi: Authors reported no conflicts of interest

f.population: 141 subjects needing single anterior maxillary or first premolar tooth replacement
f.intervention: Single implants with conical interface (OsseoSpeed TX), immediately provisionalized
f.comparison: Flat-to-flat (NobelSpeedy) and platform-switched (NanoTite Certain PREVAIL) interfaces
outcomes: plaque index and bleeding on probing
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss at 5 years was -0.16 mm (conical), -0.92 mm (flat-to-flat) and -0.81 mm (platform-switched) (P<.0005); mucosal changes were minimal in all groups.
f.funding_coi: First author receives research grants and honorarium from Dentsply Implants

f.population: 14 patients with clinically healthy peri-implant soft tissue, 37 samples
f.intervention: Platform-switching implant restorations with 0.25-0.85 mm mismatch (test groups)
f.comparison: Traditionally restored (platform-matching) implants (control group)
f.main_result: No significant differences between switching and traditional platform implants in inflamed connective tissue area, microvascular density or collagen content at 48 months
f.sample_size: 37 peri-implant soft tissue samples from 14 patients
f.funding_coi: Self-funded by the authors and their institution; no conflict of interests

f.population: One 32-year-old partially edentulous male patient with bilateral posterior mandibular restoration
f.intervention: Immediately loaded implants with platform-switched abutment, one 3i implant retrieved by trephine after 6 weeks for histology
f.main_result: Histology of the retrieved platform-switched implant showed 1 mm crestal resorption on one side and none on the other, with BIC 65.1 ± 6.3%
f.funding_coi: Partially supported by the Italian Ministry of Education, University, Research (MIUR)

f.population: 2D finite element model of an osseointegrated implant in posterior mandible
f.intervention: Microthread implant neck with abutment diameters 4.0, 4.5 and 5.0 mm (platform switching)
f.comparison: Smooth-neck implant and 5.0 mm standard abutment
outcomes: von Mises crestal bone stress under vertical and oblique 100 N load
f.main_result: Microthread model had 29% greater crestal stress than smooth-neck (31.61 vs 24.51 MPa oblique; 9.31 vs 7.20 MPa vertical); narrower abutments reduced stress.
f.funding_coi: Partly supported by University of Michigan student research funds; software provided by Cranes Software, whose business development head is a coauthor; authors report no conflicts.

f.population: 22 implants (in vitro, E. coli leakage model)
f.intervention: Zimmer Tapered Screw-Vent with slip-joint connection, abutments torqued to 30 Ncm
f.comparison: Argon Konus K3pro with conical connection
outcomes: bacterial leakage (E. coli colony counts) at 6, 24, 48, 72 h, 7 and 14 days
f.main_result: Type of connection significantly affected bacterial leakage (P<0.001); leakage did not change significantly over time.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared

f.population: 45 patients receiving 131 implants
f.intervention: Platform-switched implants (4.8 mm platform, 4 mm body) with a healing abutment 1 mm narrower than the platform
f.comparison: Standard implants with healing abutment of same diameter as platform
outcomes: vertical crestal bone loss on periapical radiographs
f.main_result: Mean bone loss 0.95 mm for platform-switched vs 1.67 mm for control implants after 12 months of loading (P = .001).
f.limitations: Histologic evaluation and longer follow-up are needed to confirm results.

f.intervention: Review of implant-abutment connection designs (external hex, internal hex, Morse taper, cone screw, platform switch)
f.main_result: No evidence points to a single best connection type; external hex suits multiunit, internal hex and Morse cone favour single units and esthetic regions.

f.population: Three 3D finite element models of an external-hex implant with bone and single crown
f.intervention: Platform switching: 5.0 mm implant with 4.1 mm UCLA abutment, 100 N axial or oblique load
f.comparison: Regular platform (4.1/4.1 mm) and wide platform (5.0/5.0 mm) models
outcomes: von Mises, maximum and minimum principal stress in bone, implant, screw and prosthesis
f.main_result: Platform switching reduced von Mises stress in peri-implant bone by 17.5% (axial) and 9.3% (oblique).
f.limitations: Stress was influenced more by implant diameter than by platform switching; platform switching did not improve screw behaviour.

f.population: Five hound-type dogs; 12 implants per dog in the mandible
f.intervention: Bone-level implants with 3.3 mm abutment on 4.1 mm implant (horizontal offset, Morse taper connection) placed even with, 1 mm above or 1 mm below the crest, submerged or non-submerged, with gold crowns
f.comparison: Placement level (crest, 1 mm above, 1 mm below) and submerged versus non-submerged healing
f.main_result: Bone change for submerged implants even with, 1 mm below and 1 mm above the crest was -0.34, -1.29 and 0.04 mm; non-submerged -0.38, -1.13 and 0.19 mm.
f.funding_coi: Supported by Institute Straumann; two authors are Straumann employees

f.population: 2D and 3D finite element models of a mandible with a commercial implant (Frialit-2)
f.intervention: Topological shape optimization (soft kill option) giving tapered implant necks with larger crestal radius
f.comparison: Commercially available implant (3.8 mm, no taper)
outcomes: peak von Mises stress in bone at implant neck under axial and oblique load
f.main_result: Tapered optimized implants cut peak neck stress by 62-77% (2D, 30-45 degree taper) and 3D peak stress from 27.8 to 11.3 MPa axial and 54.0 to 22.4 MPa oblique.

Crestal bone loss is multifactorial and tied to crest module design and connection; a rocket-shaped sloping-shoulder module is proposed as ideal and long-term crestal bone preservation makes short implants predictable.

f.population: 80 patients, lower molar area, thin (<=2 mm) or thick (>2 mm) mucosa
f.intervention: Bone-level platform-switched implants (4.1 mm, Straumann) placed one-stage in thin soft tissue
f.comparison: Same implants placed in thick soft tissue (>2 mm)
outcomes: crestal bone loss on radiographs at 2 months, restoration and 1 year
f.main_result: Crestal bone loss was 1.17 mm in thin tissue versus 0.21 mm in thick tissue at 1 year (p < .001).
materials_brands: Straumann Bone Level 4.1 mm platform-switched implant

f.population: 12 Göttingen minipigs, 96 implants in the mandible
f.intervention: Three bone-level implants (Astra Tech Osseospeed, Straumann Bone Level, NobelReplace Tapered Groovy) placed at crest level or 1 mm above, submerged healing
f.comparison: Straumann Tissue Level implant as control
outcomes: histologic and radiographic crestal bone levels
f.main_result: At crest-level placement, Astra Osseospeed and Straumann Bone Level preserved more crestal bone than NobelReplace Tapered Groovy at 12 weeks (P < 0.01).
materials_brands: Straumann Tissue Level Implant SP RN

f.population: Fifteen clinical studies of platform-switched vs non-platform-switched implants (8-80 patients, 50-360 implants per study)
f.intervention: Platform-switched implants (narrower abutment on wider implant platform)
f.comparison: Non-platform-switched implants with matching abutment and implant diameters
f.main_result: Seven of 15 studies found PS did not reduce crestal bone loss versus NPS; implant positioning, ridge width and micromotion control matter more.
f.sample_size: 15 clinical studies; 8-80 patients and 50-360 implants each
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest and no external funding
f.limitations: Most included studies did not address ridge width, and some measured bone on panoramic radiographs, possibly imprecisely.

f.population: Ten controlled trials, 1,239 implants, platform-switched vs platform-matched
f.intervention: Platform-switched implants
f.main_result: Marginal bone loss was significantly less around platform-switched implants (MD -0.37 mm); no difference in implant failure (RR 0.93).
f.follow_up: mean follow-up of at least 12 months required for inclusion
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Authors call for further long-term, well-conducted randomized controlled studies.

f.population: 35 patients with 67 bone-level implants in premolar areas
f.intervention: Bone-level implants restored with platform switching, single metal-ceramic crowns
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone change was -0.28 mm from baseline to 5 years; papilla-to-contact distance fell from 2.08 to 1.31 mm; buccal margin unchanged.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: 20 dental implants (BioHorizons) in two groups of 10
f.intervention: Internal hexagonal vs tri-lobe internal implant-abutment connection, challenged with S. aureus for 14 days
f.comparison: Internal hexagon vs tri-lobe connection against each other
f.main_result: Internal hexagon implants showed significantly higher mean log CFU than tri-lobe implants (P<0.001).

f.population: 80 partially edentulous patients with missing posterior teeth
f.intervention: 8.5 mm platform-switched implants (Certain Prevail)
f.comparison: Platform-matched implants (XP Certain)
f.main_result: At 5 years interproximal bone loss was 0.38 mm (test) vs 0.41 mm (control), p=0.201, no progression since year 1.
f.funding_coi: Unrestricted grant from Biomet 3i; no conflicts declared

f.intervention: Working instructions for VITA In-Ceram YZ and VITA YZ HT presintered zirconia: design, milling, coloring, sintering, finishing, veneering, bonding
Flat (F) and step (S) pontic designs for ridges previously reconstructed periodontally
f.main_result: F and S pontics contact the mucosa broadly without excessive pressure, easing cleaning and supporting a natural emergence profile in reconstructed ridges.
f.limitations: Needs prior surgical augmentation; S pontic fabrication is more time consuming than ovate.

f.population: 65 patients with 383 implants supporting 81 zirconia-based fixed prostheses; 219 pontic sites measured
f.intervention: Zirconia implant-supported restoration with a modified ovate pontic (biologic pontic designed interface)
outcomes: alveolar ridge mucosa thickness under pontic
f.main_result: Mean mucosal thickness under the pontic was 2.32 mm in the maxilla and 2.20 mm in the mandible, with 98.7% implant survival at 3 years.

f.population: In vitro studies of bond strength between layering materials and zirconia frameworks
f.intervention: Layering porcelain or indirect composite applied to zirconia frameworks
f.comparison: Metal-ceramic systems as reference in some studies
f.main_result: Available data give considerable information on stable layering, but few in vitro studies exist on indirect composite bonding to zirconia.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Few in vitro studies on indirect composite-zirconia bond strength; more controlled clinical trials needed.

f.intervention: Newer-generation metal-ceramic porcelains with fine leucite crystals and high-gold alloys such as Captek
f.comparison: Conventional metal-ceramic alloys and porcelains

f.intervention: Stepwise grinding of ceramic to mimic natural morphology (transition ridges, thirds, grooves) and gold-powder marking to copy surface texture
f.main_result: Labial transition ridges determine visual width and general morphology, and gold powder helps identify and mimic surface texture.

f.population: 12 porcelain-fused-to-metal central incisor crowns rated by 18 evaluators (prosthodontists, general dentists, students)
f.intervention: Air abrasion and diamond-paste polishing of the glazed porcelain surface
f.comparison: Retained autoglazed (reglazed) surface
f.main_result: In phase 1 polished crowns rated higher than glazed for outline sharpness, reflectance and general esthetics (p<.01), with differences largely reversing in phase 2.

f.population: 42-year-old woman needing a lower right second premolar and first molar restoration
f.intervention: Monolithic ZLS crown and partial crown via complete digital workflow (intraoral scan, printed model, CAD/CAM)
f.main_result: Two weeks after cementation the patient had no postoperative sensitivity, healthy tissues and good shade adaptation.
f.limitations: Clinical study data on ZLS ceramics are still missing.

f.main_result: Clinical data for all-ceramic systems are increasingly available to guide indications, and fracture toughness is a more inherent measure than strength rating.

A trend to monolithic restorations avoids chipping and delamination seen with more esthetic multilayered restorations, and CAD-CAM composites offer intermediate properties that are easier to mill and polish.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no commercial or associative conflict of interest

f.population: Bar-shaped specimens cut from 4 CAD/CAM blocks
f.intervention: 3-point bending test (ISO 6872) for flexural strength and modulus
f.comparison: Two glass-ceramics vs two nanoceramic resin composites, before and after firing
f.main_result: IPS e.max CAD (crystallized) had the highest flexural strength (334.1 MPa) and modulus (44.8 GPa); Vita Enamic had lowest FS (124 MPa) and Lava Ultimate lowest FM (9.75 GPa).
f.limitations: Authors note flexural tests have limitations and do not reproduce complex intraoral stresses.

f.population: Lithium disilicate glass samples melted at 1400 C, annealed and nucleated
f.intervention: Crystallization under an imposed temperature gradient
f.main_result: Imposing a temperature gradient during crystallization produced a lithium disilicate microstructure-graded glass-ceramic with crystallinity gradients dependent on processing, with cracking in the glassy region.
f.limitations: Microhardness variability was too great to draw conclusions.

f.population: Lithium disilicate (LS2) glass samples
f.intervention: Variable frequency microwave (VFM) crystallization
f.comparison: Conventional heating
f.main_result: VFM crystallized lithium disilicate glass in significantly shorter time and at lower temperature than conventional heating, with a slightly different mechanism.
f.funding_coi: Egyptian government scholarship program

f.population: LZS and LZSA glass-ceramic specimens and human fetal osteoblasts
f.intervention: Lithium-zirconium silicate glass-ceramics produced by melting, milling, pressing and sintering
f.comparison: LZS vs LZSA (alumina-containing) and polystyrene control
