f.main_result: Median mid-facial mucosal margin change was -0.02, -0.13 and -0.14 mm in collagen matrix, palatal graft and control groups, with no significant differences.
f.sample_size: 75 patients randomized, 70 re-examined at one year
f.funding_coi: Implants provided by Straumann AG and biomaterials by Geistlich Pharma AG; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: 8-week healing may be too short for graft consolidation; keratinized mucosa width not measured

f.population: 75 patients with single tooth extraction in the maxillary incisor/premolar area
f.intervention: Ridge preservation with xenogeneic bone substitute (DBBM-C) covered with collagen matrix or free palatal graft, then implant at 8 weeks
f.comparison: Spontaneous healing
outcomes: need for GBR at implant placement
f.main_result: Horizontal bone resorption was -0.9 mm (collagen matrix) and -1.0 mm (palatal graft) versus -3.2 mm in controls, and GBR was needed in 32%, 24% and 72%.
f.funding_coi: Implants by Straumann AG and biomaterials by Geistlich Pharma AG; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Buccal bone thickness and integrity were not calculated

f.population: Adult patients with extraction sites or edentulous areas needing implant rehabilitation
f.intervention: Biologics (autologous blood-derived products, EMD, rhBMP-2, rhPDGF-BB) in ridge preservation/reconstruction, ridge augmentation or sinus floor augmentation
f.comparison: Conventional modalities without biologics
f.main_result: Biologics did not give superior clinical or radiographic outcomes than conventional therapy, but histomorphometric results improved.
f.follow_up: Minimum 2 months for ridge preservation, 4 months for sinus and ridge augmentation
f.funding_coi: Consensus meeting sponsored by BioHorizons, Geistlich, Lynch Biologics and Straumann; authors declare no conflicts
f.limitations: High heterogeneity prevented quantitative analysis

f.main_result: Alveolar ridge preservation is not indicated when an implant can be placed within 0-2 months of extraction; otherwise it should be considered.
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Clinic of Fixed and Removable Prosthodontics, University of Zurich

f.population: 36 patients with 40 extraction sockets
f.intervention: Socket grafting with a 1:1 mixture of biphasic calcium phosphate (4BONE) and calcium sulphate (BOND BONE)
f.comparison: Ungrafted sockets left to heal naturally
outcomes: horizontal ridge width at 0, 3 and 6 mm
f.main_result: At 3 mm below the crest, control sites lost 2.28 mm of ridge width versus 0.03 mm gained in the test group (p=.007).
f.funding_coi: Partly supported by an educational grant from MIS implants technology

f.population: Patients who have received a ridge preservation procedure
f.intervention: Minimally invasive ridge preservation approaches, with or without immediate implant placement
f.comparison: Other ridge preservation procedures
f.main_result: Limited studies and methodological discrepancies made it impossible to confirm a significant benefit of minimally invasive approaches in ridge preservation.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Very few RCTs reported the same outcomes and pre-extraction site dimensions were not reported

f.population: Lower incisor sockets of 120-day-old male rabbits
f.intervention: Standardized 5 mm buccal plate defect created in one socket
f.comparison: Contralateral socket with intact buccal bone wall
f.main_result: Sockets with buccal plate loss had reduced width compared with intact sockets, and the difference decreased with time.

f.population: Patients planned for tooth extraction with subsequent grafting and/or membrane procedure
f.intervention: Graft and/or membrane placement after tooth extraction
f.comparison: Control sites with no intervention
outcomes: clinical ridge width and height change
f.main_result: Socket interventions reduced ridge dimensional change but could not prevent resorption (control width loss 2.46-4.56 mm vs 1.14-2.5 mm in test sites)
f.limitations: Limited data on effectiveness of ridge preservation compared with control

f.population: Patients scheduled for single tooth extraction and implant restoration (27 subjects, 28 extraction sites)
f.intervention: Socket filled with collagen-enriched deproteinized bovine bone mineral and covered with collagen membrane
f.comparison: Blood clot with collagen membrane only
f.main_result: Total volume reduction after 6 months was 21.3% with grafting vs 20.0% without (NS); grafting helped only at sites with thin (≤1 mm) buccal bone wall
f.funding_coi: Materials provided by Geistlich Pharma and Dentsply Sirona
f.limitations: Hard and soft tissue changes were not evaluated separately

f.population: Healthy humans with fresh extraction sockets
f.intervention: Alveolar ridge preservation: socket grafting with bone substitute, GBR with membranes or soft tissue graft, or bioactive materials
f.comparison: Unassisted socket healing
f.main_result: ARP reduced resorption versus unassisted healing by about 1.31-1.54 mm in width and 0.91-1.12 mm in height
f.funding_coi: No conflicts declared by authors
f.limitations: Limited data prevented reliable histological conclusions or a recommendation of a specific technique

f.intervention: Pontic-shield: modified socket-shield (partial extraction) to develop pontic sites
f.main_result: The pontic-shield technique can successfully develop pontic sites and preserve the ridge (14 sites, 10 patients)
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: Two patients with late failure of implants near retained root fragments
f.main_result: Both late implant failures (4 and 10 years) were associated with retained root fragments in close contact with the implant and bacterial infiltration
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Limited case reports and no prospective analyses exist

f.population: Single-rooted teeth
f.intervention: Socket-shield technique at immediate implant placement with provisionalization
f.main_result: Outlines an up-to-date step-by-step partial extraction therapy protocol for socket-shield with immediate implant placement

f.population: 10 consecutive patients with a single maxillary anterior implant replacement (first premolar to first premolar)
f.intervention: Immediate implant placement with the socket shield technique (buccal root portion retained)
f.main_result: Volumetric analysis showed low facial contour change (mean oro-facial tissue loss 0.33 mm), mean marginal bone loss 0.33/0.17 mm and mean PES 12 at about 5 years
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Descriptive retrospective study; technique should not be used routinely until prospective trials are available

f.population: One 68-year-old patient with an immediate implant in the anterior maxilla, retrieved after five years
f.intervention: Immediate implant placement with the root membrane technique
outcomes: tissue in gap between root membrane and implant
f.main_result: Buccal bone plate was maintained without resorption with a healthy PDL; bone-to-implant contact 76.2% after five years
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: Further studies needed to confirm; role of graft in gap unclear

f.population: Three beagle dogs (premolar sites) plus one clinical case
f.intervention: Socket shield with buccal root segment separated vertically into two pieces, implant placed lingually
f.main_result: Shield segments showed healthy PDL and new bone between implant and shield; the clinical case lost 0.88 mm mean labial volume
f.funding_coi: Funded by Thommen Medical research grant; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Only three dogs, no control, no histomorphometry, short follow-up

f.population: Patients with anterior immediate implants placed with the root membrane technique in 3 private practices
f.intervention: Root membrane technique: periodontal ligament-mediated immediate implant placement
f.main_result: 5 failures in 250 implants; 10-year cumulative implant survival 96.5% and success 87.9%

f.population: 40 patients each needing one anterior tooth replaced after extraction
f.intervention: Socket shield technique with immediate post-extraction implant and immediate provisional crown
f.comparison: Conventional post-extraction implant with labial gap grafted with allograft
f.main_result: Survival 100% in both groups at 3 years; socket shield group had less marginal bone resorption (0.605 vs 1.115 at 3 years) and higher PAS (12.15 vs 10.3), P<0.05
f.funding_coi: Funded by the authors' own institutions; no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Low power of the evidence; larger sample and longer follow-up needed

f.population: 23 published studies on the socket-shield technique (1 case-control, 4 animal histological, 1 abstract, 17+2 case reports)
f.intervention: Socket-shield technique (intentional retention of a root section at immediate implant placement)
f.main_result: Complications in 58/70 (82.86%) animal-study implants and 33/136 (24.26%) clinical-study implants; buccal/crestal bone loss most common
f.sample_size: 23 studies; 70 animal implants and 136 clinical implants
f.follow_up: 18 of 23 studies lasted 12 months or less
f.funding_coi: No funding; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: No meta-analysis possible (heterogeneity, no RCTs); 4 of 5 quality-assessed studies scored low

f.population: Postextraction ridge sites (review; no study subjects)
f.intervention: Partial extraction therapies: root submergence, socket-shield, pontic shield, proximal socket-shield
f.main_result: Proposes PET as a collective term with a classification and indications; supporting literature is limited to case reports, case series and two animal histology reports
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Literature very poor (case reports, case series, animal histology); randomized and long-term data needed

f.population: 30 adults with nonrestorable single anterior teeth with intact buccal periodontal tissues
f.intervention: Modified socket shield technique (1.5 mm buccal root shield) with immediate implant and immediate single-crown restoration
f.main_result: 100% implant survival at 1 year, ISQ 72.9 at placement and 74.6 at 1 year, no biologic complications, prosthetic complications 2.5%
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported (text truncated); funding not stated
f.limitations: Limited follow-up time and no volumetric analysis

f.main_result: Letter argues the systematic review misapplied its own eligibility criteria: 4 of 23 studies were not socket-shield, 3 were misrepresented as adverse effects, so bone loss was overstated
f.funding_coi: No funding; three authors are paid to lecture on the socket-shield technique

f.population: One 45-year-old patient with a failing maxillary right central incisor adjacent to an implant crown
f.intervention: Proximal socket shield with immediate implant placement and provisionalization
f.main_result: At 1 year the interimplant papilla between the central incisors was well maintained with satisfactory esthetic results
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Single case, short-term (1 year) follow-up, technique-sensitive, limited long-term evidence

f.population: Evidence from three systematic reviews on biologics in periodontal plastic surgery, infrabony defects and ridge preservation/implant site development
f.intervention: Biologics: autologous blood-derived products, EMD, rhPDGF-BB, rhBMP-2
f.comparison: Conventional treatment approaches
outcomes: ridge preservation/reconstruction and implant site development
f.main_result: Appropriate use of biologics is generally safe and adds benefit to conventional treatment; benefit and risk vary by biologic and patient factors; evidence limited for gingival augmentation, ARP/ARR and ISD
f.funding_coi: Sponsored by BioHorizons, Geistlich, Lynch Biologics and Straumann; authors report advisor/lecture fees from industry
f.limitations: Limited clinical evidence for some indications (gingival augmentation, ARP/ARR, ISD)

f.population: 65 patients with a single implant site in a healed alveolar ridge with lingual-buccal sloped configuration
f.intervention: Implants with modified (sloped) marginal geometry placed with the slope at the buccal side
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss 0.57 mm over 3 years, CAL gain 0.11 mm, BoP with PPD >=5 mm at <10% of implants, no implant lost
f.sample_size: 65 patients enrolled; 57 patients with 57 implants at 3 years
f.funding_coi: Supported by grants from Dentsply Sirona Implants/Astra Tech; some authors report honoraria and grants from industry
f.limitations: Observational multicenter design without a well-defined control group

f.population: Patients with dental implants and keratinized peri-implant mucosa
f.intervention: Soft-tissue substitutes versus autogenous grafts to augment keratinized peri-implant mucosa; exposure KT <2 mm
f.comparison: KT >= 2 mm; autogenous grafts
f.main_result: Reduced KT width associated with biofilm, inflammation, discomfort, recession, bone loss and peri-implantitis; autogenous grafts are standard of care, xenogeneic substitutes similar to CTG
f.sample_size: Systematic review 1: 22 articles (21 studies); review 2: 11 articles (10 investigations)
f.funding_coi: Participants filed COI disclosures; industry funding, consultant and speaker fees declared
f.limitations: Grafting review studies had unclear or high risk of bias

f.population: 96 patients with 195 implants placed with simultaneous lateral GBR, at least 5 years after loading in a supportive periodontal therapy program
f.intervention: Lateral GBR at implant placement (DBBM and/or autogenous bone with resorbable or non-resorbable membrane)
f.comparison: Within-cohort predictors: resorbable vs non-resorbable membrane, implant diameter, soft tissue graft or not
f.main_result: 44% of implants showed recession (mean 0.6 mm); recession was linked to non-resorbable membrane and wider implants, soft tissue grafting predicted stability
f.follow_up: At least 5 years after loading; mean SPT 8.3 years
f.funding_coi: Funded by Geistlich Pharma AG
f.limitations: Retrospective analysis without formal sample size calculation

f.population: Adult (over 18 years) subjects needing one or more dental implants, in prospective controlled trials of transcrestal sinus floor elevation
f.intervention: Transcrestal sinus floor elevation, irrespective of technique, technology and timing
f.comparison: Any other transcrestal sinus floor elevation procedure differing in at least one technical element (e.g. grafting protocol)
outcomes: number of surgical sessions and chair time
f.main_result: Transcrestal sinus floor elevation is minimally invasive and effective; invasiveness can be reduced further without losing effectiveness by using powered instruments (drills, piezoelectric inserts, electrical mallet) instead of manual osteotome and hand mallet.
f.funding_coi: Supported entirely by the Research Centre for the Study of Periodontal and Peri-implant Diseases, University of Ferrara
f.limitations: Differences in design, outcome measures and observation interval prevented meta-analysis; the review was not registered.

f.population: Four illustrative patients with anterior (esthetic zone) implant sites, including a congenitally missing lateral incisor, a fractured central incisor, a resorbed incisor and an underdeveloped ridge
f.intervention: Site preservation and overbuilding (orthodontic eruption, bone and connective tissue grafting, punch uncovering) before implant restoration
f.main_result: Overbuilding the implant site with orthodontic, grafting and punch-uncovering techniques allowed the restorative clinician to mold an ideal gingival framework; no numeric outcomes reported.

f.population: Systemically healthy adults with at least one implant-supported fixed restoration
f.intervention: Thin peri-implant soft tissue (buccal thickness <2 mm or probe shimmering)
f.comparison: Thick peri-implant soft tissue (buccal thickness 2 mm or more)
f.main_result: Post-follow-up PES did not differ between thin and thick tissue (MD 0.15, p=.46), but PES change favoured thick tissue (p=.05) and thin tissue showed more recession (-0.62 mm); evidence quality was very low.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded by two University of Zurich clinics; authors declared no conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Evidence quality was very low because of non-randomized studies, high risk of bias and residual confounding.

f.population: Peri-implant soft tissues around osseointegrated implants (literature review)
f.main_result: Supracrestal soft tissues around implants show structures analogous to non-inflamed gingiva, but the connective tissue has a different, scar-like spatial orientation; keratinized mucosa is not a prerequisite for long-term implant maintenance.
f.limitations: Most studies have described structure only, with little data on the true biologic function of peri-implant soft tissues.

f.population: One patient with multiple retained maxillary roots and periodontally compromised mandibular teeth, treated with interim complete dentures
f.intervention: Cross-mounting buccal index (CMBI) made from the interim restoration for abutment selection and framework fabrication
f.main_result: The index lets the clinician use a duplicate of the interim restoration to select abutments and fabricate the framework without a new denture setup, reducing chairtime and laboratory time.
f.limitations: The method depends on a well-established provisional prosthesis and is contraindicated if the provisional has poor esthetics or function.

f.population: Periodontally compromised teeth with increased mobility
f.intervention: Splinting of mobile teeth to stronger adjacent teeth
f.main_result: Splinting is an essential adjunct to cause-related therapy that can prolong the life of periodontally compromised mobile teeth, but it does not remove the cause of mobility and mobility may return after splint removal.
f.limitations: Further research is required on the exact role of splints and on patient selection criteria.

f.population: 45 completely edentulous patients with poorly retained mandibular dentures (plus 2D finite element models)
f.intervention: Two mini-implants splinted with a prefabricated bar retaining a mandibular overdenture
f.comparison: Two single, non-splinted ball-type mini-implants
outcomes: bone stress by finite element analysis
f.main_result: At 24 months marginal bone loss was 1.43 mm (ball) vs 0.92 mm (bar), not significant (P=.116); FEA minimum principal stress was -118 MPa unsplinted vs -56.8 MPa splinted, and vertical bone loss was more prevalent in the ball group (51% vs 29%, P=.04).
f.funding_coi: Grant from CONICYT (Chile), FONDEF Project Di1109

f.population: 198 patients with posterior partially edentulous jaws (Kennedy Class I/II) and 453 short implants (10 mm or shorter)
f.intervention: Short implants supporting splinted posterior prostheses
f.comparison: Short implants supporting non-splinted (single crown) prostheses
f.main_result: Success was 97.7% for splinted vs 93.2% for non-splinted short implants, with similar marginal bone loss (1.22 vs 1.27 mm); non-splinted implants had higher failure risk in men and at 8.5 and 7 mm lengths.
f.funding_coi: Authors report no conflicts of interest

f.population: 30 completely edentulous participants with problems retaining mandibular dentures
f.intervention: Two splinted immediately loaded canine-region implants with bar attachment retaining a mandibular overdenture
f.comparison: Two nonsplinted immediately loaded implants with ball attachments
outcomes: vertical and horizontal circumferential bone loss on CBCT
f.main_result: After 3 years vertical bone loss was 1.36 mm (ball) vs 1.0 mm (bar) and horizontal 0.88 vs 0.77 mm, with significantly more vertical bone loss around nonsplinted implants (P<.001); survival 93.3% vs 100% (P=.156).
f.limitations: CBCT has higher radiation dose than conventional imaging and metal beam-hardening artefacts.

f.population: 18 patients (9 men, 9 women, aged 49-76) with at least two consecutive posterior implants bilaterally
f.intervention: Splinted prostheses on short internal-connection implants (one side)
f.comparison: Nonsplinted restorations on the contralateral side
f.main_result: Bone levels did not differ between splinted and nonsplinted implants longer than 6 mm; nonsplinted 6-mm implants gained bone at 24 and 36 months, and all screw loosening occurred on the nonsplinted side (5 of 15 patients).
f.sample_size: 82 implants in 18 patients (15 analyzed at 3 years)
f.funding_coi: Authors reported no conflicts of interest

f.population: Bone level and tissue level implants in 14 included controlled clinical trials
f.intervention: Apico-coronal implant position (supracrestal, equicrestal, subcrestal)
f.comparison: Equicrestal versus subcrestal versus supracrestal placement
f.main_result: For bone level implants, early CBL differed by 0.15 mm (P=.18) and late CBL by 0.03 mm between equi- and subcrestal placement; authors recommend tissue level implants equicrestally and bone level implants subcrestally.
f.sample_size: 14 articles included, 12 in the quantitative synthesis
f.funding_coi: University of Michigan Periodontal Graduate Student Research Fund

f.population: 200 partially or fully edentulous patients with 657 Ankylos implants placed 1-3 mm subcrestally
f.intervention: Examination of peri-implant health, mucositis and peri-implantitis around subcrestally placed implants
f.main_result: Prevalence of peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis was 66.5% and 15.0% at patient level (62.6% and 7.5% at implant level); peri-implantitis was associated with history of periodontitis (OR 5.33).
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared

f.population: Four patients; implants harvested en bloc with surrounding tissues
f.intervention: Implants with a Laser-Lok microchannel collar
f.main_result: There was connective tissue attachment to the Laser-Lok microchannels with no signs of inflammation.
f.funding_coi: Sponsored by a grant from BioHorizons

f.population: Canine model
f.intervention: Laser-ablated microgrooves (Laser-Lok) placed on the abutment
f.comparison: Traditional machined abutment surfaces
f.main_result: Laser-microgrooved abutments gave significantly improved peri-implant hard and soft tissue healing compared with machined abutments.
f.funding_coi: Sponsored by a grant from BioHorizons
f.limitations: Loss of 11 abutments reduced the number available and precluded quantitative analysis.

f.population: Two healthy partially edentulous adult patients
f.intervention: Healing abutments with a 0.7-mm Laser-Lok microgrooved band
f.main_result: Laser-ablated microgrooves allowed direct connective tissue attachment to the abutment, prevented apical migration of the junctional epithelium and protected the crestal bone.
f.funding_coi: Supported by a grant from BioHorizons

f.population: Six dogs
f.intervention: Titanium implants coated with purified porcine type I collagen
f.comparison: Uncoated titanium implants
f.main_result: Epithelial and connective tissue dimensions and connective tissue composition were similar at collagen-coated and uncoated implants after 4 and 8 weeks, with no adverse reactions.
f.sample_size: 6 dogs, two test and two control implants each
f.funding_coi: Grants from Implant Innovations Inc.; no conflicts declared

f.population: Patients with treated periodontal disease receiving implants in partially edentulous premolar and molar areas
f.intervention: Implants with a macro-thread neck (Group A, EZ Plus Internal)
f.comparison: Implants with a micro-thread neck (Group B, Megafix Internal) placed adjacent in the same patient
outcomes: marginal bone loss after 1 year of loading
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss was 0.154 mm with macro-thread and 0.125 mm with micro-thread, not significantly different (P = 0.669).

f.population: 2005 patients receiving cylindrical implants of the same trademark and type
f.intervention: RBM surface implants
f.comparison: SLA surface implants
f.main_result: RBM implants had 96.06% success (74 of 1877 failed) and SLA 96.53% (93 of 2675 failed); no significant difference in osseointegration success.
f.sample_size: 4793 implants in 2005 patients (abstract); 4552 implants in the results
f.funding_coi: No funding; no conflict of interest

f.main_result: Osseointegration is redefined as a foreign body reaction; moderately rough isotropic surfaces such as TiUnite show improved clinical results, while clinical evidence for nanoroughness, chemistry and hydrophilicity is lacking.
f.funding_coi: Both authors are scientific advisors to Nobel Biocare

f.population: Six commercial implant surfaces (7 surface areas) from different manufacturers
f.intervention: Topographical characterization with FESEM, SEM and light interferometry
f.main_result: Modern implant surfaces are highly complex with multiple scales of topography; Sa was lowest for the machined surface and about 1.5 micron for the BIOMET 3i blasted/dual-acid-etched/DCD, OsseoSpeed and SLActive surfaces.
f.funding_coi: Authors are employees of BIOMET 3i

f.population: Animal studies (in vivo) of implants with measured surface roughness and 3-month bone healing
f.intervention: Implants with increasing surface roughness (Ra/Sa)
f.main_result: 15 of 16 comparisons showed higher bone-to-implant contact with higher roughness (6 significant); studies were too heterogeneous to pool.
f.limitations: Selected studies were too heterogeneous for inference of data.

f.population: 12 adult mini-pigs, implants placed in mandibles after premolar extraction
f.intervention: Anodized (TiUnite) and HA-coated implants
f.comparison: Machined surface implants
f.main_result: Overall BIC was 19.39% for machined, 39.05% for HA-coated (P=0.0092) and 42.72% for anodized implants (P=0.0011), so anodized matched HA-coated.

f.population: 5 young adult mongrel male dogs, implants placed in healed premolar sites of the mandible
f.intervention: Implants with TPS, HA-coated and sandblasted (SBM) surfaces
f.comparison: Smooth machined implants
f.main_result: Mean BIC was 41.7% machined, 48.9% TPS, 57.9% HA and 68.5% SBM; only SBM differed significantly from machined.
f.funding_coi: Study supported by Paragon Implant Company

f.population: 10 totally edentulous patients receiving transitional implants in the posterior maxilla
f.intervention: Tapered Anyridge implant with knife-edge threads and nanostructured calcium-incorporated surface
f.comparison: Cylindrical EZPlus implant with self-tapping threads and sandblasted surface
f.main_result: Mean BIC was 35.9% with test and 29.9% with control implants (p = 0.16, not significant); BD was similar (31.8% vs 32.5%, p = 0.9).
The authors argue marginal bone loss around implants reflects an immune imbalance rather than primary bacterial disease; massive immune overreaction affects only about 1-2% of implants at 10 years.
f.funding_coi: Supported by grants from the Swedish Research Council, King Gustaf V and Queen Victoria Freemason Foundation and the Osteology Foundation; no conflicts of interest reported

f.intervention: Surface topography (micro- and nanometer level) and surface chemistry modifications of oral implants, with reference to OsseoSpeed
f.main_result: Moderately rough surfaces give the strongest bone response experimentally, but randomised clinical studies found no significant difference versus minimally rough implants; the benefit of nanosurfaces and hydrophilic/bioactive surfaces remains unproven.
f.limitations: Evidence for nanotopography and surface chemistry effects is lacking in vivo and clinically.

f.population: Twenty Labrador dogs with mandibular premolars extracted; implant sites in the mandible
f.intervention: Screw implants with SLA surface and a circumferential trough creating a wound chamber, to model early healing/osseointegration
outcomes: histology of soft and hard tissue formation
bone formation and remodeling over time
f.main_result: The wound chamber model allowed study of early bone formation: bone formation started within the first week, woven bone was replaced by parallel-fibered/lamellar bone, and implants stayed clinically stable despite temporary loss of hard tissue contact at 1-2 weeks.
materials_brands: ITI Dental Implant System solid screw implant, SLA surface (Institut Straumann AG)

f.population: Göttingen minipigs with a buccal acute-type dehiscence model in the mandible
f.intervention: Gradient anodized implant (NobelActive TiUltra) placed in buccal dehiscence defects
f.comparison: Custom-made geometric replica with superhydrophilic sandblasted acid-etched (SLActive) surface, and a commercial BLX implant with the same surface
f.main_result: At 8 weeks, de novo crestal bone and osseointegration were significantly greater around the SLActive control implants than around the gradient anodized test implant.
f.sample_size: 15 minipigs; n = 6 per group at 2 weeks and n = 8 at 8 weeks
f.funding_coi: Funded by Institut Straumann AG; two authors receive speaker honorariums from Straumann

f.population: Patients treated with endosseous dental implants in published longitudinal human studies (edentulous, overdenture, partially edentulous, single tooth)
f.intervention: Implants with roughened titanium surfaces
f.comparison: Relatively smooth (machined) titanium implants; also hydroxyapatite-coated implants
outcomes: implant success rate (odds ratio, Peto meta-analysis)
f.main_result: Predictably high success was achieved with rough and smooth titanium and HA-coated implants; rough surfaces had higher success in most indications except single-tooth replacements, and mandibular implants outperformed maxillary ones.
f.limitations: The success criteria used in each study were not critically analyzed and different studies used different criteria.

f.population: 50 edentulous or to-be-edentulous patients needing an implant-supported cross-arch prosthesis
f.intervention: Immediately loaded cross-arch prostheses on four to eight roughened-surface implants (iRES Shape 1BC)
f.comparison: Machined/turned surface implants (iRES iPerio), 25 patients
f.main_result: At 1 year no prosthesis failed; two machined implants failed in one patient; marginal bone loss -0.64 mm (rough) vs -0.68 mm (turned), no significant difference.
f.funding_coi: I-RES, the implant manufacturer, donated implants and components; no interference declared
f.limitations: Small sample size (pilot) and baseline imbalance in implant length and number of implants per patient.

f.population: 36 patients receiving ITI SLA implants in maxilla and mandible
f.intervention: Immediately loaded implants with ISQ measured by resonance-frequency analysis
f.comparison: Implants loaded after 3 months (delayed loading)
outcomes: ISQ at placement and over 12 weeks
f.main_result: All implants passed the 1-year loading control; two implants failed (ISQ at placement 48 DL and 53 IL), and RFA was not a reliable tool to identify mobile implants.
materials_brands: ITI SLA implants (Straumann); Osstell RFA device

f.intervention: Surface roughness, wettability and cleanliness modifications of dental implant surfaces
f.main_result: Hydrophilic implants improve initial blood contact, support wound healing and accelerate osseointegration, and roughness and wetting parameters can help predict bioresponse.
f.limitations: Knowledge of surface-related reactions is fragmentary and complex multi-scale surfaces are hard to manufacture reproducibly.

f.intervention: RBM (hydroxyapatite/calcium phosphate blasting with soft etching) implant surface compared to SLA
f.comparison: SLA (alumina large-grit blasted and acid-etched) surface
f.main_result: Manufacturer states RBM avoids alumina contamination but yields a less porous surface; reported survival is 97.2% at 4 years for RBM and 95% at 5 years for SLA.
materials_brands: DSI implants of Ti6Al-4V ELI alloy

f.intervention: Implant surface modifications (micro/nano topography, biomimetic coatings) and their effect on osseointegration
f.main_result: Most in vitro and in vivo studies indicate micro and submicro (nano) topographies benefit bone cell interaction, accelerating and increasing the quality of bone-to-implant contact.

f.intervention: Periodontal microsurgery with the surgical microscope, instruments and microsuturing
f.main_result: Microsurgery offers enhanced outcomes over macrosurgery, especially passive wound closure and reduced tissue trauma, with more rapid healing.
f.limitations: Microsurgery is technique-sensitive and more demanding than periodontal macrosurgery.

f.intervention: Selective pressure method with concave transmucosal profile of implant provisional restorations
f.main_result: The selective pressure method and concave transmucosal profile delivered esthetically and functionally successful implant restorations in the presented cases.

f.population: A prepared extracted mandibular molar with a thermal probe in the pulp chamber, in a water bath
f.intervention: Direct fabrication and relining of provisional crowns with five resins (PMMA, PEMA, PVEMA, Bis-acrylic, VLP urethane dimethacrylate)
f.comparison: The five resin materials compared with each other
f.main_result: Mean temperature rise at crown fabrication ranged from 37.76 C (PVEMA) to 39.40 C (PMMA); PMMA produced the highest exothermic reaction (P<.0001)
f.sample_size: 10 provisional crowns and 10 relines per material, 100 recordings

f.population: 28 patients with single-tooth edentulism (anterior and premolar sites)
f.intervention: Immediate implant placement with connective tissue graft, Bio-Oss Collagen gap fill and immediate screw-retained provisional with concave transmucosal profile
f.main_result: Buccal soft tissue stayed stable with very little recession; mean mesial papilla loss 0.21 mm, distal 0.021 mm, crestal bone loss 0.28 mm mesially and 0.24 mm distally; no implant failures
f.limitations: Short-term study; longer studies needed

f.population: Single implant restorations in the anterior region
f.intervention: Direct and indirect techniques to modify the emergence profile and peri-implant soft tissue, and ways to record and transfer it to the laboratory
outcomes: accuracy of soft tissue profile transfer
f.main_result: Gradual modification of an interim restoration (e.g. with composite) lets the clinician assess tissue response; each technique has listed advantages and disadvantages, and tissues must not be manipulated to cause undue trauma

f.population: Patients with compromised implant fixture angulation, position or selection
f.intervention: Transitional custom abutment: a temporary cylinder abutment built up with light-cured composite and progressively modified intraorally to sculpt supraimplant soft tissue
f.main_result: The technique allows progressive intraoral modification of the abutment to develop emergence profile and gingival contours, compensating for compromised implant angulation; no quantitative results

f.population: One 27-year-old woman with peri-implant recession at a maxillary right lateral incisor implant
f.intervention: Replacement of the restoration with a screw-retained, undercontoured titanium and composite resin interim restoration, then a new zirconia abutment and crown
f.main_result: At 3 months the midfacial gingiva had migrated about 1 mm coronally, enough to proceed to the definitive restoration
f.follow_up: 3 months with the interim restoration, then 2 months after the definitive restoration
f.limitations: Success is limited by the volume and position of the hard and soft tissues, and the approach can be expensive

f.population: Partially edentulous patients with fixed implant-supported single crowns and FDPs
f.intervention: Ceramic or metal abutments with internal implant-abutment connection
f.comparison: Ceramic or metal abutments with external implant-abutment connection
f.main_result: Estimated 5-year survival was 97.6% (SCs) and 97.0% (FDPs) with internal connections versus 95.7% and 95.8% with external; ceramic abutments had significantly more abutment fractures than metal
f.follow_up: Mean follow-up of at least 3 years in included studies
f.funding_coi: No specific conflict of interest declared

f.population: Patients in RCTs and CCTs with zirconia and titanium implant abutments in the same patient
f.intervention: Zirconia abutments
f.comparison: Titanium abutments
f.main_result: Meta-analysis (soft tissue color only) favored Zr abutments; no significant differences for recession, probing depth, bleeding, marginal bone level or patient-reported outcome; one study found higher PES with Zr
f.limitations: Heterogeneity in study design, statistics and reported results limited meta-analysis to soft tissue color

f.population: Three adult female Göttingen minipigs, mandibular premolar extraction sockets
f.intervention: Socket preservation with porous titanium granules (PTG) or heat-oxidized white PTG, collagen membrane, implants placed after 11 weeks
f.comparison: Empty sockets (sham)
f.main_result: PTG sockets matched sham: bone volume 61.7% PTG vs 50.3% WPTG (P=0.03) vs 57.1% sham; BIC 68.2% PTG, 36.6% WPTG, 60.9% sham (n.s.); apical defects seen in all groups
f.sample_size: 30 implants in 3 minipigs (12 PTG, 12 WPTG, 6 sham)
f.follow_up: 11 weeks socket healing plus 6 weeks submerged implant healing
f.limitations: Apical osseous defects were seen in all groups and a single cause could not be determined; small animal pilot

f.population: One 62-year-old woman with a peri-implant osseous defect at an IMZ implant (right central incisor)
f.intervention: Open flap debridement, surface decontamination with 24% EDTA gel, grafting with porous titanium granules (PTG) and resubmersion
outcomes: histology and element analysis of the graft
f.main_result: After 12 months PTG was in close contact with new bone growing into the granule porosities and onto the implant surface; radiographic defect heights fell from 9.24/5.70 mm to 0.97/0.74 mm (mesial/distal)
f.limitations: Only one case; further evaluation in patients with thinner mucosa is necessary; buccal graft height was lost

f.population: Five New Zealand white rabbits, both maxillary sinuses
f.intervention: Sinus floor elevation grafted with Bio-Oss mixed with Tisseel fibrin sealant
f.comparison: Bio-Oss mixed with normal saline
f.main_result: New bone formation 14.8% (Bio-Oss+saline) vs 18.5% (Bio-Oss+Tisseel); residual grafted bone 70.5% vs 60.4%; difference in bone formation insignificant
f.funding_coi: Funded by a research grant of Pusan National University; no competing interests
f.limitations: Pilot experiment with only five animals

f.population: Two patients (30-year-old and 59-year-old women) with extraction sites and bone defects needing implant site reconstruction
f.intervention: Bone grafting with human fibrin sealant mixed with deproteinized bovine bone, covered with a collagen resorbable membrane, then delayed implant placement
outcomes: clinical bone regeneration for implant placement
f.main_result: The protocol gave good clinical results for bone regeneration in implant surgery with a relatively simple, non-invasive procedure.
f.follow_up: 20 months and 36 months post-op in the two cases
f.limitations: Literature on xenograft plus fibrin sealant is controversial; more cases and long-term clinical and histological studies are needed.

f.population: Two patients with horizontal bony deficiency: a 64-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man, both with periodontitis
f.intervention: F.I.R.S.T. technique: fibrin sealant mixed with collagenated porcine xenograft and used to glue a cortical lamina membrane over the defect
f.main_result: Case 1 gained 4.05 mm of horizontal width, stable at 3 years, with newly formed trabecular bone on histology; case 2 widened a 1 mm ridge to 5 mm and implants were stable 3 years after loading.
f.limitations: Only two cases; further studies are needed to confirm the modification.

f.population: Two patients: a 57-year-old woman needing anterior maxillary ridge augmentation and a 65-year-old woman needing mandibular ridge augmentation
f.intervention: Tisseel fibrin sealant as binder for particulate bone grafts (autogenous plus xenograft), no membrane
outcomes: graft form and bulk retention on CBCT
f.main_result: Tisseel-bound composite grafts maintained ridge form and position, with excellent retention at the 10-year scan in patient 1.
f.funding_coi: First author has stock with X-Nav; other author none.
f.limitations: Small sample, no randomization, and no comparative volume measurements because of differing imaging.

f.population: 2,858 patients each with a posterior tooth with at least one visible crack, enrolled by 209 US dentists
f.intervention: Practitioner-chosen treatment or monitoring of cracked posterior teeth, followed annually
f.comparison: Teeth recommended for treatment versus teeth recommended for monitoring at baseline; intracoronal versus full/partial coverage restorations
f.main_result: Over 98% of cracked teeth survived 3 years (37 extractions); 14% of restored teeth failed; about 80% of monitored teeth stayed on monitoring.
f.funding_coi: NIH/NIDCR grants; authors declare no competing interests

f.population: Zirconia crowns on custom abutments fabricated on a master cast with an Astra Tech EV implant analog (maxillary right first premolar)
f.comparison: Interrupted digital Atlantis workflow (abutment received and rescanned)
f.main_result: All three workflows gave clinically acceptable marginal gaps (<120 um); full digital Atlantis had the smallest marginal gap (SEM 22 um, Geomagic 14 um) and split-file the smallest internal fit (59 um).
f.sample_size: 7 specimens per group (5-7 analyzed in Geomagic)
f.funding_coi: Stanley D. Tylman Research Grant (AAFP) and Texas A&M Restorative Dentistry; funders had no role

f.population: 10 healthy young volunteers with thick gingival biotype, 40 maxillary premolars
f.intervention: Expasyl retraction paste
f.comparison: Single KnitTrax cord size 0 with aluminum chloride
f.main_result: Paste produced a gap 0.041 mm smaller than cord (P=.014); both gaps were clinically acceptable (cord 0.282 mm, paste 0.241 mm) and height change did not differ.
f.follow_up: 2 weeks between sessions, plus a further 2 weeks final assessment
materials_brands: KnitTrax cord size 0 (Pascal) with aluminum chloride
f.limitations: Small sample, unprepared teeth in thick-biotype patients, and measurement points relying on researcher judgment.

f.intervention: Second retraction cord (double cord technique) before subgingival impression for fixed prosthesis
f.comparison: Single cord retraction technique
outcomes: impression quality grade of the prepared supports (poor/good/excellent)
f.main_result: Poor impressions were 41.7% with one cord versus 3.6% with two cords; excellent were 23% versus 82.4%.

f.population: 75 STL datasets of left upper first molar preparations for zirconia crowns made by 75 general dentists
f.intervention: Digital (CAD software and 3D inspection) evaluation of preparation geometry against clinical recommendations
f.main_result: No preparation met all recommendations; mean convergence angle was 26.7 degrees, abutment height 4.1 mm, and over 30% had insufficient interocclusal reduction.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared

f.population: Zirconia crown copings on acrylic maxillary molar dies prepared at 4, 8 and 12 degrees
f.intervention: Preparation angle of 4, 8 or 12 degrees total taper, with copings made by a laboratory or milling-center CAD/CAM system
f.comparison: Laboratory versus milling-center CAD/CAM fabrication; 4 versus 8 versus 12 degrees
outcomes: cement gap at chamfer, axial wall, occlusal and marginal locations
f.main_result: Preparation angle and measurement location significantly affected fit; 12 degrees gave best overall fit; marginal openings were 36.6 to 45.5 um in all groups and did not differ by fabrication site.
f.sample_size: 10 copings per angle per CAD/CAM system (60 copings)
materials_brands: Cercon zirconia (Cercon Base, Cercon Brain, DeguDent)
KetacCem Aplicap glass ionomer cement (3M ESPE)

f.population: Gingival tissues around vital and nonvital human teeth in adults (10 included studies, 400 teeth)
f.intervention: Gingival retraction with cords, pastes, surgery, cautery or lasers
f.comparison: The methods served as their own comparators
f.main_result: Of 145 articles, 10 studies (400 teeth) were included; chemomechanical retraction was most common and no method was clearly superior; clinical parameters were not significantly affected.
f.funding_coi: Authors deny any conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Heterogeneous results; English only and no grey literature search.

f.intervention: Conventional and modern gingival retraction methods (mechanical, chemical, surgical) for tooth- and implant-supported fixed prostheses
f.main_result: Gingival retraction techniques are classified as mechanical, chemical or surgical; the review discusses cords, cordless techniques, hemostatic agents, lasers, rotary curettage, electrosurgery, implants and digital impression.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared

f.population: 40 extracted sound human maxillary first premolars (from patients aged 18-22 years)
f.intervention: Monolithic zirconia crowns (traditional IPS e.max ZirCAD LT vs translucent ZirCAD MT) on teeth prepared with shoulder or feather-edge margin
f.comparison: Shoulder (1 mm) vs feather-edge margin design; traditional vs translucent zirconia
f.main_result: Mean fracture resistance was highest for traditional zirconia with shoulder margin (A1 2.903 kN), then A2 2.3, B1 1.854 and B2 1.523 kN; shoulder beat feather-edge and traditional beat translucent zirconia.
materials_brands: IPS e.max ZirCAD MT Multi A3 (Ivoclar)
RelyX U200 self-adhesive resin cement (3M ESPE)

f.intervention: Mechanical, chemicomechanical and surgical retraction of periodontal and peri-implant soft tissues
f.main_result: In peri-implant tissues contemporary retraction means should be avoided; technique choice should consider medical history, working zone and soft-tissue biotype.

f.population: 40 gingivally healthy adult probands (upper premolars), later with mild artificial gingivitis
f.intervention: Gingival displacement before impression: double cord technique with aluminum chloride, or kaolin paste (Expasyl) containing aluminum chloride
f.comparison: Contralateral quadrant without gingival displacement (split-mouth), and cord vs paste
outcomes: marginal gingiva height change / gingival recession
f.main_result: Cord gave better sulcus representation than paste in healthy gingiva, but mild gingivitis worsened it for cord and not for paste; no permanent palatal recession up to six months.
f.funding_coi: Investigator-initiated trial partly supported by 3M Oral Care; no conflict of interest declared

f.intervention: Tissue displacement methods: mechanical, mechanico-chemical, rotary gingival curettage and electrosurgery
f.main_result: Four families of gingival displacement are described with advantages and disadvantages; electrosurgery is safe and effective when variables are controlled.

f.population: Seven studies (four RCTs) on patients needing indirect fixed restorations or with unprepared teeth, healthy gingiva
f.intervention: Gingival retraction techniques without cord (cordless, e.g. paste)
f.comparison: Cord technique
f.main_result: Both cord and cordless techniques reliably retract gingiva; paste gives a drier field and is less injurious but displaces tissue less than cord.
f.sample_size: 7 studies included (4 RCTs), 8 to 252 participants per study
f.limitations: No meta-analysis because of heterogeneity of measurement variables across studies

f.population: 60 extracted third molars sectioned into enamel halves, worn against porcelain or gold discs
f.intervention: Wear of enamel against four porcelain systems and a type III gold alloy in electro-mechanical wear machines at pH 6.1 and pH 1.2
f.comparison: Enamel worn against enamel (control)
outcomes: wear volume loss of enamel and ceramic (3D scanning)
f.main_result: At pH 6.1 only the leucite-reinforced pressable ceramic significantly increased enamel wear versus enamel controls; under acid conditions enamel wear rose sharply but gold did not exceed enamel controls.
materials_brands: Authentic (Ceramay) leucite-reinforced veneering and pressable ceramic
Vita Mark II (Vita Zahnfabrik) machinable ceramic
f.limitations: Findings should be cautiously extrapolated to in vivo conditions

f.intervention: Ceramic laminate veneers: materials, applications and techniques
f.main_result: Clinical success of laminate veneers depends on suitable patient indications and correct application of the materials and techniques.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared

f.intervention: Less invasive adhesive and CAD/CAM-based restorative concepts: polymer pre-treatment, veneers, onlays and fixed dental prostheses
f.main_result: Overview of advances in fixed prosthodontics with support in material selection for single-tooth restorations through fixed dental prostheses.

f.population: 66-year-old man with bruxism and severe tooth wear
f.intervention: Full-mouth rehabilitation at increased vertical dimension: lithium disilicate veneers (anterior), CAD/CAM lithium disilicate overlays (posterior) and monolithic zirconia crowns on canines and first molars for four-point stability
f.main_result: After 4 years of function no complications were registered.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: Longer-term randomized studies on ceramics in grinders are needed

f.population: Clinical studies of patients with tooth wear restored with direct or indirect restorations
f.intervention: Indirect restorations (ceramics, composites, metal) for tooth wear
f.comparison: Direct restorations (resin composite)
outcomes: clinical performance by FDI or USPHS criteria
f.main_result: No evidence was found for the superiority of any restoration technique for treating tooth wear.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Most included studies were at high risk of bias and heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis.

f.population: 7 patients with severe tooth wear
f.intervention: Full-mouth adhesively bonded monolithic lithium disilicate occlusal onlays (IPS e.max Press)
f.main_result: Monolithic lithium disilicate occlusal onlays showed 100% survival up to 11 years; 3.9% marginal discoloration and 1% marginal crack.

f.population: Published treatment reports of generalized, complete-arch tooth wear
f.intervention: Minimally invasive adhesive rehabilitation of generalized tooth wear, analyzed in five steps (waxing, occlusal position, VDI, restoration, follow-up)
f.main_result: Eleven studies (16 publications) were included; diagnostic waxing was used in 9, VDI tested in 8, and composite resin and glass ceramic were each used in 6 for definitive treatment.
f.sample_size: 11 studies (16 publications), each of 1 to 4 patients
f.follow_up: 0 to 20 months after definitive treatment in included studies
f.limitations: Included studies were case reports and small case series.

f.population: Patients with severely worn occlusal surfaces (posterior teeth)
f.intervention: Minimally invasive glass-ceramic (lithium disilicate) occlusal onlays with supragingival margins, adhesively cemented
f.comparison: Traditional full crowns and direct composite restorations (discussed)
f.main_result: Occlusal onlays of high-strength glass-ceramics with supragingival margins reduce loss of dental hard tissue and increase enamel available for bonding compared with full crowns, provided the protocol is followed.
f.limitations: Highly technique-dependent; lack of long-term clinical data for CAD/CAM polymer restorations.

f.population: Two patients in their mid-thirties with localised anterior tooth wear
f.intervention: Gold palatal veneers on maxillary canines plus direct composite restorations, using the Dahl concept and canine-guided mutually protected occlusion
outcomes: posterior dento-alveolar compensation and occlusal contact
canine guidance and mutually protected occlusion
f.main_result: In both cases posterior dento-alveolar compensation occurred within 18 weeks with full occlusal contact re-established and a canine-guided mutually protected occlusion.
f.limitations: Any interventive restorative treatment is subject to maintenance, repairs or replacement.

f.population: Published literature on the lithium disilicate glass-ceramic IPS e.max (mainly e.max CAD)
f.intervention: IPS e.max CAD lithium disilicate glass-ceramic (materials science, properties, clinical use)
f.main_result: IPS e.max CAD shows excellent mechanical properties and acceptable esthetics with promising short- and medium-term single-crown survival, but long-term survival data are insufficient.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared
f.limitations: Clinical studies are limited in scope and time; lack of long-term data and of data on multi-unit FPDs.

f.population: New mechanical torque-limiting devices (friction-style and spring-style) from 6 implant manufacturers
f.intervention: Measurement of delivered torque of friction-style and spring-style devices with a digital torque gauge
f.comparison: Friction-style versus spring-style devices
outcomes: absolute difference between delivered and target torque
f.main_result: No difference in accuracy between friction-style and spring-style devices (P=.872); all devices were within ±10% of target torque.
f.sample_size: 30 devices (5 per manufacturer), each tested 10 times
f.limitations: In vitro study using only new devices; wear with use was not tested.

f.population: Controlled human (4) and animal (6) studies of implants placed with high vs low insertion torque
f.intervention: High insertion torque (>25 Ncm, up to 176 Ncm)
f.comparison: Low insertion torque (<30-35 Ncm)
f.main_result: No significant difference in marginal bone resorption (ES 0.13, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.38, human studies) or implant failure (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.01-20.77) between high and low insertion torque.
f.sample_size: 591 implants (348 high torque, 243 low torque) in 4 human and 6 animal studies
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no financial interest
f.limitations: High risk of bias in nearly all studies, few implants and large between-study heterogeneity; overall body of evidence is weak.

f.population: Patients rehabilitated with dental implants (6 studies: 3 RCTs, 3 prospective)
f.intervention: Implant placement with high insertion torque (50 Ncm or more)
f.comparison: Regular or low insertion torque (less than 50 Ncm)
f.main_result: No significant difference between high and regular/low torque in implant survival (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.06-4.06, P=.52) or marginal bone loss (MD 0.15 mm, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.44, P=.30).
f.sample_size: 651 implants (437 high torque, 214 regular/low) in 389 participants from 6 studies
f.follow_up: at least 6 months (inclusion criterion); 6 to 36 months in included studies
f.limitations: Authors recommend further research; consensus on definition of high/low torque is lacking.

f.population: 21 patients with edentulous mandibles (mean age 67.4 years)
f.intervention: Implants placed with low (<20 Ncm) or high (>50 Ncm) insertion torque, with machined or anodized neck design
f.comparison: Low versus high insertion torque; machined versus anodized neck (split-mouth)
outcomes: peri-implant bone level change on radiographs
probing depth and bleeding on probing
f.main_result: No influence of insertion torque (p=.912) or implant neck design (p=.682) on peri-implant bone level at 1 year; bone loss was 0.69 and 0.68 mm for the two torque groups.
materials_brands: Osstell mentor with Smartpeg abutments (Integration Diagnostics)
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest; supported by the authors' department (Department of Oral Surgery, Medical University of Vienna)

f.population: 48 patients (38 analysed) with 66 Tapered Screw-Vent implants, 4.5 mm diameter
f.intervention: Implants placed with maximum insertion torque of 70 Ncm or more (mean 110.6 Ncm, up to 176 Ncm)
f.comparison: Implants placed with insertion torque of 30-50 Ncm (9 implants, mean 37.1 Ncm)
outcomes: marginal bone resorption at loading and 1 year
f.main_result: Mean marginal bone loss was 1.03 mm (low torque) vs 0.72 mm (high torque) at loading and 1.09 vs 1.24 mm at 1 year, with no significant difference between groups.
f.sample_size: 66 implants in 48 patients in the abstract; 66 implants in 38 patients analysed
f.limitations: Nonrandomized, non-blinded design with a small control group and limited access to posterior sites for torque measurement.

f.main_result: Trauma from occlusion does not cause gingivitis or periodontal pockets but affects the supporting tissues; inflammation and occlusal trauma act as co-destructive factors in periodontitis.
f.funding_coi: Research supported by NIDR, USPHS grant DE-00646-0 5

f.population: 64 sets of human jaws from autopsy; 106 interdental spaces examined histologically
f.intervention: Bite analysis, then histological mesio-distal sectioning and radiographs of jaw specimens
f.main_result: Angular defects and attachment loss were related to subgingival plaque downgrowth and CEJ level, with no evidence that trauma from occlusion acts as a co-factor.
f.sample_size: 106 interdental spaces from 31 persons' specimens analysed (of 64 collected)

f.main_result: Periodontal staging and grading should start every implant case so that treatment planning maximizes conservation of teeth and preservation of alveolar bone ahead of restoratively driven plans.
f.funding_coi: Authors report grants/honoraria from implant and biomaterial companies (e.g., Straumann, Geistlich, BioHorizons)

f.main_result: A prosthodontically driven virtual plan combining CBCT, intraoral/facial scans and a diagnostic wax-up supports computer-guided implant surgery, with treatment difficulty assessed beforehand.
f.funding_coi: No disclosures

f.population: 20 adults with single implants replacing a second molar
f.intervention: Single-implant prosthesis on a second molar, tested with peanut chewing test, questionnaire and VAS
f.comparison: Same patients before insertion of the implant prosthesis
f.main_result: Masticatory performance rose from 67.8% to 84.3% after the implant prosthesis (P<0.0001), and over 90% of patients were satisfied.
Prosthetic design in the edentulous jaw depends on number and location of implants, which in turn determine whether a fixed or removable (overdenture) prosthesis is chosen.

f.population: 50 subjects with stage III or IV periodontitis and a tooth with attachment loss to or beyond the apex
f.intervention: Periodontal regeneration (papilla preservation flaps with EMD, membranes, bone grafts)
f.comparison: Extraction and replacement with implant- or tooth-supported fixed partial denture
f.main_result: Survival was 88% for regeneration and 100% for extraction and replacement, with similar complication-free survival and lower cost for regeneration.
f.funding_coi: Funded in part by the European Research Group on Periodontology
f.limitations: Sample size was based on logistic considerations given the pilot nature of the study.

f.main_result: Many patients prefer fixed prostheses for the edentulous jaw, but patient-centred studies do not confirm this, and overdentures may offer advantages in cost and hygiene.

Tooth maintenance is suitable when the tooth is not extensively diseased, has high strategic value, lies in an intact arch and gingival preservation is paramount; otherwise strategic use of implants and short-span FDPs is recommended.

f.population: Adult General Dental Services patients in England and Wales, 1990-2006
f.intervention: Restorations (amalgam, resin composite, glass ionomer, crowns, veneers) placed in permanent teeth
outcomes: time to extraction of the restored tooth
f.main_result: At 15 years 32-42% of restorations survived to re-intervention and 77.8-84.2% of restored teeth were not extracted; larger restorations did worse and crowns beat direct restorations for re-intervention but not extraction.
f.sample_size: 13,896,048 tooth restorations in more than 3 million patients

f.population: Adult General Dental Services patients in England and Wales with restored incisor teeth, 1990-2006
f.intervention: Direct restorations, crowns and veneers in incisor teeth
f.comparison: Restoration types, patient and dentist factors compared
outcomes: time to extraction of the restored incisor
f.main_result: 35% of incisor restorations survived without re-intervention at 15 years and 81% of restored incisors were not extracted; crowns did best for re-intervention (48%) but worst-but-one for extraction (75%) versus composite 84% and veneers 93%.

f.population: Partially and totally edentulous patients with implant-supported fixed reconstructions (nine studies, 1,369 patients)
f.intervention: Partial FDPs on 2-4 implants and full-arch FDPs on 4-6 implants
f.main_result: Partial FDP survival was 98.9% at 5 and 97.8% at 10 years, full-arch FDP survival on 4-6 implants 97.5%/95.0% maxillary and 97.9%/95.9% mandibular, but evidence on the optimal number and distribution is lacking.
f.sample_size: 9 studies, 5,642 implants and 1,448 reconstructions in 1,369 patients
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Substantial lack of evidence; no controlled trials comparing implant numbers and implant-to-replaced-unit ratios not reported

f.population: 18 patients (14 partially, 4 fully edentulous), age 38-71, with insufficient vertical bone height
f.intervention: Implants placed with exposed threads (2-7 mm), autogenous bone chips from a bone filter aspirator and a barrier membrane, flaps coronally displaced, 12-month healing
outcomes: regenerated tissue filling the space under the membrane
f.main_result: 3 of 22 membranes became exposed; in the 19 covered cases the space beneath the membrane filled with regenerated tissue, shown histologically to be vital bone.
f.limitations: Technique-sensitive, with risk of early membrane exposure; further research needed on load-bearing capacity and long-term results.

f.population: 20 partially edentulous patients with vertical jawbone deficiencies, 58 implants
f.intervention: Titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membrane with demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft (Group A) condensed under the membrane
f.comparison: Autogenous bone chips under the membrane (Group B)
f.main_result: Mean vertical bone gain was 3.1 mm (124%) with allograft and 5.02 mm (95%) with autogenous chips; new bone-titanium contact ranged 39.1-63.2% depending on pre-existing bone quality.
f.sample_size: 20 patients, 58 implants (22 in Group A, 30 extending beyond bone crest in Group B)

f.population: Partially edentulous adults needing vertical bone augmentation with single or multiple implants
f.intervention: Resorbable collagen barriers supported by an osteosynthesis plate with particulate autogenous bone
f.comparison: Nonresorbable titanium-reinforced e-PTFE barriers
f.main_result: Mean bone level at 6 years was 1.33 mm (resorbable) vs 1.00 mm (nonresorbable); adjusted difference 0.15 mm (95% CI -0.39 to 0.69, P = .5713), no failures or complications after loading.
f.sample_size: 22 patients (11 per group), one control dropout
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; no conflicts of interest

f.population: 35 patients with 36 three-dimensional vertical bone defects (single, multiple missing teeth, posterior maxilla)
f.intervention: Vertical GBR with titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membranes and particulated autografts, with simultaneous sinus augmentation in group C
f.comparison: Three clinical scenarios (single missing tooth, multiple missing teeth, posterior maxilla with sinus augmentation) compared
f.main_result: Mean vertical augmentation was 5.5 mm, crestal remodeling 1.01 mm at 12 months and stable through 6 years; implant survival 100%, cumulative success 94.7%.
f.limitations: Retrospective design; results should be verified by more rigorous studies.

f.population: 19 patients with vertically deficient alveolar ridges (20 procedures)
f.intervention: GBR with a 1:1 mixture of autogenous bone and ABBM covered by a titanium-reinforced high-density PTFE membrane
f.main_result: Average vertical bone gain was 5.45 mm with no complications; biopsies showed 36.6% autogenous/regenerated bone, 16.6% ABBM and 46.8% marrow space without inflammation.
f.follow_up: Mean 8.24 months of graft healing before biopsy
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Case series without controls; randomized controlled studies are needed.

f.population: 21 patients (29 mandibular surgical sites) needing vertical bone regeneration in the posterior mandible
f.intervention: Titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membrane with autograft, allograft or auto-xenograft, simultaneous or staged implant placement
f.comparison: Simultaneous vs staged implant placement; implants with vs without keratinized mucosa
f.main_result: Cumulative implant survival was 93.6% with mean bone remodeling 0.34-1.04 mm over 6 years; success was higher with simultaneous (82.5%) than staged (66.8%) placement and with keratinized mucosa (82.1% vs 58.4%).
materials_brands: W. L. Gore titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membrane
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported

f.population: 21 patients with edentulous, severely atrophic anterior maxillae needing horizontal and vertical augmentation
f.intervention: Bilaminar cortical tenting graft from a split ramus block, filled with particulate autograft, covered with ABBM and collagen membrane
f.main_result: Vertical and horizontal bone gain were 5.70 and 8.45 mm with 10.20% and 6.15% resorption; peri-implant bone reduction was 0.77 mm after about 6 years with 100% implant survival.
f.funding_coi: No specific grant funding; no competing interests

f.population: 49 partially edentulous patients with 123 Brånemark implants in 53 vertically augmented ridges
f.intervention: Implants protruding 2-7 mm placed with titanium-reinforced e-PTFE membrane protecting blood clot (A), allograft (B) or autograft (C)
f.comparison: Three techniques compared: blood clot, allograft, autograft under the membrane
f.main_result: Only 1 of 123 implants failed; mean bone loss was 1.35 mm (A), 1.87 mm (B) and 1.71 mm (C), so vertically augmented bone behaved like native bone.
f.limitations: Annual bone levels came from non-standardized periapical radiographs, so minor measurement errors are possible.

f.population: 40 partially edentulous patients with 66 implants in previously augmented bone
f.intervention: Titanium implants (TPS surface) placed 6-9 months after horizontal ridge augmentation with autografts and barrier membranes
f.main_result: No implant was lost among the 61 examined (survival 100%); one had peri-implant infection, giving a 5-year success rate of 98.3%.
f.sample_size: 66 implants in 40 patients (61 implants examined at 5 years)
materials_brands: ITI Dental Implant System (Straumann), TPS surface

f.population: Patients with vertical bone defects needing implant-supported restorations (literature on vertical ridge augmentation)
f.intervention: Surgical strategies, flap designs and devices proposed to reduce invasiveness of vertical ridge augmentation
f.main_result: Vertical augmentation remains inherently invasive; digital planning, customized meshes/blocks and modified flap designs may simplify it, but evidence is mostly short-term case reports and retrospective series without PROMs.
f.funding_coi: Self-funded; no conflict of interest declared.
f.limitations: Techniques are described mostly in retrospective case series, not tested in randomized trials with patient-reported outcomes.

f.population: 142 consecutively treated patients with 154 grafted sites (vertical defects in the posterior maxilla)
f.intervention: Split bone block (SBB) technique with autogenous retromolar blocks and sinus floor elevation via a tunnel approach, implants after 3 months
f.main_result: Mean vertical gain was 7.6 mm; resorption was 0.63 mm at 10 years (8.3%), with 4 implants lost.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest reported.

f.population: Adult patients with anterior tooth wear, compensatory eruption and deep overbite needing restorative space
f.intervention: Orthodontic intrusion of maxillary and/or mandibular incisors (or jaw surgery) to create restorative space, guided by four diagnostic principles
f.comparison: Crown lengthening with endodontic and post-and-core treatment, or opening the vertical dimension by restoring posterior teeth
f.main_result: Orthodontic intrusion of abraded incisors is a viable method for restoring them more conservatively, rather than increasing vertical dimension.

f.population: Seven completely edentulous complete-denture wearers aged 45-70 years
f.intervention: Complete dentures with occlusal vertical dimension reduced by about 3 mm
f.comparison: Complete dentures with an appropriate OVD
outcomes: masseter EMG amplitude during maximum clenching
f.main_result: Mean masseter EMG during maximum clenching was 435.35 uV with appropriate OVD versus 299.25 uV with reduced OVD (significant).
f.follow_up: EMG two months after first denture delivery, repeated two weeks after the second set

f.intervention: Increasing or decreasing the vertical dimension of occlusion in treatment planning

f.population: 30 dental students (12 men, 18 women), aged 21-30
f.intervention: Occlusal vertical dimension increased by 2, 4, 6 and 8 mm with polyvinyl siloxane occlusal registrations while posed smiles were photographed
f.comparison: Existing occlusal vertical dimension (+0 mm)
outcomes: incisal edge to upper lip distance
incisal edge to lower lip distance
f.main_result: Increasing OVD significantly increased interlabial gap height, incisal edge to lower lip distance and display zone area, and decreased smile index; smile width and upper lip length were unchanged.
materials_brands: Imprint Bite (3M ESPE) silicone occlusal registration
Nikon D7000 camera with Micro-NIKKOR 105 mm lens

f.population: 10 patients with generalised moderate to severe occlusal wear (attrited dentition) and loss of vertical dimension >3 mm
f.intervention: Canine-to-canine and full-arch occlusal splints at 1 mm and 4 mm vertical dimension, each worn one week
f.comparison: Splint type (canine-to-canine vs full arch) and splint thickness (1 mm vs 4 mm), compared with pre-splint baseline
outcomes: masseter and anterior temporalis surface EMG
f.main_result: All splints reduced masseter EMG (left masseter from 263.10 to about 135-147 uV, p<.001), more with 4 mm than 1 mm; condylar position did not change significantly.
f.follow_up: Each splint worn one week with one-week washout

f.intervention: Definition, measurement and clinical significance of vertical dimension in prosthodontics
f.main_result: Understanding the relationship between VD, TMDs, facial esthetics and psychological well-being is essential for effective prosthodontic treatment.
f.funding_coi: No financial support or relationships declared.

f.population: One 77-year-old woman with severely worn dentition, missing mandibular posterior teeth and reduced vertical dimension
f.intervention: Occlusal overlay splint to raise vertical dimension, then provisional fixed restorations and definitive metal-ceramic crowns with mandibular RPD
f.main_result: A satisfactory result was achieved by restoring the vertical dimension, with improved esthetics and function
f.follow_up: 1 month splint trial and 3 months provisional restorations
f.limitations: Trial period shorter than in other case reports

f.population: One 49-year-old patient with increased VDO, anterior open bite, masticatory muscle pain and periodontal involvement
f.intervention: Extraction of teeth 18 and 17, RPD clasp removal and occlusal adjustment by selective grinding to reduce VDO
f.main_result: Over 90 days there was complete remission of the initially reported symptoms after VDO was reduced
f.funding_coi: No funding; no conflict of interest

f.population: 96 general-practice patients whose occlusal vertical dimension had been increased (aged 36-84, mostly female)
f.intervention: Increase in vertical dimension of occlusion using acrylic pivots on a training plate or existing mandibular denture
f.main_result: 79.7% of responding patients and 81.2% by the panel judged patients to look younger after the treatment
f.sample_size: 96 patients surveyed, 69 responded (72%); panel of 5 judges
f.limitations: Patients' subjective opinions could be biased, so an independent panel was added

f.intervention: Phonetic (closest speaking space) method of locating the vertical dimension of occlusion

f.population: Human and animal studies on changes in occlusal vertical dimension
f.intervention: Critical review of claims that changes in occlusal vertical dimension harm the masticatory system
f.main_result: Current evidence does not support that moderate OVD changes harm the masticatory system
f.funding_coi: U.S. Public Health Service grants
f.limitations: The state of the science in this field is found wanting

f.intervention: Alteration of occlusal vertical dimension (reasons, five areas of concern, methods of establishing it)
f.main_result: The author concludes there are several correct approaches; altering vertical dimension does not harm the TMJ or produce muscle pain with an ideal occlusal scheme, muscle activity returns to baseline after 3-4 months, and stability is unknown.

f.intervention: A decision-making table relating overjet, overbite, prosthetic space, mandibular morphology, profile and skeletal type to increasing or decreasing VDO
f.main_result: There is an optimal adaptive space for the vertical dimension rather than a single point

f.population: Patients with complete or incomplete tooth fracture, especially over 40 years of age
f.intervention: Predisposition index, transillumination diagnosis and full-coverage cast restorations
f.main_result: Incomplete tooth fracture may be involved in up to 20% of patients referred to endodontists
f.limitations: No significant long-term study on the incidence of tooth loss from fracture exists

f.intervention: Vestibular deepening (vestibuloplasty) techniques
f.main_result: Vestibular deepening gives easier access for daily hygiene and improves patient comfort

f.population: School children aged 11.5 to 12.5 years in South Glamorgan
f.intervention: Classification of frenal attachment, upper lip coverage and mandibular vestibular depth
f.main_result: Plaque and bleeding fell with greater mandibular vestibular depth and rose with decreasing lip coverage; the effects were small and independent
f.funding_coi: Grant from the Department of Health and Social Security

f.population: Patient with multiple aberrant frenum and shallow vestibule in the mandibular anterior region
f.intervention: Conventional vestibular deepening procedure
f.main_result: Conventional vestibular deepening was successful in gaining vestibular depth and attached gingiva width

f.population: 17 healthy edentulous patients with existing conventional complete dentures
f.intervention: Two anterior mandibular implants with the existing denture converted to an overdenture using O-ring or magnet attachments
f.comparison: Conventional mandibular denture (baseline) and the other attachment system in a crossover design
f.main_result: O-ring attachments gave greater force-gauge retention (925 vs 479 g) and stability (984 vs 756 g) than magnets, and both exceeded conventional dentures.
f.follow_up: at least 6 months per attachment system (12 months total)
f.funding_coi: Supported by the National Institute for Dental Research and Calcitek Inc.

f.population: 19 patients with inadequate attached gingiva at single-rooted mandibular teeth
f.intervention: Free gingival graft from the palate (1.5 mm mucotome graft) to a partial-thickness recipient bed
f.main_result: Six months after FGG, vertical and area shrinkage (34% and 42%) correlated negatively with vestibular depth (r=-0.614 and r=-0.476); horizontal shrinkage (13%) did not.
f.funding_coi: Grant from Kerman Oral and Dental Diseases Research Center; no competing interests

f.population: Edentulous or soon-to-be edentulous mandibles receiving implants with alveolar ridge reduction (technique report, no formal sample)
f.intervention: Transalveolar sutures through inter-implant osteotomies securing facial and lingual flaps apically to hold vestibular depth and keratinized tissue
f.main_result: The authors report the technique prevented tissue overgrowth onto the implants, caused no extra discomfort, and the osteotomies re-ossified within 6 months.
f.limitations: Ideal vestibular depth for the two restoration types is still to be analysed in an IRB-sanctioned study.

f.population: One 21-year-old male with Miller class II recession at mandibular right central incisor
f.intervention: Lateral pedicle flap combined with subepithelial connective tissue graft
f.comparison: Functional probing versus Lugol's iodine staining for measuring keratinized gingiva
f.main_result: At 1 and 3 months there was 3 mm root coverage and 3 mm increase in keratinized gingiva width, with no difference between the two measurement methods.
f.limitations: Partial root coverage only; complete coverage may need a second-stage coronally advanced flap, and the technique is limited to one or two teeth.

f.population: 61 periodontal patients on supportive periodontal therapy with 234 implants in function at least 12 months
f.intervention: Exposure: shallow vestibular depth (4 mm or less) adjacent to implants
f.comparison: Sites with adequate vestibular depth (more than 4 mm)
f.main_result: Shallow-VD sites had higher mucosal recession (0.91 vs 0.47 mm), higher RAL (4.23 vs 3.59 mm), higher bone level value (2.18 vs 1.7 mm) and less keratinized mucosa (1.24 vs 2.38 mm).
f.follow_up: Implants in function at least 12 months (retrospective, 6-year longitudinal)
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest; no external funding
f.limitations: Authors state that further prospective and interventional studies are required.

f.population: 25 patients (aged 17-55) with very shallow lower labial vestibule
f.intervention: Vestibular deepening by the technique of Edlan and Mejchar with periosteum elevated
f.main_result: Mean vestibular depth increased from 2.24 to 6.96 mm (difference 4.72 mm, P<0.01), with improved gingival state and plaque index.
f.follow_up: 3 months to 4 years 7 months (mean 1 year 11 months)

f.population: Ceramic specimens (Empress II, InCeram-Alumina, InCeram-Zirconia, Frialit ZrO2), 10 per group
f.intervention: PyrosilPen flame treatment (2.5, 5, 10 s/cm2) followed by silane and luting composite (Variolink II)
f.comparison: Etched and silanated Empress II control
f.main_result: Optimal flame time was 5 s/cm2, giving shear bond strengths of 23, 23, 13 and 16 MPa (Empress II, InCeram-Alumina, InCeram-Zirconia, Frialit) versus 27 MPa for the control.
f.sample_size: 4 ceramics x 3 flame times x 10 specimens
f.limitations: Sandblasting before flame treatment may be recommendable and needs further investigation.

f.population: Alumina/30 vol% zirconia composite specimens (2.2 mol% Y2O3), slip cast
f.intervention: Heat treatment in unstabilized ZrO2 powder at 1400 C to remove Y2O3 from the surface
f.comparison: As-fired, annealed, ground and impacted surfaces
f.main_result: Y2O3 removal at 1400 C for 16 h raised monoclinic fraction to 0.67 and gave surface stress of -550 MPa, with smaller indentation cracks than as-fabricated surfaces.
f.funding_coi: Office of Naval Research
f.limitations: At higher loads the crack size exceeds the compressive zone depth, so the benefit diminishes.
