f.population: One patient with a discolored nonvital maxillary right central incisor and gingival level discrepancy (plus an FPD example)
f.intervention: Transfer of the adjusted subgingival contour of the interim restoration to the definitive cast using a zirconia coping customized with casting wax
f.main_result: The technique replicates the interim restoration's subgingival contour on a rigid definitive cast; symmetric gingival contours around the central incisors were achieved in the case shown.
materials_brands: NobelProcera FCZ Crown zirconia coping (Nobel Biocare)
f.funding_coi: JSPS KAKENHI grant 17K11781
f.limitations: Limited amount of apical gingival movement attainable; finish line should stay about 1 mm subgingival.

f.population: 86 included publications (in vitro studies, clinical studies, one systematic review) on zirconia-to-composite adhesion
f.intervention: Zirconia surface conditioning methods and bonding materials (airborne-particle abrasion, silica coating, MDP primers, cements)
outcomes: bond strength of zirconia to composite resin
f.main_result: Airborne-particle abrasion and tribochemical silica coating have the most evidence; combined mechanical and chemical (10-MDP or silane) conditioning is essential and no universal protocol is supported.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Heterogeneous protocols, tests and storage times make results difficult to compare; few clinical studies.

f.population: 52 in vitro studies on bond strength of luting cements to zirconia
f.intervention: Surface conditioning methods (169 different protocols) before resin or glass-ionomer luting
f.comparison: Non-conditioned control zirconia ground with SiC paper
outcomes: effect of cement type, test method, aging
f.main_result: Bond strength was significantly influenced by surface conditioning, cement type, test method and aging

f.population: Published literature on monolithic zirconia restorations
f.intervention: Monolithic zirconia restorations
f.comparison: Veneered zirconia restorations
f.main_result: In vitro studies suggest monolithic zirconia may be the best choice for posterior FPDs under high occlusal load and minimal space; clinical evidence is lacking
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Further in vitro and especially in vivo studies with larger samples and longer follow-up are needed

f.population: 57 clinical studies of ceramic restorations (tooth- and implant-supported)
f.intervention: All-ceramic restorations (feldspathic, hybrid, silicate, oxide ceramics)
f.main_result: Established silica- and oxide-based ceramics show high long-term clinical survival; recent materials lack long-term clinical validation
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Great heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis

f.population: 76 patients needing a single implant crown in the molar/posterior region
f.intervention: Monolithic zirconia crown on Ti-Zr reduced-diameter (3.3 mm) implant
f.comparison: Porcelain-fused-to-metal crown
f.main_result: At 3 years estimated implant survival was 80% (14 implants lost: 11 fractures, 3 aseptic); prosthetic complications (minor chipping) occurred only with PFM crowns
f.sample_size: 76 patients enrolled; 59 analysed at 3 years (32 test, 27 control)
materials_brands: Straumann Roxolid Tissue Level Standard Plus implant, 3.3 mm
f.funding_coi: Funded by University of Zurich clinic and ITI Foundation; several authors reimbursed by Straumann and 3M

f.intervention: Lava / Lava Plus zirconia restorations: indications, preparation, shading, handling and cementation
f.funding_coi: Published by manufacturer 3M Deutschland GmbH
f.limitations: Manufacturer notes higher failure risk from adhesion failure and secondary caries for adhesive and inlay/onlay bridges

f.population: Discs of conventional and high-translucency zirconia and lithium disilicate
f.intervention: Transmittance measurement and FE-SEM of two zirconia and two lithium disilicate materials
f.comparison: Zirconia versus lithium disilicate; conventional versus high translucency
f.main_result: High-translucency lithium disilicate was most translucent; high-translucency zirconia exceeded conventional zirconia but stayed below even conventional lithium disilicate

f.population: 40 disk-shaped zirconia specimens in 4 groups, plus 10 controls
f.intervention: Grinding with high-speed handpiece or micromotor, continual or periodic
f.comparison: Unground control specimens (n=10)
f.main_result: All grinding reduced flexural strength; high-speed handpiece groups 815 MPa vs micromotor 718 MPa; micromotor grinding reached 127 C vs 63 C

f.population: 18 Prettau zirconia crowns cemented on Co-Cr implant substitutes
f.intervention: Inner crown surface melt-etching with KHF2
f.comparison: Sandblasting and ceramic-stone grinding
outcomes: tensile adhesion strength to resin cement
f.main_result: Adhesion strength: sandblasted 5.2 MPa < ground 7.3 MPa < melt-etched 9.8 MPa (p<.05)

f.population: Literature on zirconia restorations (ceramics, CAD/CAM, bonding, surface finish, clinical results)
f.intervention: Zirconia-based ceramic fixed dental prostheses
outcomes: bonding to veneering ceramic and resin cements
f.main_result: Most frequent clinical complication was veneering porcelain chipping; zirconia frameworks rarely failed
f.limitations: Larger and longer clinical studies are needed

f.population: 30 densely sintered zirconia cylinders
f.intervention: Low-pressure air abrasion, 50 um Al2O3 at 1 bar, before self-adhesive cement
f.comparison: Unconditioned control and standardized 2.8 bar air abrasion
f.main_result: Sand_H 16.24 and Sand_S 16.01 MPa did not differ (P=0.8580); both exceeded control 13.29 MPa (P<0.001)

f.population: Zirconia ceramic (Cercon Base) and leucite glass-ceramic (GN-1) specimens
f.intervention: Internal coating technique (fusing silica-based porcelain onto zirconia) with or without silane, bonded with Panavia F 2.0 or Superbond C&B
f.comparison: Untreated air-abraded zirconia (Zr) and GN-1 glass-ceramic, with and without silanization
f.main_result: Silanization significantly improved bond strength to INT and GN-1 for both cements, and INT plus silane gave the highest strength (18.9 MPa with Superbond C&B, 14.5 MPa with Panavia F 2.0).
f.sample_size: n=7 per group; 56 zirconia and 28 glass-ceramic specimens
f.funding_coi: Supported by a GCOE Program grant of Tokyo Medical and Dental University
f.limitations: Conclusions limited to the study conditions; only 24 h water storage was tested.

f.population: Premolar crowns (porcelain fused to metal and glass-infiltrated alumina) cemented on stainless-steel dies
f.intervention: Modified framework design: core thickened to 1 mm at the cervical margin, 2.0 mm height lingually, with a 3.5 mm proximal strut
f.comparison: Standard even 0.5 mm framework design, and PFM versus In-Ceram alumina
f.main_result: Modified design raised characteristic strength (PFM 1,760 to 2,418 N; alumina 994 to 1,308 N), and PFM groups were stronger than alumina groups.

f.population: Monolithic high-translucency zirconia crowns (90) on a stainless-steel molar-like die
f.intervention: Margin thickness (light 0.8 mm vs heavy 1.2 mm chamfer) combined with collar height (none, 0.5 mm, 1.0 mm)
f.comparison: Light chamfer vs heavy chamfer, and no collar vs low vs high collar
f.main_result: Heavy chamfer crowns were significantly stronger than light chamfer (4362 vs 3055 N mean); collar height had no significant effect.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared; no funding statement found

f.population: 3Y-TZP zirconia discs (10 mm diameter, 2 mm thick)
f.intervention: Sandblasting with alumina at two particle sizes (110, 250 um), two pressures (2, 4 bar) and two impact angles (30, 90 degrees)
f.comparison: Polished unblasted control specimens, and annealed blasted specimens
f.main_result: Sandblasting with 110 um particles raised biaxial strength (characteristic 1572 vs 1306 MPa control at 90 degrees, 2 bar) via compressive residual stress; 250 um particles lowered it (1192 MPa).
f.funding_coi: Funded by Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovacion of Spain research grants
f.limitations: Conclusions hold only within the sandblasting conditions studied; failure origins were hard to identify in specimens broken into multiple pieces.

f.population: Y-TZP zirconia discs (Cercon), 1.2 mm thick, 15 mm diameter
f.intervention: Sandblasting with 110 um alumina at 2 bar for 10 s at 15 or 25 mm distance and 45 or 90 degree angle
f.comparison: Unsandblasted control group
f.main_result: No significant difference in biaxial flexural strength among groups (p = 0.40), but surface roughness differed significantly (p < 0.001), highest at 15 mm/90 degrees (0.51 um).
f.funding_coi: Supported by Dental Research Center, Tehran University of Medical Sciences; conflict of interest none
f.limitations: The in vitro setting could not perfectly simulate the oral clinical setting.

f.population: Ceramic specimens (Y-TZP zirconia, lithium disilicate, feldspathic porcelain) worn against extracted human enamel cusps
f.intervention: 3-body wear simulation for 50,000 cycles against enamel on rough, smooth or glazed ceramic surfaces
f.comparison: Three ceramics (zirconia, lithium disilicate, feldspathic porcelain) and three surface finishes (rough, smooth, glazed)
outcomes: change in surface roughness (Ra) after wear
f.main_result: Smooth porcelain became significantly rougher (P<.004) and rough lithium disilicate became smoother (P=.012); zirconia and lithium disilicate did not become as rough as feldspathic porcelain.
f.sample_size: 72 ceramic specimens (9 groups of 8) and 72 enamel cusps
f.follow_up: 50,000 wear cycles (about 1 year of simulated wear)
f.limitations: Conclusions are limited to the study conditions.

f.population: CAD/CAM zirconia single-crown copings and 3-, 4- and 5-unit bridge frameworks on stainless-steel master abutment models
f.intervention: Post-machining sintering of KATANA CAD/CAM zirconia frameworks, then cementation and measurement of marginal gap and cement layer thickness
f.main_result: Marginal gap was 3.6 um for the coping and 4.2 vs 43.2 um on non-pontic vs pontic side of 3-unit frameworks; the 5-unit framework showed no pontic/non-pontic difference.
f.sample_size: 3 copings or frameworks of each type
f.funding_coi: Supported in part by a JSPS Grant-in-aid for Scientific Research (C)

f.population: Monolithic zirconia disks (10 mm diameter) of 0.8 mm and 1.3 mm thickness
f.intervention: Two thicknesses combined with airborne-particle abrasion (50 um Al2O3) or grinding plus polishing
f.comparison: Untreated control disks and the other thickness
f.main_result: 1.3 mm disks were stronger than 0.8 mm disks and airborne-particle abrasion increased strength, while grinding followed by polishing had no effect (P<.05).

f.population: Square zirconia (Kavo Everest) specimens, 5 x 10 x 10 mm, veneered with Cerabien ceramic
f.intervention: Airborne-particle abrasion with 110 um Al2O3, liner application, or both, before veneering
f.comparison: Control group ground with #320 diamond disc
f.main_result: Shear bond strength ranged from 27.87 MPa (liner) to 36.63 MPa (airborne-particle abrasion); abrasion was significantly higher than the liner groups (P<.05).

f.population: Y-TZP zirconia cubes (10 mm) veneered with five veneering ceramics (in vitro specimens)
f.intervention: Zirconia surface treatments (polishing, sandblasting, silica-coating), liner application, and regeneration firing before veneering
f.comparison: Polished zirconia surface without liner or regeneration firing
f.main_result: Shear strength ranged 23.5±3.4 to 33.0±6.8 MPa with no clear correlation to surface treatment; sandblasting did not improve bonding and regeneration firing reduced it.
f.sample_size: 10 specimens per combination of veneering ceramic and treatment
materials_brands: Veneering ceramics: Cerabien ZR, IPS e.max, Triceram, Vintage ZR, VM9
f.funding_coi: Vita Zahnfabrik manufactured the Y-TZP cubes; ceramic materials supplied by manufacturers

f.population: Five commercial zirconia frameworks (Cercon white/yellow, Lava white/yellow, Procera) as discs veneered with two ceramics
f.intervention: Surface treatment (as-milled, airborne-particle abrasion, liner) before veneering with Noble Rondo or Cercon Ceram Express
f.comparison: White versus colored zirconia and as-milled surface versus other treatments
f.main_result: Bond strength to colored zirconia was significantly weaker than to white zirconia, and the effect of each surface treatment depended on the zirconia material.
f.sample_size: 30 test groups (5 zirconias x 2 veneers x 3 treatments), 18 microbars per group
f.funding_coi: Test materials supplied by Nobel Biocare and 3M ESPE

f.population: Densely sintered zirconia and cp2 titanium specimens
f.intervention: Sandblasting at distances of 5, 10 and 15 mm and angles of 45, 60, 75 and 90 degrees, then silane and resin cement bonding
f.comparison: Unblasted control specimens and the other angle/distance groups
f.main_result: Sandblasting angle significantly affected shear bond strength, with 75 degrees best and not different from 90 degrees; sandblasting distance had no significant effect.
f.sample_size: n=8 per group for each material
materials_brands: RelyX Unicem Aplicap resin cement (3M ESPE)
Rocatec Pre silica-coated alumina powder (3M ESPE)

f.population: Thirty extracted sound premolars restored with veneered zirconia crowns
f.intervention: Three CAD/CAM zirconia frame designs (flat, PFM-like, anatomically guided) veneered with pressure-layered porcelain
f.comparison: Flat design versus PFM-like design versus anatomically guided design
f.main_result: Anatomically guided frames had higher fracture load (1721.6 N) than PFM-like (1004.6 N) and flat (1179.5 N) frames, which were comparable.

f.population: 120 monolithic crowns on resin abutments replicating a mandibular first molar preparation
f.intervention: High- and low-translucent zirconia crowns at 0.3 to 1.5 mm thickness and lithium disilicate crowns at 1.0 and 1.5 mm, aged then loaded to fracture
f.comparison: High-translucent versus low-translucent zirconia versus lithium disilicate, across thicknesses
f.main_result: Fracture load of high- and low-translucent zirconia crowns was equal and significantly greater than lithium disilicate at equal thickness; load fell with decreasing thickness.
f.funding_coi: Conducted without third-party or manufacturer influence; materials provided by 3M ESPE and Ivoclar Vivadent

f.population: 45 zirconia crown copings on 15 metal master dies (maxillary second molar preparation)
f.intervention: CAD/CAM lithium disilicate veneering cap sintered onto the zirconia coping (ST)
f.comparison: Conventional layering (VT) and overpressing (PT/OT) of veneering porcelain
f.main_result: Sintered CAD/CAM veneer caps had a mean fracture load of 6262.67 N versus 3700.39 N (layering) and 3523.73 N (overpressing), P<0.001.
f.limitations: Fatigue was not taken into account in this study.

f.intervention: APC zirconia-bonding concept: air-particle abrasion, zirconia primer, adhesive composite resin
f.main_result: Durable resin bonding to zirconia is recommended through air-particle abrasion, an MDP-containing primer and an adhesive composite resin cement (APC concept).

f.population: Procera AllZirkon zirconia specimens with airborne-particle-abraded intaglio surfaces
f.intervention: Resin luting agents (Panavia F, RelyX ARC) with different bonding/silane coupling agents, tested after 3 days and after 180 days plus thermal cycling
f.comparison: Panavia F without any bonding/silane agent (control)
f.main_result: Aging significantly reduced bond strength; a bonding/silane agent containing an adhesive phosphate monomer gave superior long-term bond strength (about 15 to 17 MPa versus 1.08 MPa for the RelyX ARC primer system).

f.population: Three-unit zirconia fixed partial dentures on PMMA molar abutments
f.intervention: Different surface treatments and adjustment procedures (sintered, glazed, sandblasted and glazed, ground, polished) followed by chewing simulation and fracture testing
f.comparison: Control group without thermal cycling and mechanical loading, and a veneered anatomically reduced design
outcomes: failures during thermal cycling and mechanical loading
f.main_result: No FPD failed during chewing simulation and median fracture force (1173.5 to 1316.0 N) did not differ between groups or from the control.
f.follow_up: chewing simulation of about five years of oral service

f.population: Fifty zirconia plates (LavaMulti, 3M ESPE) with steatite ball antagonists
f.intervention: Surface treatments: as fired, sandblasted, ground, ground and polished, ground and glazed, tested in a pin-on-disk wear apparatus
f.comparison: The five surface-treatment groups against each other
f.main_result: Polished zirconia caused the lowest antagonist wear (66 um) versus 81-85 um for other treatments; zirconia wear was measurable only for the glazed group (46 um).

f.funding_coi: Published by the manufacturer, Ivoclar Vivadent AG Research & Development

f.population: Stereolithography additively manufactured zirconia bar specimens (25x4x3 mm)
f.intervention: Printing zirconia bars with an SLA ceramic printer and sintering to 0%, 20% or 40% porosity
f.comparison: 0% versus 20% versus 40% porosity groups
f.main_result: The 40%-porosity group had the highest manufacturing accuracy and lowest volume change; volumetric changes ranged from -20.33% to +3.5% and were uneven across axes.
f.limitations: None of the groups tested were able to perfectly match the virtual design of the specimens.

f.intervention: Monolithic zirconia ceramics (conventional and ultra-translucent/multicolor)
f.main_result: Monolithic zirconia causes minimal antagonist wear if polished and shows promising 5-7 year survival, but evidence on ultra-translucent types is limited.
f.follow_up: up to 5 or 7 years (short-term studies reviewed)
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Due to limited studies evaluating the wear properties of ultra-translucent material, no sound conclusions can be made.

f.population: 32 extracted human maxillary premolars in 4 groups of 8
f.intervention: Monolithic 3Y zirconia full crown (control), MODF onlay, MODL onlay and MODBL overlay, bonded by air abrasion, MDP primer and composite resin cement, then 1.2 million thermomechanical cycles
f.comparison: Full crown preparation (group 1, control) versus three partial coverage designs
f.main_result: One MODF onlay debonded at 632,000 cycles, none fractured, and all seven intact MODF specimens showed marginal deterioration where the antagonist contacted.
f.follow_up: 1.2 million loading cycles (about 5 years of function)
f.funding_coi: Authors deny any conflicts of interest
f.limitations: Within the limitations of this in vitro study (no specific limitations listed).

f.intervention: Resin-bonded, all-ceramic and metal-ceramic fixed dental prostheses
f.main_result: Metal-ceramic FDPs show the highest survival; all-ceramic can be comparable but chip more; resin-bonded FDPs act as long-term provisionals.
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest

f.population: Pre-sintered zirconia (Y-TZP) disks, 15 mm diameter, 2.4 mm thick
f.intervention: Sandblasting with 50 um aluminum oxide before sintering (Z-PRE) or after sintering (Z-POS)
f.comparison: Z-CTR, no surface treatment
f.main_result: Pre-sintering sandblasting gave rougher surfaces and more defects but did not raise shear bond strength over post-sintering sandblasting; both beat control.
f.funding_coi: Supported by FAPESP grants
f.limitations: Long-term consequence of pre-sintered treatment on the zirconia-veneer interface needs further investigation.

f.population: 10 patients (5 women, 5 men; mean age 52.8) receiving 17 posterior four-unit zirconia FDPs
f.intervention: Lava zirconia-based four-unit posterior FDPs veneered with Lava Ceram, cemented with RelyX Unicem
f.comparison: Contralateral untreated control teeth for periodontal parameters
f.main_result: After 4 years cumulative survival of the four-unit FDPs was 76.5%, with three framework fractures at the distal connector.
f.funding_coi: University Complutense of Madrid grant no. 229-2006
f.limitations: Within the limitations of this prospective clinical study; small sample and short follow-up, more long-term observation needed.

f.intervention: Zirconia and alumina core materials for all-ceramic restorations
f.funding_coi: Grant-in-Aid, Japan Society for the Promotion of Science No. 18390521

f.intervention: Dental zirconia types, properties, applications and cementation
f.main_result: Monolithic translucent zirconia has shown promising results and high survival rates, and cementation methods have improved.
f.funding_coi: No external funding; no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Data are scarce; well-designed clinical trials are needed.

f.population: 160 disks of four 4Y/5Y translucent zirconia materials
f.intervention: Surface treatments: as-machined, glass bead abraded, alumina abraded
f.comparison: Hand-polished control with 2000-grit silicon carbide paper
f.main_result: 4Y zirconia was stronger than all 5Y materials; alumina abrasion slightly strengthened 4Y but weakened 5Y materials and produced the roughest surfaces.
f.funding_coi: No specific grant funding

f.population: Prospective and retrospective cohort studies of all-ceramic and metal-ceramic FDPs
f.intervention: All-ceramic fixed dental prostheses
f.comparison: Metal-ceramic FDPs
f.main_result: 5-year survival was 94.4% for metal-ceramic FDPs versus 88.6% for all-ceramic FDPs (P<0.0001).
f.follow_up: mean follow-up of at least 3 years
f.limitations: Assumption of a constant annual event rate; mean observation period was 3.8 years for all-ceramic versus 8 years for metal-ceramic FDPs.

f.population: Studies of tooth-supported single crowns: 4663 metal-ceramic and 9434 all-ceramic
f.intervention: All-ceramic tooth-supported single crowns
f.comparison: Metal-ceramic single crowns
f.main_result: Estimated 5-year survival of metal-ceramic SCs was 94.7%, similar to reinforced glass-ceramic (96.6%), alumina (96%) and zirconia (92.1%) crowns; zirconia had more veneer fractures and loss of retention.
f.follow_up: mean follow-up of at least 3 years; 5-year estimates
f.funding_coi: No conflict of interest

f.population: Bar-shaped bilayered specimens: three zirconia core ceramics with their veneering ceramics plus a metal ceramic control
f.intervention: Core-veneer shear bond strength of three zirconia core/veneering ceramic systems by the Schmitz-Schulmeyer method, with half of each group thermocycled
f.comparison: Metal ceramic control (Degudent U94 / Vita VM13) and dry storage versus thermocycling
f.main_result: All-ceramic groups reached about 9-12.5 MPa, unaffected by thermocycling, and all were significantly below the metal ceramic control (about 26-28 MPa).
f.sample_size: 30 specimens per group, four groups (n = 15 thermocycled per group)
materials_brands: Vita In-Ceram YZ Cubes / Vita VM9
Degudent U94 / Vita VM13 (metal ceramic control)

f.population: Bilayered ceramic core-veneer specimens of four all-ceramic systems and a metal ceramic control, all made from one master die
f.intervention: Shear loading of the core-veneer interface of IPS-Empress2/Eris, Procera AllZircon/CZR, DC-Zircon/Vita D and Procera AllCeram/AllCeram until failure
f.comparison: Metal ceramic (MC) control
f.main_result: Shear strength of IE (30.86 MPa), PZ (28.03) and DC (27.90) did not differ significantly from the metal ceramic control (30.16), whereas PA (22.40) was lower.

f.population: Lithium disilicate glass-ceramic, Y-TZP and metal-ceramic molar crowns (in vitro) and patients with zirconium oxide-based or lithium disilicate restorations (in vivo)
f.intervention: Step-stress fatigue testing of crowns, clinical recall of Lava zirconium oxide and IPS e.max Press restorations, and a wear trial of ceramic crowns against enamel
f.comparison: Metal-ceramic and veneered Y-TZP crowns in vitro; enamel-to-enamel wear and veneer porcelains in vivo
outcomes: wear of ceramic and antagonist enamel
f.main_result: LDGC crowns had the highest characteristic strength in vitro (eta 1,719 N vs 1,304 N for MCR and 631 N for Y-TZP), and 2.8% of zirconium oxide crowns at 7 years were replaced versus none of the LDGC restorations at 4 years.
f.sample_size: n = 21 crowns per in vitro group; 574 zirconium oxide restorations and 236 LDGC restorations recalled; 31 patients with 36 teeth in the wear trial
f.funding_coi: Two authors are co-owners of Dental Consultants (publisher of The Dental Advisor) and Apex Dental Milling

f.population: Standardized zirconia crown frameworks (maxillary canine analog) cemented on CoCr abutments
f.intervention: Veneering with overpressed porcelains (PressX Zr, GC Initial LF, VITA PM9, IPS e.max ZirPress)
f.comparison: Layered veneering porcelains (Zirox, GC Initial ZR, VITA VM9, IPS e.max Ceram)
f.main_result: Overpressed crowns had similar or higher fracture load than layered ones; IPS e.max ZirPress (1519 N) exceeded IPS e.max Ceram (894 N).

f.population: Bar-shaped zirconia specimens (3 mol% Y2O3, Zirluna ACF), glazed or veneered with feldspathic ceramic
f.intervention: Clinically simulated sequential grinding (NTI diamond burs 20, 10, 7.5 um) and polishing of glazed full-contour zirconia
f.comparison: Zirconia veneered with feldspathic ceramic and glazed (group 2)
f.main_result: Glazed full-contour zirconia had significantly lower roughness than veneered zirconia, and fine polishing gave roughness comparable to glazing, while veneered zirconia stayed rougher after polishing.
materials_brands: NTI diamond burs and polishing kit

f.population: Tooth-supported monolithic ceramic single crowns and fixed partial dentures in human clinical studies
f.intervention: Monolithic ceramic (lithium disilicate, zirconia, PICN) single crowns and FPDs
f.comparison: Veneered ceramic restorations (5 studies with direct comparison)
f.main_result: Pooled failure was 1% for monolithic single crowns and 3% for FPDs, with no significant difference from veneered restorations in survival (RR 0.68).
f.sample_size: 18 studies: 1061 monolithic single crowns and 104 FPDs
f.funding_coi: No specific grant from funding agencies

f.population: Thirty zirconia disks in three thickness groups on nine backgrounds
f.intervention: Spectrophotometric CIELab measurement of zirconia disks of 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8 mm placed on nine backgrounds
f.comparison: A2 composite resin background as the reference for color difference
f.main_result: Mean delta E ranged 1.44 to 7.88 and was affected by thickness and background; 0.4 mm masked most backgrounds, 0.6 mm amalgam and 0.8 mm nickel-chromium alloy.
materials_brands: DD Bio ZX2 monolithic zero zirconia

f.population: 46 patients (49 teeth) needing full-crown restoration of first and/or second molars
f.intervention: Monolithic zirconia crowns for posterior teeth
f.main_result: Marginal adaptation was excellent in 100% of crowns, color match acceptable in 6.1%, with no significant change in wear of antagonist teeth over 96 weeks.
f.funding_coi: Funded by Guangxi Province and Guilin City research plans; no conflicts of interest

f.population: 35 zirconia specimens (ICE Zirkon) bonded with Variolink II resin cement
f.intervention: Sandblasting alone or combined with Monobond S, Monobond Plus or Z-Prime Plus before cementation
f.comparison: Untreated control (Group I)
f.main_result: MDP-containing primers (Monobond Plus, Z-Prime Plus) with sandblasting gave the highest shear bond strength and the untreated control the lowest.

f.population: Y-TZP ceramic specimens (in vitro studies)
f.intervention: Grinding of Y-TZP
f.comparison: As-sintered Y-TZP without grinding
f.main_result: Grinding generally decreased flexural strength and increased roughness of Y-TZP; slow-speed handpiece, grit size under 50 um and plenty of coolant limited the damage.

f.population: Disc-shaped specimens of partially stabilized (Prettau) and fully stabilized (Prettau Anterior) monolithic zirconia
f.intervention: Staining (A2 liquid) and vacuum sintering
f.comparison: Non-stained specimens sintered without vacuum
f.main_result: Staining lowered translucency of fully stabilized zirconia and raised its flexural strength but lowered that of partially stabilized zirconia; vacuum sintering gave minimal benefit.
f.sample_size: n=15 per subgroup, two zirconia types, three conditions

f.population: Pressureless-sintered biomedical grade Y-TZP ceramic specimens
f.intervention: Dental grinding and sandblasting
f.comparison: Pristine as-sintered specimens
outcomes: survival under cyclic loading (dry and artificial saliva)
f.main_result: Grinding at high rotation speed lowered mean strength and cyclic survival, whereas sandblasting strengthened the surface and raised cyclic survival; testing in artificial saliva lowered survival strength by about 10-15%.
f.funding_coi: Supported by the Slovenian Research Agency

f.main_result: Zirconia can withstand posterior physiologic loads, but veneer chipping and the poorly understood zirconia-veneer bond are the main weaknesses.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared

f.main_result: Zirconia materials can withstand posterior physiologic loads, yet zirconia cores are not problem free.
Third-generation zirconia has improved optical properties, while data on its mechanical properties are still scarce.
Newer zirconia generations are more translucent but generally weaker, and lower masking potential can be a drawback.
f.funding_coi: Translucency measurements financed by pritidenta, which also supplied crowns; authors state they were not influenced

f.population: 36 CAD/CAM monolithic translucent zirconia discs (10 mm x 0.8 mm)
f.intervention: Classic, speed and super speed sintering cycles, with or without thermodynamic aging
f.comparison: Classic sintering cycle (1510 C, 120 min hold)
f.main_result: Rapid sintering reduced translucency and biaxial flexural strength (super speed 863.8 MPa vs classic 1169.4 MPa before aging); aging reduced translucency only.
f.sample_size: 36 discs, n=12 per sintering group, n=6 per subgroup

f.population: 80 milled monolithic molar crowns
f.intervention: Cubic ultratranslucent (UT) and supertranslucent (ST) zirconia crowns at 1.0 and 1.5 mm
f.comparison: Lithium disilicate (IPS e.max CAD LT) crowns, 1.5 mm
f.main_result: Translucency ranked UT1.0 > ST1.0 > UT1.5 > lithium disilicate 1.5 by total transmission; UT and ST cubic zirconia were more translucent than lithium disilicate LT.
f.funding_coi: Kuraray Europe Italia supplied materials and technical assistance; no funding statement

f.population: Yttria-stabilized zirconia (8 mol% Y2O3) ceramic samples with and without TiO2
f.intervention: Addition of 10 mol% TiO2, sintering and hot isostatic pressing
f.comparison: TiO2-undoped ZrO2 (8 mol% Y2O3) sample
f.main_result: 10 mol% TiO2 dissolved into cubic 8Y-ZrO2, promoted grain growth and pore migration, and gave transparent ceramics for 0.35 to 7 um wavelengths.

f.population: 3Y-TZP zirconia specimens of different grain sizes and 3Y-TZP-MWCNT nanocomposites
f.intervention: Sandblasting with two particle sizes (110 and 250 µm), two pressures (2 and 4 bars) and two impact angles (30 and 90 degrees)
f.comparison: Non-sandblasted control material
f.main_result: Mild sandblasting (110 µm, 2 bars) raised biaxial strength and left surface mechanical properties unchanged, while 250 µm particles at 90 degrees lowered strength; 10-15% monoclinic phase formed to a depth of about 10-13 µm.
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Spanish Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Cooperation (MAEC-AECID)
f.limitations: Conclusions apply within the limits of the sandblasting conditions studied.

f.population: In vitro studies (and a few clinical studies) of bonding to zirconia ceramics
f.intervention: Surface treatments, primers/adhesive monomers and aging conditions used to improve adhesion to zirconia
f.main_result: Airborne-particle abrasion and tribochemical silica coating are reference pretreatments, adhesive monomers are necessary for chemical bonding, and contamination and aging reduce adhesion; results across 134 publications were hard to compare.
f.limitations: Results were difficult to compare because parameters varied between research protocols, and laboratory studies need clinical confirmation.

f.population: ZiReal Post (Biomet 3i) zirconia abutments, as-received and porcelain-coated
f.intervention: Characterization by XRD, XRF, EDS, optical, scanning and transmission electron microscopy
f.comparison: As-received versus fluoroapatite-porcelain-coated abutments
f.main_result: The abutments are high-purity tetragonal zirconia with 3-4 mol% yttria and homogeneous equiaxed grains averaging 0.30 µm, with only 1 µm machining ring marks.
f.funding_coi: Partial support from the Spanish Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación; Biomet 3i supplied the abutments

f.population: VITA YZ T, HT, ST and XT zirconia blanks and VITA VM 9 veneering material (laboratory testing)
f.funding_coi: Manufacturer (VITA Zahnfabrik) document

f.population: Porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns on an Ankylos implant abutment analog (mandibular first molar form)
f.intervention: Three metal substructure designs: minimum thickness (A), conventional 1.5 mm cutback (B), wrinkled design (C)
f.comparison: Conventional design (Group B)
f.main_result: Mean fracture resistance was 236.13 kg for the conventional design, 188.63 kg for the wrinkled design and 111.13 kg for the minimum-thickness design (P < 0.05).
f.limitations: The authors state the theory that PFM can provide better support requires further corroboration.

f.population: Zirconia bars (17 x 2 x 1 mm), ground-and-polished or milled with Cercon CAD/CAM
f.intervention: Airborne-particle abrasion with 50 or 120 µm aluminum oxide, with or without a veneer-baking heat treatment
f.comparison: Polished zirconia bars
outcomes: surface and subsurface damage on SEM
f.main_result: Flexure strength ranged from 546 MPa (ground bars abraded with 120 µm) to 1166 MPa (polished), correlating strongly with surface roughness (R2 = 0.912); heat treatment had no significant influence.

f.population: Sixty alumina-core all-ceramic crowns on brass dies
f.intervention: Procera AllCeram crowns with 0.4 mm (Group 1) or 0.9 mm (Group 2) AllCeram veneer porcelain
f.comparison: In-Ceram crowns with 0.9 mm Vitadur Alpha veneer (control)
f.main_result: Mean load at fracture was 2197.6 N, 2401.4 N and 2581.0 N for the three groups, with no significant difference between them.
f.limitations: Values are useful for comparative purposes only and cannot be extrapolated to the clinical situation.

f.population: 182 zirconia frameworks with 305 abutment teeth prepared by general dentists in Germany
f.intervention: 3D analysis of STL framework data for total occlusal convergence, abutment height and finish line design
f.comparison: Literature-based criteria for adequate zirconia preparations
f.main_result: Only 13 of 305 teeth (4.3%) met the adequacy criteria; mean total occlusal convergence was 17.9 degrees, higher in molars (23.2) than premolars (14.2), and 92.5% of finish lines were not ideal.
f.funding_coi: BEGO Medical GmbH supplied the data sets

f.population: 53 monolithic all-ceramic maxillary first molar crowns on a metal abutment analog
f.intervention: Axial static loading to fracture of monolithic zirconia, lithium disilicate and feldspar ceramic crowns, adhesively luted or conventionally cemented
f.comparison: Lithium disilicate and feldspar ceramic crowns; adhesive versus glass-ionomer cementation
f.main_result: Zirconia crowns fractured at the highest loads (5,620 N luted, 4,340 N cemented) versus about 2,700 N for lithium disilicate and 1,340 N for feldspar ceramic.
f.funding_coi: DeguDent provided material and financial support; no conflicts of interest reported
f.limitations: Limitations of the in vitro setting do not allow conclusions for clinical practice.

f.population: Disk specimens (10 mm diameter, 1.3 mm thick) of 3 mol% yttria-stabilized zirconia with and without 0.3 mol% alumina dopant
f.intervention: High-pressure spark plasma sintering (400 MPa) of alumina-doped 3Y-TZP powder (TZ-3Y-E)
f.comparison: Undoped 3 mol% yttria zirconia powder (TZ-3Y)
f.main_result: Alumina dopant lowered transparency despite similar 80 nm grains and porosity below 0.05%, because alumina along grain boundaries caused strong birefringent scattering.
f.funding_coi: Grants-in-Aid from the Japanese Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology and JSPS

f.population: Y-TZP and alumina ceramic plates bonded to polymer (polycarbonate) substrates, simulating crowns on dentin; no patients
f.intervention: Sandblasting of the ceramic undersurface (50 um Al2O3, 5 s) before bonding, then dynamic and cyclic Hertzian loading to radial crack initiation
f.comparison: As-polished (unblasted) specimens
outcomes: strength at radial crack initiation (dynamic and cyclic loading)
f.main_result: Sandblasting lowered strength by under 10% in single-cycle loading but by 20-30% in 10 Hz cyclic loading; extrapolation still suggests sandblasted Y-TZP crowns can cope with masticatory forces up to 400 N.
f.funding_coi: National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research (PO1 DE10976)
f.limitations: The 10 Hz cyclic frequency is high relative to mastication (about 1 Hz), so the fatigue effect is probably overestimated.

f.population: One transparent cubic 8 mol% yttria-stabilized zirconia (c-YSZ) disk (no patients)
f.intervention: High-pressure spark plasma sintering (400 MPa) followed by annealing in air for 100 h
f.comparison: As-sintered versus annealed disk
f.main_result: The as-sintered zirconia strongly absorbed light because of oxygen vacancies; annealing in an oxidizing atmosphere improved transparency despite increased porosity, and fine residual pores scattered light.
f.sample_size: one sintered disk, 10 mm diameter, about 1 mm thick after polishing
f.funding_coi: World Premier International Research Center Initiative (MEXT, Japan) and a Japanese Grant-in-Aid for Scientific Research

f.population: Theoretical 3 mol% yttria-stabilized tetragonal zirconia (3Y-TZP) plates 0.3-2.0 mm thick (no specimens or patients)
f.intervention: Rayleigh scattering model of in-line transmission versus grain size and thickness
f.comparison: Threshold in-line transmission of a suite of dental porcelains (about 2.5% at 1 mm, 555 nm) and one published experimental data set
outcomes: critical grain size for porcelain-like translucency
f.main_result: To match dental porcelain translucency, the mean 3Y-TZP grain size must be about 82 nm at 1.3 mm thickness, 77 nm at 1.5 mm and 70 nm at 2 mm.
f.funding_coi: NIDCR grant R01 DE017925 and NSF grant CMMI-0758530; author declares no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Theoretical predictions were higher than the single available experimental data set across the visible spectrum.

f.population: Dental zirconia ceramics (Y-TZP, 4Y/5Y-PSZ, graded and nanostructured variants); no patients
f.intervention: Narrative review of generations of dental zirconia and routes to greater translucency
f.comparison: Lithia-based glass-ceramics
f.main_result: More translucent zirconia generations (more cubic phase) lose strength and toughness, so the most durable ceramics are the least translucent; grain size below about 100 nm is predicted to be needed for translucent Y-TZP.
f.funding_coi: US NIH/NIDCR and NSF grants; no conflicts declared
f.limitations: Nanostructured zirconia is still at an early stage, and standardized laboratory tests give only a cautionary glimpse of clinical performance.

f.population: Modern zirconia materials grouped into four generations; no study population
f.intervention: Classification of zirconia generations by composition, translucency and strength, with guidance on luting and finishing
f.main_result: More cubic crystals (higher yttria content) raise translucency but lower flexural strength and fracture toughness, so each of the four zirconia generations has its own indications.
f.limitations: Clinical long-term data on the newest zirconia generations are scarce and only in-vitro data exist.

f.population: 30 patients (aged 27-75) needing a three- or four-unit posterior FPD replacing one or two missing teeth
f.intervention: Three- and four-unit posterior FPDs with CAD/CAM yttria-stabilized zirconia frameworks, veneered and cemented with glass-ionomer cement
f.comparison: No comparator restoration; periodontal parameters of abutment teeth compared with contralateral control teeth
outcomes: Gingival, Plaque and sulcus bleeding indices and pocket depth
f.main_result: After a mean 34.2 months all 27 examined FPDs were intact (100% framework survival); one had a major veneer chip, giving a cumulative success rate of 96.3%.
f.sample_size: 30 patients enrolled; 27 patients with 27 FPDs (19 three-unit, 8 four-unit) examined
f.limitations: Only medium-term (3-year) follow-up; 3 of 30 patients were lost to recall.

f.sample_size: 5102 articles retrieved by a Web of Science search for 'dental zirconia'
f.funding_coi: CNPq (Brazil), US NIH/NIDCR and UFMG research funding acknowledged

f.population: in vitro studies of fixed prosthetic restorations (intra-coronal, extra-coronal, FPDs, implant overdentures)
f.intervention: translucent zirconia as the primary material for fixed prosthetic restorations
f.comparison: traditional zirconia or other materials commonly used in fixed prosthodontics
f.main_result: Translucent zirconia has complex esthetic properties with potential for high translucency and color adaptability, and is a versatile material in restorative and implant dentistry (70 studies included, mostly in vitro).
f.funding_coi: Internal grant of Iuliu Hatieganu University; no conflict of interest declared

f.main_result: Higher yttria content increases zirconia translucency but reduces strength; zirconia is classified into 3Y-, 4Y-, 5Y-TZP and combined multilayer types.
f.funding_coi: No funding; one author is an academic editor of PeerJ

f.population: Ultra-high translucent zirconia (Shofu Disk ZR Lucent Ultra)
f.intervention: Ultra-high translucent zirconia made with Cyclic CIP and Plus Y Technology
f.comparison: 5Y and 3Y zirconia, lithium disilicate
f.main_result: UHTZ has translucency comparable to lithium disilicate while its flexural strength is comparable to 5Y zirconia.
f.funding_coi: No funding stated; Shofu Inc. supplied specimens and technical help

f.population: Translucent zirconia, 3Y-TZP and lithium disilicate specimens
f.intervention: Two translucent zirconias (Katana UTML, Lava Esthetic)
f.comparison: Conventional 3Y-TZP (Lava Plus) and lithium disilicate (IPS e.max Press)
f.main_result: As translucency increased with increased cubic content, edge toughness decreased (Katana UTML 304 N/mm vs Lava Plus 717 N/mm).
f.sample_size: n=20 per material for translucency and edge chipping, n=3 for XRD

f.population: 60 monolithic zirconia molar crowns on prefabricated implant abutments
f.intervention: Speed sintering (about 2 h) of 3Y-TZP and 4Y-TZP crowns
f.comparison: Long-term sintering (about 7 h)
f.main_result: Shortening sintering time increased marginal gaps only for 4Y-TZP crowns; all groups stayed under 120 µm.
f.funding_coi: Hacettepe University research funds; no competing interests

f.population: 108 zirconia FDPs (single-unit, three-unit, cantilever) on a mandibular model
f.intervention: High-speed sintering (1,580°C, about 20 min) of multi-layer 4Y-TZP
f.comparison: Conventional sintering (1,450°C, about 10 h)
f.main_result: High-speed sintering reduced accuracy of three-unit FDPs but had no clinically relevant effect on fit.
f.funding_coi: Amann Girrbach supplied materials; no conflicts of interest

f.intervention: 90-minute sintering of KATANA Zirconia
90-minute sintering of KATANA Zirconia HT/LT
54-minute high-speed sintering of KATANA Zirconia UTML/STML

f.main_result: Higher yttria content gives higher translucency and lower strength; adequately selected zirconia suits implant superstructures and fixtures.
f.funding_coi: No external funding

f.population: Rectangular bar specimens of high-translucent and low-translucent Y-TZP zirconia
f.intervention: High-translucent Y-TZP (Prettau Anterior), also tested after autoclave aging
f.comparison: Low-translucent Y-TZP (Diazir) and aged high-translucent Y-TZP
f.main_result: High-translucent zirconia had markedly lower flexural strength (427 vs 805 MPa) and fracture toughness (4.9 vs 8.9 MPa.m1/2) than low-translucent zirconia; aging did not significantly change flexural strength.
f.funding_coi: Funded by authors' university funds; no conflict of interest declared

f.population: Bar-shaped specimens cut from each of four layers of pre-sintered multilayer zirconia blocks
f.intervention: Three Katana multi-layered zirconias (HTML, STML, UTML) tested at 0.4, 0.8 and 1.2 mm thickness
f.comparison: Comparison among the three Katana grades (HTML vs STML vs UTML)
f.main_result: Flexural strength and fracture toughness were significantly higher for Katana HTML (652.85-887.64 MPa; 4.25-5.01) than STML (280-436 MPa) and UTML (258-331 MPa), with no differences between layers.
f.sample_size: 15 specimens per group per layer and thickness
f.funding_coi: Supported by Kuraray Noritake; authors declare no conflict of interest
f.limitations: Conclusions are limited to the in vitro design

f.population: One 31-year-old female patient with an endodontically treated upper first molar
f.intervention: Chairside fabrication of a monolithic crown from multilayer super-translucent zirconia (CEREC MTL Zirconia) with speed-sintering
f.main_result: A monolithic multilayer zirconia crown could be fabricated chairside in about 75-90 minutes with a good color match.
f.limitations: Clinical data for this type of restoration are still sparse.

f.intervention: Air abrasion of cubic-containing high-translucent zirconias, with laboratory processing and an anterior monolithic case
f.comparison: Original high-strength tetragonal zirconia without a cubic phase
f.main_result: Cubic-containing zirconia responds differently to air abrasion than conventional tetragonal zirconia, so clinical decisions should not be based on tetragonal data.

f.population: Sol-gel synthesized zirconia powders with progressively increasing yttrium content (5YZ to 100YZ)
f.intervention: Progressive yttrium additions with heat treatment at 1300 and 1500 C, analysed by XRD, Raman and Rietveld refinement
f.main_result: Tetragonal, mixed tetragonal-cubic and fully cubic phases formed depending on yttrium content; cubic compositions resisted tetragonal-to-monoclinic transformation at 1500 C.
f.funding_coi: DST-SERB India financial assistance

f.population: Zirconia specimens (32 specimens from 17 zirconia blanks) supplied by 9 dental laboratories for posterior and anterior indications
f.intervention: Laboratory-fabricated zirconia specimens ordered for posterior (high strength) and anterior (high translucency) indications, tested for flexural strength, hardness, composition and transmittance
f.comparison: Posterior (HS) versus anterior (HT) intended zirconia, and 3 mol% versus 5 mol% yttria grouping
f.main_result: Strength scattered widely (posterior 490 MPa, anterior 581 MPa) because of mixed yttria use; grouped by yttria it was 584 MPa for 3 mol% and 373 MPa for 5 mol%.
f.funding_coi: None of the authors reported any disclosures.
f.limitations: Strength was highly dependent on laboratory processing and finishing; all fractures originated from machining flaws.

f.population: In-vitro studies on translucent zirconia with yttria content higher than 3 mol%
f.intervention: Changing yttria content and other material-related variables in zirconia
f.comparison: 3 mol% yttria stabilized zirconia
f.main_result: Fifty-three in-vitro studies showed that changing yttria content significantly affected translucency, and zirconia of the same generation varies in translucency.
f.funding_coi: No funding to report; no competing interests

f.intervention: Airborne particle abrasion of zirconia fixed dental prostheses before adhesive cementation
f.main_result: Air-abrasion improves resin adhesion to zirconia but can raise monoclinic phase and lower strength, so it should be brief (about 20 seconds), below 2.8 bar, with 30-50 um silica-coated or silica particles.
f.limitations: Whether air-abrasion contributes to long-term zirconia degradation is not clinically proven.

f.intervention: Surface treatment methods for bonding resin cement to zirconia-based ceramics
f.main_result: Silica coating with aluminum oxide particles is the surface treatment of choice for bonding Y-TZP with resin cements, and functional monomers add chemical bonding.
f.limitations: Further clinical studies are necessary to establish the ideal technique and materials.

f.population: Patients with bonded zirconia restorations (resin-bonded FPDs, inlay-retained FPDs, veneers) in 8 included clinical studies
f.intervention: Bonded zirconia restorations: posterior inlay-retained FPDs and anterior cantilevered resin-bonded FPDs
f.main_result: Anterior resin-bonded FPDs showed 100% survival at 3 to 10 years; posterior inlay-retained FPDs ranged from 12.1% at 10 years to 95.8% at 5 years; debonds occurred in all studies but prostheses could usually be rebonded.
f.follow_up: 20 months to about 10 years across studies (12 months minimum for inclusion)
f.limitations: Heterogeneity in study design hampered any meta-analysis, and the role of bonding efficacy in survival is unknown.

f.population: Zirconia disks (7 mm diameter, 3 mm height) of two commercial systems, Cercon and Biodenta, veneered with their matching ceramics
f.intervention: Veneering of each zirconia core with its manufacturer-recommended layering ceramic, then thermocycling and shear testing
f.comparison: Cercon zirconia with Cercon ceram versus Biodenta zirconia with 2 in 1 ceramic
f.main_result: Mean SBS was 27.19 MPa (Cercon) and 28.22 MPa (Biodenta) with no significant difference; Biodenta failed mostly adhesively, Cercon with mixed failures.
materials_brands: Biodenta zirconia with 2 in 1 ceramic (Biodenta Swiss AG)

f.population: 4Y-TZP zirconia blocks (9.0x7.0x5.0 mm, n=72 per group assignment) contaminated with human saliva
f.intervention: Precoating the zirconia bonding surface with ethyl cellulose before saliva contamination, then removal with ethanol in an ultrasonic bath
f.comparison: Uncontaminated control; saliva then ultrasonic ethanol cleaning; saliva then zirconia cleaner; zirconia primer then saliva then water spray
f.main_result: Shear bond strength was significantly higher in the ethyl cellulose group than in the other cleaning methods, and no saliva contaminants were found after removal of the coating.
f.sample_size: 72 zirconia blocks in 5 groups, each divided into 3 aging subgroups (n=24)
f.follow_up: Artificial aging equivalent to up to 2.2 years in an oral environment
f.funding_coi: Supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) grant funded by the Korea government (MSIT)

f.population: 100 cylindrical 3Y-TZP zirconia disks (Ceramill Zi)
f.intervention: Etching with hydrofluoric acid at 40%, 9.5% and 5% concentration for 1, 5 or 15 minutes
f.comparison: Control specimens polished with SiC abrasive paper (baseline surfaces)
f.main_result: 40% HF significantly increased Ra and Rz at all times, 9.5% HF only after 15 minutes, and 5% HF produced no significant change.
f.sample_size: 100 disks: 9 etching subgroups of 10 plus a control of 10

f.intervention: Zirconia and other all-ceramic systems versus porcelain-fused-to-metal as framework materials for crowns and fixed partial dentures
f.comparison: Conventional metal-ceramic restorations
f.main_result: Zirconia shows favourable mechanical properties and suits single crowns and short-span FPDs, but clinical results are not yet comparable with metal-ceramic and long-term data are insufficient.
f.limitations: Zirconia long-term clinical performance, bonding to veneering ceramic, cementation, aging and wear need further investigation.

f.population: Fifty identical epoxy resin replicas of a prepared molar, each restored with an all-ceramic or PFM crown
f.intervention: Monolithic CAD/CAM lithium disilicate crowns; zirconia core veneered by hand-layering, heat-pressing, or CAD/CAM lithium disilicate veneer (CAD-on)
f.comparison: Porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns as control
f.main_result: All LDG and CAD-on crowns survived 500,000 cycles, whereas all PFM, ZVP and ZVL crowns failed.

f.population: 48 cylindrical Y-TZP zirconia specimens (6 mm diameter, 4 mm height) veneered with porcelain cylinders
f.intervention: Surface treatments before veneering (heat treatment, airborne-particle abrasion, or both), with or without cyclic loading
f.comparison: Control group with no treatment after grinding
f.main_result: Surface treatment had no significant effect on shear bond strength; air-particle abrasion without heat treatment gave significantly lower strength after cyclic loading (10.7 vs 34.1 MPa).
f.sample_size: 48 specimens, 12 per group (6 with and 6 without cyclic loading)

f.population: Cubes (10 mm edge) of ceria-stabilized zirconia/alumina nanocomposite (Ce-TZP/A, NANOZR) layered with veneering ceramics, with Y-TZP as control
f.intervention: Veneering ceramics (Cerabien ZR, IPS e.max, Initial ZR, Triceram, Vintage ZR, VITA VM 9) applied with or without liner on polished or airborne-particle abraded Ce-TZP/A
f.comparison: Polished Y-TZP veneered with Cerabien ZR and Vintage ZR
f.main_result: Mean shear bond strengths ranged from 14.2 MPa (IPS e.max with liner) to 27.5 MPa (VITA VM 9); airborne-particle abrasion was unnecessary and liners impaired bond strength to Ce-TZP/A.

f.intervention: Low-pressure alumina air abrasion plus MDP-containing zirconia primer (Z-PRIME PLUS) with dual-cure resin cement
f.comparison: Self-adhesive resin cements (BisCem, RelyX Unicem, SmartCem2) on sandblasted zirconia
f.main_result: Z-PRIME PLUS/DuoLink gave the highest shear bond strengths to zirconia (28.7 MPa initial light-cured) and kept them after aging, unlike the self-adhesive cements.
f.sample_size: n = 8 per group in the Table 1 data
f.funding_coi: Three authors are founder or employees of Bisco Dental, maker of the featured products

f.population: 54 beams of yttria-partially-stabilized tetragonal zirconia with a feldspathic porcelain button
f.intervention: Three heating rates (25/50/75 C/min) and three cooling regimens (fast/moderate/slow) during porcelain firing
f.comparison: Fast and moderate versus slow heating and cooling regimens
outcomes: delamination (failure) force in modified 4-point flexural test
f.main_result: Cooling regimen and heating rate significantly affected failure load, with cooling having the greater effect; slow cooling and slow heating strengthened porcelain fused to zirconia.

f.population: Specimens of zirconia ceramic and cobalt-chromium alloy (plus aluminum oxide in part 1)
f.intervention: Sandblasting with 50-um aluminum oxide, with or without ultrasonic cleaning afterwards
f.comparison: Ultrasonic cleaning versus no ultrasonic cleaning after sandblasting
outcomes: shear bond strength of resin luting material
f.main_result: Specimens not ultrasonically cleaned after sandblasting had significantly higher shear bond strength than cleaned ones, for zirconia (13.11 vs 9.67 MPa, P<0.001) and Co-Cr (13.60 vs 9.80 MPa, P=0.006).
f.funding_coi: JSPS KAKENHI grant; no competing interests

f.population: Y-TZP plates (10 x 10 x 1 mm) veneered with porcelain
f.intervention: Three porcelain application methods (wash-dentin firing, thicker moist layer, no liquid) on Y-TZP, analysed by XRD2 micro-diffraction
f.comparison: Porcelain applied with versus without liquid medium; thin versus thick layer
outcomes: tetragonal/monoclinic phase content at the interface

f.population: In vivo and in vitro studies of zirconia-based fixed dental prostheses
f.intervention: Literature review of zirconia-based fixed dental prostheses
f.comparison: Ceramo-metallic restorations
f.main_result: Porcelain-veneered zirconia restorations showed fracture rates of 6-15% over 3-5 years versus 4-10% over ten years for ceramo-metallic restorations.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared

f.population: Zirconia blocks (80 specimens, 8 groups) contaminated with human saliva
f.intervention: Cleaning of saliva-contaminated zirconia with water, 35% phosphoric acid, Ivoclean or particle abrasion, before or after MDP primer
f.comparison: Control group bonded without saliva contamination
f.main_result: Water rinsing after MDP application (20.6 MPa) and particle abrasion or Ivoclean before MDP (23.1 and 22.7 MPa) preserved bond strength relative to control (25.8 MPa); phosphoric acid did not.
f.funding_coi: Materials donated by manufacturers; authors deny conflicts of interest

f.population: Fully sintered IPS e.max ZirCAD zirconia micro-specimens bonded in pairs
f.intervention: Tribochemical silica sandblasting (CoJet) and/or silane/MDP primers (Clearfil Ceramic Primer, Monobond Plus) before bonding with two composite cements
f.comparison: No sandblasting and/or no primer; BisGMA-based versus MDP-based cement; three ageing protocols
outcomes: micro-tensile bond strength (Weibull scale and shape)
f.main_result: Best bond durability came from CoJet sandblasting plus a silane/MDP primer (highest Weibull scale 54.04 MPa and shape 3.47 with Clearfil Ceramic Primer and Panavia F2.0 at 10 d); sandblasting was indispensable for Panavia F2.0.
f.follow_up: 10 days, 10,000 thermocycles or 6 months water storage

f.population: Air-abraded Lava zirconia disks (20 mm x 1.5 mm) contaminated with fresh human saliva
f.intervention: Cleaning of saliva-contaminated zirconia with Ivoclean, SDS, hydrogen peroxide or sodium hypochlorite solutions
f.comparison: Additional air-abrasion, water-spray rinsing and a no-contamination control
outcomes: failure mode and SEM of fractured surfaces
f.main_result: Ivoclean and 1% NaOCl restored shear bond strength (9.1 and 10.9 MPa) to the level of the uncontaminated control (10.4 MPa) and air-abrasion (9.5 MPa); SDS, H2O2 and water spray alone gave 4.4-6.7 MPa.
f.sample_size: 28 zirconia disks, 12 resin cylinders per group
f.limitations: Long-term clinical studies are still required to confirm efficacy of the cleaning solutions.

f.population: Alumina-blasted yttria partially stabilized zirconia discs
f.intervention: MDP-salt primer (experimental MDP-containing cleaner) applied to zirconia before resin cement
f.comparison: Untreated control, 1% MDP, and MDP+silane (Clearfil Ceramic Primer Plus)
f.main_result: MDP-salt gave the highest characteristic tensile bond strength before (51.6 MPa) and after 5,000 thermocycles (35.5 MPa) versus MDP and MDP+silane.
f.funding_coi: Grant 17K11701 from the Japanese Ministry of Education; Kuraray Noritake provided experimental materials; no conflicts declared

f.population: Published zirconia bond-strength studies (1,371 tests from 144 papers)
f.intervention: Pooled analysis of luting techniques (mechanical and chemical pre-treatments, cements, test methods) for bonding to zirconia
outcomes: bond strength by pre-treatment, cement, test method and aging
f.main_result: Combined mechanical and chemical pre-treatment was crucial for durable zirconia bonding; cement choice did not matter after aging if composite cement was used, and macro-shear tests gave lower, less discriminative values.
f.funding_coi: Flemish scholarship, FWO-Flanders and KU Leuven projects; no conflicts declared

f.population: Polished yttria-stabilized zirconia (LAVA) plates
f.intervention: Gas-phase plasma fluorination of the zirconia surface
f.comparison: Three commercial zirconia primers (Clearfil Ceramic Primer, Monobond Plus, Z-Prime) and an untreated control
f.main_result: Fluorinated zirconia gave the lowest contact angle (7.8 deg) and highest shear bond strength (37.3 MPa), ahead of Z-Prime (24.3 MPa), control (9.2), Clearfil (10.0) and Monobond Plus (7.5).
f.funding_coi: RTI Fellows Program, RTI International

f.population: 30 participants needing a single maxillary implant-supported crown (14 to 24)
f.intervention: Monolithic high-translucency multilayer zirconia crowns on implants
f.comparison: Traditional veneered zirconia crowns (3Y zirconia core, feldspathic veneer)
f.main_result: No significant difference in patient VAS satisfaction, but WES differed significantly between the two crown types (P<0.05).
f.sample_size: 30 participants, each receiving both crown types
f.funding_coi: Research Discipline fund from Ninth People's Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University

f.population: 80 disk-shaped specimens (10 mm diameter; 0.8 and 1.5 mm thick) of 3Y, 4Y and 5Y zirconia and lithium disilicate
f.intervention: Zirconia of 3, 4 and 5 mol% yttria (Katana HT, STML, UTML) measured for translucency parameter and masking ability
f.comparison: Lithium disilicate (Rosetta SM)
f.main_result: TP increased with yttria content (3 to 4 to 5 mol%), all zirconia less translucent than lithium disilicate; zirconia masked normal dentin but not severely discolored dentin at 0.8 or 1.5 mm.
f.funding_coi: Grant from Korea Health Industry Development Institute (KHIDI); no conflict of interest declared

f.population: 60 ceramic crowns (30 zirconia, 30 alumina) cemented on resin models
f.intervention: Zirconia-core crowns tested for fracture load after water storage, heat treatment and cyclic preloading
f.comparison: Alumina-core crowns
f.main_result: Zirconia crowns were about 3 times stronger and tougher than alumina crowns (about 1200 vs 400 MPa); all fractures occurred in the alumina group (p<0.001).

f.population: A1-shaded ceramic specimens of 5 indirect restorative systems cemented on three tooth-colored resin substrates (ND3, ND8, ND9)
f.intervention: Five indirect restorative systems (lithium disilicate, translucent zirconia, PICN, bilayer zirconia, CAD-on) resin-cemented on different substrates
f.main_result: The bilayer YLD-T (zirconia plus veneer) showed delta E values below the acceptability threshold on all substrate comparisons and the lowest translucency, i.e. the best masking ability.
f.sample_size: n = 5 specimens per system, cemented on 3 substrates (n = 15)
f.funding_coi: Supported by CNPq and CAPES (Brazil), Junta de Andalucia and Spanish Ministry of Economy

f.population: 15 anterior zirconia crowns (n = 5 per group) placed on 11 substrates (ND1-ND9, zirconia, metal)
f.intervention: Monolithic, bi-layer and tri-layer 3Y-TZP zirconia crowns
f.comparison: Layered (bi-layer and tri-layer) crowns versus monolithic
f.main_result: Monolithic crowns had better masking ability than bi-layer and tri-layer crowns, but color differences were below the acceptability threshold only for ND2, ND3 and ND7 substrates in cervical and middle areas.
f.funding_coi: Grant of the Romanian Ministry of Education and Research, CCCDI-UEFISCDI

f.population: 1 mm-thick specimens of five monolithic zirconia systems, two lithium disilicate glass-ceramics and bovine enamel/dentin
f.intervention: Highly translucent 5Y-PSZ zirconias and 3Y-TZP zirconias tested for optical and mechanical properties
f.comparison: e.max CAD HT and LT lithium disilicate, bovine enamel and dentin as references
f.main_result: Higher yttria content (5 mol%) significantly improved zirconia translucency, but zirconia remained less translucent than lithium disilicate (p < 0.05).
f.sample_size: n = 10 per zirconia group for optical tests; n = 10 flexural, n = 5 toughness

f.population: Disc-shaped ceramic specimens (8 mm diameter, 1.8 mm thick), 11 ceramic groups, over resin composite and metal substrates
f.intervention: Bilayer and monolithic ceramic systems, with and without an opaque resin-based luting agent (OLA), over discolored substrates
f.comparison: Bilayer versus monolithic ceramics; with versus without OLA; control substrate A1
f.main_result: Bilayer structures showed significantly lower delta E00 than monolithic ones; OLA reduced delta E00 for monolithic ceramics and CAD-on with OLA masked metal substrates at a non-perceptible level.

f.population: Specimens (1.2 x 1.2 x 3.0 mm) of amalgam, dental ceramic, gold alloy, dental resin, zirconia and titanium alloy; enamel and dentin values from a prior study
f.intervention: Compression testing of dental restorative materials at 0.1 mm/min
f.comparison: Enamel and dentin mechanical properties
f.main_result: Gold alloy had hardness lower than enamel and higher maximum stress, strain and elastic modulus than dentin; zirconia (2206 MPa max stress, 3895 MPa modulus) differed markedly from enamel and dentin.
f.funding_coi: Korea Institute of Industrial Technology (KITECH); no conflict of interest declared
f.limitations: Aspect ratio of the specimens may change the stress-strain relationship

f.population: Co-precipitated 4 mol.% GdO1.5-4 mol.% SmO1.5 doped zirconia nanopowders (4Gd4SmSZ)
f.intervention: Calcination at 873 to 1273 K and annealing at 1573 K for up to 100 h
f.main_result: Powders stayed single-phase tetragonal from 873 to 1273 K (crystallite size 11.98 to 18.90 nm) and showed excellent phase stability after 100 h at 1573 K.

f.population: In vitro studies of Y-TZP zirconia specimens of any geometry
f.intervention: Airborne-particle abrasion protocols of any particle size and pressure
f.comparison: Control group without surface conditioning (nonabraded)
f.main_result: Airborne-particle abrasion improved flexural strength of Y-TZP regardless of abrasion parameters and aging; monoclinic content tended to rise after abrasion initially but was lower than control after 12 h or more of aging.

f.population: Disc-shaped specimens of lithium disilicate glass-ceramic and Mg-PSZ zirconia, 13 mm diameter
f.intervention: Glazing, HF etching, sandblasting, veneering-like heat treatment and autoclave hydrothermal aging of the ceramics
f.comparison: Untreated (crystallized or as-delivered) specimens and the other ceramic
f.main_result: Mg-PSZ was significantly stronger than e.max Cad (p<0.001); glazing reduced strength of 0.4 mm e.max Cad, and autoclaving reduced strength of as-delivered ZirMagnum (p<0.05).
f.funding_coi: Specimens donated by Cad.esthetics AB; one author is part-time employed by Cad.esthetics AB

f.population: Disc-shaped 3Y-TZP zirconia specimens (140)
f.intervention: Bonding to zirconia after different delays (15 min, 1 h, 4 h, 24 h, 72 h) following airborne-particle abrasion with 50-µm Al2O3
f.comparison: Shortest delay (15 min / 1 h) versus longer delays
outcomes: tensile bond strength after 3 days and 150 days with thermocycling
f.main_result: Surface free energy fell significantly within 24 h after abrasion; 3-day TBS ranged from 38.3 MPa (1 h) to 28.4 MPa (24 h) and 150-day TBS from 38.3 MPa (15 min) to 24.8 MPa (24 h).
f.follow_up: 150 days water storage with 37,500 thermal cycles
f.funding_coi: No specific grant; materials provided free by Kuraray Noritake and DeguDent

f.population: Y-TZP zirconia ceramic samples machined by face and peripheral grinding
f.intervention: Simulated inner-surface grinding with varied feed velocities and cutting depths
f.comparison: Lapped control samples
f.main_result: Grinding halved mean flexural strength (about 600-690 MPa versus 1419.5 MPa in the lapped control) and lowered reliability.
f.sample_size: 24 samples per test group (Weibull n = 24), 9 grinding settings plus control
f.funding_coi: Supported by TMWFK grant and in part by Girrbach-Dental GmbH

f.population: Disc-shaped specimens of three Y-TZP ceramic grades containing 3 mol% yttria
f.intervention: Dry and wet grinding with 150 and 50 µm diamond burs, sandblasting with 110 µm alumina, and combinations, plus extraction in acetic acid and ammonia solutions
f.comparison: As-sintered untreated control discs
f.main_result: Dental grinding lowered mean strength and Weibull modulus, whereas sandblasting significantly increased strength of all materials but with somewhat lower reliability.
f.sample_size: Groups of ten disc-shaped specimens per surface treatment per material
materials_brands: TZ-3YB, TZ-3YSB and TZ-3YS-E Y-TZP ceramics

f.population: A plaster die replicated from a plastic maxillary right first molar prepared for all-ceramic crowns
f.intervention: Three virtual zirconia framework designs created in CAD software: uniform 0.5 mm, full cutback (1 mm reduction), and vestibular-only reduction
f.main_result: Three different framework designs for molar zirconia-ceramic crowns could be created, with the cutback design controlling veneer thickness without compromising strength.
f.funding_coi: Supported by UEFISCDI project PN-II-RU-TE-2014-4-0476
f.limitations: The authors note the multitude of design parameters limits the conclusions

f.population: Published clinical reports (2010-2013) on zirconia all-ceramic restorations, plus the authors' own clinical and laboratory work
f.intervention: Zirconia all-ceramic restorations with porcelain veneering, and measures to prevent porcelain chipping
f.comparison: Porcelain fused to metal restorations
outcomes: influence of frame thickness and firing schedule on chipping
f.main_result: Reports describe porcelain fracture in zirconia all-ceramic restorations at 0.9-29.1%, with chipping the most common clinical failure and higher than for porcelain fused to metal.
f.sample_size: 23 clinical reports tabulated, 11 to 1,132 cases each
f.limitations: The authors call for a prospective study taking the chipping factors into consideration

f.population: 84 veneered Y-TZP mandibular molar crowns cemented on aged composite dies
f.intervention: Anatomically designed (cusp-support) zirconia cores veneered by hand-layering (VM9) or pressing (PM9)
f.comparison: Conventional 0.5 mm uniform-thickness core, and press versus hand-layer veneering
outcomes: fatigue reliability at 50,000 cycles and 200 N
f.main_result: Hand-layer veneering on a conventional core had reliability 0.99 versus 0.50 for press veneering, and anatomic core design raised reliability to 0.98 (PM9) and 1.00 (VM9) with smaller chips.
f.funding_coi: Partly supported by NIDCR grant and by Vita Zahnfabrik, which also provided the crowns
f.limitations: Long-term in vivo studies are needed to confirm the results

f.population: 24 zirconia-framed porcelain-faced crowns on a stainless steel abutment die
f.intervention: Three zirconia frame designs: 0.5 mm uniform cover, 1 mm reduced outer crown, and a frame with an occlusal surface table about half the crown
f.comparison: Conventional 0.5 mm-thick frame (Design 1)
f.main_result: Fracture strength was 645.9 MPa with Design 1, 759.5 MPa with Design 2 and 989.7 MPa with Design 3, significantly higher for Design 3 than for Designs 1 and 2.
f.funding_coi: Authors declare no conflict of interest

f.population: Forty-eight zirconia crowns on metal dies replicating a prepared maxillary central incisor
f.intervention: Collarless zirconia coping (0.5 mm, no facial collar) and thicker coping (0.7 mm)
f.comparison: Standard coping (0.5 mm thickness, 0.2 mm facial collar height)
f.main_result: The thicker coping group (3179.3 N) had significantly greater fracture load than the standard (2126.9 N) and modified thicker (2112.7 N) groups, while the collarless group (2329.1 N) did not differ from the others.
f.sample_size: 48 crowns in 4 groups (n=10 per group stated for the dies), plus 10 crowns for cyclic loading
materials_brands: IPS e.max Ceram veneering ceramic (Ivoclar Vivadent)
f.funding_coi: Faculty research grant of Yonsei University College of Dentistry

f.population: 20 zirconia-framework all-ceramic premolar crowns cemented on a cobalt-chromium die
f.intervention: Cutback framework design (0.8 mm veneer thickness) of full contour crown anatomy
f.comparison: Conventional 0.5 mm even-thickness framework
f.main_result: Mean failure load was 1,170.1 N for the even-thickness design and 1,450.4 N for the cutback design (P<.05); cutback crowns more often failed through the zirconia framework (8 of 10).

f.population: 40 all-ceramic zirconia molar crowns (10 per coping design) on a prepared mandibular first molar model
f.intervention: Four zirconia coping designs (flat, shoulder collar, cuspal-following concave, occlusal-supporting) veneered with porcelain and loaded to fracture vertically and at 45 degrees
f.comparison: Conventional uniform-thickness zirconia coping with flat occlusal surface
f.main_result: The conventional uniform-thickness coping gave the lowest fracture load and the cuspal-configuration coping (c) the highest in both vertical and lateral loading.
f.sample_size: 40 crowns, 5 per design per loading direction
f.funding_coi: Nobel Biocare supplied the zirconia copings; no funding or conflict statement
f.limitations: Conclusions apply within the limitation of this model study

f.population: Layers of KATANA Zirconia YML and ZirCAD Prime discs tested for translucency and bending strength at Tokyo Medical and Dental University
f.intervention: KATANA Zirconia YML, a four-layer (one enamel, three body) multilayer zirconia disc
f.comparison: ZirCAD Prime (Ivoclar Vivadent)
f.main_result: The enamel layer of YML had significantly greater bending strength than that of ZirCAD Prime, while Prime's enamel layer was significantly more translucent.
f.funding_coi: Document issued by the manufacturer (Kuraray Noritake Dental Inc.); comparative data courtesy of Tokyo Medical and Dental University

f.population: Bar specimens (2 x 2 x 16 mm) milled from three multilayer Y-TZP CAD/CAM discs, n = 20 per material
f.intervention: Three-point flexural strength test with SEM and PXRD analysis of multilayer Y-TZP bars
f.comparison: The three multilayer zirconias (ZirCAD Prime, Cercon ht ML, Katana YML) compared with each other
f.main_result: ZirCAD Prime had the highest flexural strength (879.42 ± 107.36 MPa) versus Cercon ht ML 701.63 ± 84.21 and Katana YML 644.73 ± 82.07 MPa, which did not differ.
f.funding_coi: No conflicts of interest declared; EU/Croatian project funding acknowledged

f.population: 300 monochrome and multilayer 5Y-PSZ zirconia specimens (10 x 20 x 2 mm)
f.intervention: Sintering at 1,450, 1,500 or 1,550 °C with hold times of 10, 15, 30 or 135 minutes
f.comparison: Regular sintering protocol (1,500 °C, 135 minutes)
f.main_result: Increasing sintering temperature with shorter hold time gave flexural strength acceptable relative to regular sintering (highest 315.81 ± 18.91 MPa monochrome, 335.21 ± 36.18 MPa multilayer); monochrome and multilayer did not differ.
f.funding_coi: Funded by the Faculty of Dentistry, Khon Kaen University; no conflict of interest

f.main_result: The review describes multiphase multilayered zirconia as the first dental material combining zirconia of different crystal phases in one body to reproduce enamel and dentin.

f.population: 36 extracted human molars embedded in resin to simulate 3-unit fixed partial dentures
f.intervention: 3-unit zirconia FPDs milled from a multilayer ZirCAD Prime blank at above, central or bottom position, with varied sintering time
f.comparison: Groups differing in blank position and sintering time (2:26, 4:25, 9:50 h) compared with each other
outcomes: fracture force after thermocycling and mechanical loading
f.main_result: All FPDs survived aging; fracture forces ranged from 1002 ±446 N (above, 9:50 h) to 1760 ±607 N (central, 9:50 h) with no overall significant difference (P=.059).
f.follow_up: Simulated 5 years of oral service (1.2 x 10^6 cycles)
materials_brands: Speed Cem Plus self-adhesive resin cement
f.funding_coi: Ivoclar Vivadent AG supported the study

f.population: Katana multilayer zirconia specimens (UTML, STML, ML) cut from enamel, transition and dentin layers
f.intervention: Characterisation of composition (XRF), phase fractions (XRD), microstructure (FE-SEM), low temperature degradation and translucency of each grade and layer
f.comparison: The three grades UTML, STML and ML compared with each other and layer with layer
f.main_result: Layers within a grade differed little, but the grades were distinct (UTML 5Y-PSZ, 4.05 µm grains; STML 4Y-PSZ, 2.81 µm; ML 3Y-PSZ, 0.63 µm); translucency was similar between UTML and STML and higher than ML.
materials_brands: KATANA Zirconia UTML, STML and ML (Kuraray Noritake)
f.funding_coi: Funded by US NIH/NIDCR grants; no conflicts of interest declared

f.population: Zirconia blocks of two brands (Lava, KaVo), 10 specimens (10 x 10 x 1 mm) per sintering condition
f.intervention: Microwave sintering (20 min) and conventional sintering with 20 min, 2, 10 or 40 h dwell
f.comparison: Conventional sintering at different dwell times versus microwave sintering
f.main_result: Longer sintering gave larger grains (347-1,512 nm Lava; 373-1,481 nm KaVo) and lower light transmittance (Lava 28.39-34.48%, KaVo 28.09-30.50%), with no density difference.

f.intervention: CAD/CAM veneering of oxide-ceramic bridge frameworks with feldspar-ceramic blocks, bonded with composite
Step-by-step design, milling, sintering and adhesive bonding of a CAD/CAM zirconia framework with a milled feldspar-ceramic veneer

f.population: In-house bridge specimens (three- and four-unit)
f.intervention: Zirconia framework with CAD/CAM feldspar-ceramic veneer bonded by adhesive composite (VITA Rapid Layer Technology)
f.comparison: Classically veneered In-Ceram YZ bridges (VM 9)
f.main_result: Rapid Layer bridges withstood over 2400 N static load versus 1420 N for classically veneered bridges, with 100 percent survival in thermal shock up to 150 C
f.sample_size: 26 three-unit and 5 four-unit bridges (thermal shock test)
f.funding_coi: In-house studies by the manufacturer

f.population: One patient with a loosened bridge in region 47
f.intervention: Replacement with a zirconia-framework bridge veneered by CAD/CAM feldspar ceramic (VITA Rapid Layer Technology)
f.main_result: Bridges made with the technique in the author's practice showed no chipping or framework fracture to date

f.population: Polished 3Y-TZP zirconia disks (9 mm diameter, 2 mm thick)
f.intervention: Hydrofluoric acid etching at 5, 20 and 40% concentration for varying times, with analysis of reaction products
f.comparison: Non-etched control surface
f.main_result: HF 40% gave the fastest, most uniform roughening; fluoride precipitates formed on the surface, so cleaning is essential, and roughness evolution slowed after about one hour.
f.sample_size: One cleaned sample per condition in the preliminary study; 3 (AFM) and 10 (WLI) samples per experimental point
f.funding_coi: European Commission 7th Framework Programme (Marie Curie ITN), Spanish MINECO and Government of Catalonia
f.limitations: Authors note polishing is not part of commercial implant processing and effects of precipitates on bonding and patient health are unknown.

f.population: 100 polymer-infiltrated ceramic crowns (Vita Enamic) cemented on one-piece zirconia implants (ceramic.implant CI)
f.intervention: Cementation with 13 cements (temporary, glass-ionomer, self-adhesive, adhesive resin) with or without manufacturer ceramic primer
f.comparison: Cement types against each other, with versus without ceramic primer
f.main_result: Retention was highest for Panavia 21 (605 N) and Panavia F 2.0 (318 N); other resin cements 222-270 N, above glass-ionomer (196 N) and temporary cements; primer helped only Panavia SA.
f.sample_size: 100 crowns on 100 implants, n=5 per group; shear n=6, diametral tensile n=10
materials_brands: Panavia F 2.0, Panavia 21, Panavia SA, Panavia V5
